## Adaptive Learning and Correlative Assessment of Differential Usage Patterns for Students with-or-without Learning Disabilities via Learning Analytics

MASOODA M. MODAK, Research Scholar, SP.I.T., Mumbai, Assistant professor, SIES Graduate School of Technology, India

PRACHI GHARPURE, Director, SVKM's NMIMS University, Indore Campus, India SASIKUMAR M, Director, CDAC,Santacruz, India

Learning Disabilities (LD) can be categorized into logical, analytical, grammatical, vocabulary, sequential, and inference disabilities. Analysis of such disabilities assists students to identify and strengthen their weak areas. A wide variety of analysis models is proposed by researchers to perform such tasks, but most of these models are highly complex and cannot be scaled for multimodal parameter sets. To overcome these issues, this text proposes a model for correlative assessment of differential usage patterns in students with-or-without learning disabilities via multimodal analysis. The proposed model initially collects real-time inference sets for students with Learning Disabilities (LD) and without LDs. These sets consist of question-specific recorded responses for 'Addition,' 'Carry Propagation,' 'Basic to Advanced Grammar,' 'Direct, Inference and Vocabulary Comprehension,' 'Finding odd-man-out,' 'Sequencing,' and 'Pseudo and Sight Spelling' for different question sets. Answers to these questions and their metadata were processed via a correlative engine that assisted in evaluation of correctness, time needed per question per category, number of skips, number of revisits, and unanswered ratio for different students. This evaluation was combined with temporal analysis to identify per-category progress of students. Based on this progress, students were either upgraded to next level or given lower-level questions, which assisted them to incrementally improve their grades. The model proved that the performance of LD students is 55% less than the non-LD students and an average of 18 LD students have achieved an average of 33% of improvement after having multiple attempts of the adaptive lessons. The model uses a correlation function, which enables to identify answering patterns of LD and non-LD students with 98.4% accuracy, thus can be used for clinical scenarios.

Additional Key Words and Phrases: Learning disability, correlation analysis, multiple attempt analysis, multimodal analysis

## 1 INTRODUCTION

One of the most prevalent cognitive barriers to communicating verbally or in writing is a disorder of specific learning (SLD) . It also manifests itself in problems with reading, writing, and listening. In India, the occurrence of learning disabilities varies from 2.16% to 30.77% [1]. Specific learning disorders might take the form of dyslexia, dysgraphia, or dyscalculia. Dyslexia is a disorder that makes schoolwork challenging. Since dyslexia is a neurological disorder, its effects will vary, depending on the individual who suffers from it. It has lifelong consequences on a child's ability to express themselves verbally and in writing. Due to confusion between letters and words, they read slowly and incorrectly. The experts are of the opinion that, even when the same type of disability is involved, there is no one solution that can meet all individual needs; as a result, using external tools tailored to particular special needs is preferable to create embedded facilities; and that special attention should be paid to accessibility of the content uploaded to the LMS [2]. Group learning activities must be made accessible and modified for students with and without difficulties who are participating in e-learning [3]. There are specific issues with the current elearning online models, gaming apps that still exist, such as personalizing content based on the needs of the students and identifying students who have learning disabilities [4, 5]. Students taking online lessons while wearing an EEG headband will provide real-time e-learning data. The CNN model proposed in Reference [5] will divide the students into grades and aid in the creation of an automated framework for the monitoring of a student learning curve, offering suggestions for improving the course materials for online learning. These models provide a very high level of accuracy for real-time applications, but they impose additional implementation expenditures. Moreover, these models cannot be used in normal learning settings, because they are invasive; as a result, they are inappropriate for usage in general e-learning environment.

Children who struggle with dysgraphia sometimes produce slanted, distorted, or incorrectly capitalized writing. Children who struggled with spelling tended to write or copy slowly. Children with dysgraphia often struggle with number sense and seeing patterns in mathematical formulas and situations. Dyscalculia makes it hard for children to accomplish even basic arithmetic, since they cannot grasp how operators and numbers work. Thus, each child with a different learning difficulty has a different type of struggle. This implies that it is essential to capture the learning characteristics of each of these types of learners. But the machine learning models employed in previous works are black box models, making them unable to determine the features on which the presence or absence of a learning disability is determined.

For the purpose of LD detection, several research studies employ unofficial techniques. The methods employed in these research studies to identify learning disabilities (LD) in children rely on the provided checklists, which contain the symptoms and signs of the specific LD. Many times, a certain symptom listed on the checklist is applicable to a child, but he is unaware of it. The students often struggle to admit that they experience one or more of the symptoms listed in the checklist. Furthermore, the list of signs and symptoms is static and could leave out a lot of different indications of the various learning difficulties. Given the above-mentioned difficulties, we require a system that can recognize LD and understand the learner's learning process. The system must be capable of analyzing LD symptoms, determining how they relate to one another, and diagnosing the presence of a learning disability.

Thus, the motivation of this research is to provide learning according to the dynamic requirements of the student. A unique detection model is employed to detect the presence or absence of learning disability based on the dynamic learning profile of the student. Once the difficulty is detected, the student will learn according to his capabilities and preferences using the learning analytics engine that uses the proposed statistical model for deciding the adaptive content. The adaptive content presented to user students with disabilities makes use of e-learning that has LMS software packages. The proposed model provides learning settings that are helpful to the success of children with learning disabilities. These settings recognize and accommodate the unique needs of each student. The proposed system has an analytical engine that analyzes the continuous performance of the dynamic learning pattern of the student. For analytical analysis, classifiers such as Decision Tree, SVM, Logistic Regression, and KNN are employed. The analytics engine enables the LD-detected student to study according to his learning preferences, thereby inspiring them to overcome their obstacles to learning. The article also presents the correlative assessment of the usage patterns of students with and without learning disabilities in terms of parameters such as the number of correctly answered questions, amount of time taken, the number of skips, the number of revisits, percentage of improvement or no improvements in comparison of LD versus non-LD. Based on this observation, Section 3 discusses methodology of research. Section 4 discusses the design of a model for multimodal assessment of differential usage patterns among students with and without learning disabilities. Section 5 discusses adaptive learning through dynamic profiling using statistical modeling, Section 6 presents model validation with accuracy, precision, and recall of LD detection. Section 7 presents the analysis of the reattempts for the comparison of revisits, skips, as well as the typical time delay required by LD students to improve their performance. When the proposed model's performance was compared to that of several state-of-the-art models, it was shown to perform better; this facilitates its use in clinical settings. This article concludes with some insightful observations regarding the proposed model and offers a number of suggestions for enhancing it.

## 2 LITERATURE REVIEW

Various works are been proposed and implemented in this area. The studies in References [6, 7] offer a comprehensive overview of how WebVR might be applied to dyslexia instruction. The study also discusses how spatial data may be used as an input. For richer and more dynamic display, relationships among data can be rendered into a 3D environment, which refers to a variety of connections, interactions, or relationships between distinct elements that can be represented or visualized in a three-dimensional (3D) virtual space. Datasets used in machine learning frequently contain a number of characteristics or properties that can have an impact on the result or target variable. The performance and predicted accuracy of the model may be impacted by the complex interactions between these features. However, standard two-dimensional plots might be difficult to visualize high-dimensional data (data with numerous features). We may be able to obtain a better understanding of how various aspects interact with one another by simulating these interactions in a 3D environment. The work suffers from absence of efforts or elements that would establish connections or interrelationships among the relationships that have been identified or captured. This interrelationship could help to diagnose the presence of a learning disability.

Eye-tracking motions have been demonstrated to be a reliable indicator of reading difficulties in children. Dyslexia can be identified with the use of eye-gaze behavior analysis. The study in Reference [8] aims to show the capability of gaze-based predictions, where the predictive analytics is used to improve user success and enhance user experience. This study intends to promote the development of adaptive learning according to the identified learning difficulty. According to the relevant results in Reference [9], a significant improvement has been illustrated by applying direct human eye-gaze indication, which quantitatively points out that using eye gaze can be more efficient than other human-action based inference approaches.

The design of the detection system used in Reference [10] employs Logistic Regression (LR) and Deep Forest models. The inclusive customized learning environment has a prototype app for use by people with special needs. Predicting the likelihood of a child to be a having learning disability is the major goal of this approach. Using the disability model, a profile is generated for a student who has a disability. The disability model enables the best virtual learning object to be suggested based on the learner's preferences and actions.

For students with learning difficulties, intelligent assistive technologies (IAT) are created to offer individualized help and accommodations to improve their academic progress. These tools make use of different artificial intelligence techniques, machine learning techniques, and adaptive algorithms to meet the unique demands of students who face varied learning difficulties. Assistive technology to help those with visual and learning disabilities is also used in research work proposed by researchers in Reference [11]. Concatenation synthesis is used in this suggested assistive device's Text To Speech (TTS) conversion and Optical Character Recognition (OCR) processes. The main conclusion was that instructors should use technology to teach reading to boost LD children's reading abilities. Participants in the experimental group consistently outperformed their contemporaries. According to research, the most efficient technology for teaching one reading skill utilized gaming or drill-and-practice formats.

Speech fluency is one of many language development processes that might be impacted by learning disabilities. The majority of currently used disfluency detection methods heavily rely on expensive and infrequently available human-annotated data. The authors in Reference [12] investigated how to use active learning into the fine-tuning process to close the performance gap. With a limited annotated dataset, active learning may reduce the drawback of self-supervised learning by focusing on the most significant instances to label by the fusion of self-supervised learning with active learning.

The work in Reference [13] proposes models that utilize Augmented Reality (AR) , social and collaborative technologies, and the modification of learning environments. But these models are not able to assist a large variety of students because of their infrastructure and cost requirements. These models also require students to learn about technologies before using them, which further restricts their scalability. Similar models are proposed in References [14, 15], wherein, interventionbased approaches, such as individualized reading assistance (IRA) , and the utilization of costeffective technologies are employed in order to make performance enhancement models more accessible and scalable. The drawback of this work is that the same intervention techniques are used in a variety of contexts. This technique does not consider the particular situations and requirements of various children or groups.

Extensions to these models are discussed in References [16, 17], wherein methods such as special attention for LD students, inculcation of self-determination among students, and interventionbased models (IM) for continuous assistance are proposed. Out of these models, the intervention model is highly efficient, because it showcases high student throughput performance when applied in real-time scenarios. But these models are only aimed at improving the reading fluency related to dyslexia.

Both the students' learning difficulties and criteria for measuring their performance, such as memory, attention, and language, are provided by the authors in References [18, 19]. The strengths and weaknesses of the learner, as well as potential roadblocks to e-learning, may be identified in this way. Researchers will keep tweaking the prototype and adapting it to new impairments in an effort to boost students' performance in a digital classroom [20, 21]. This web software was made to serve as a quick diagnostic tool for learning disabilities. Each of their control and experimental groups has an equal number of youngsters. The children in both sets of tests will have 10 activities to complete that will measure their literacy, numeracy, and mental acuity. Results showed that children with learning disabilities gave wrong answers at a higher rate than the control group. The number of correct responses and the amount of time spent on each assignment will be used to make these selections [22, 23]. Children who may have learning disabilities may be identified using ICT if an ontology-based ICT tool is used. It is very beneficial for both parents and educators, since this paradigm involves testing for learning impairments in youngsters. Furthermore, it provides appropriate learning opportunities [24, 25] for different use cases. The drawback of the above approaches using web software is that they lack interaction with the child being examined, which is a crucial aspect of diagnosing learning difficulties. The web-based program in these studies is not able to imitate how trained professionals can monitor nonverbal cues, clarify questions, and create a more comfortable and suitable setting for assessment.

Researchers have created a broad range of analytical models to carry out SLD identification tasks. According to the findings by the authors in Reference [26], who compared two groups-students with learning disabilities and those with no learning disabilities-students with LD reported worse social and academic personalities. Additionally, they reported lesser levels of motivation and effort put into their academic work, as well as perceiving their mood as more negative. Emotional behavior comparisons to the non-LD peer group did not reveal any noticeable changes at the same time. The work in Reference [27] makes a thorough argument from a variety of theoretical angles that five factors, including learning commitment (the learner's commitment to participating in and excelling at the learning process), course objectives (how closely the learner's expectations fit the objectives of the curriculum), learning actions (the precise behaviors, attitudes, and tactics that students use to understand and retain knowledge), learning soul (the learner's determination, passion, and sense of connection to the subject), and learning external environment, will affect the degree of learning disabilities and learning adaptability among college students. The research concluded that for better learning, adaptation of content to learner characteristics is important and needed. Research in Reference [28] suggests a model that is built using cellular automata and association rules in conjunction with fuzzy logic and machine learning. The benefit of the suggested approach is that it aids in identifying these students' needs, preventing commonly used procedures from influencing their approach to learning. Therefore, it is important to recognize that every child learns at a different speed. With Hybrid Neuro-Fuzzy (HNF) methods, however, the vast majority of these models are very sophisticated and cannot be scaled for multimodal parameter combinations.

In References [29, 30], student feedback and student misbehavior analyses are used to estimate the levels of LD and non-LD that are present in certain students, further demonstrating the effectiveness of such models. Finding out if a student has a learning difficulty is the aim of this research. The level of accuracy of these models is somewhat constrained by the use of data collection and analysis techniques, each of which has certain limitations. According to the studies described in References [31-33], continuous supervision, 1-Dimensional Convolutional Neural Network (1D-CNN) models based on electroculography, and app-based scanning of students may all be used to increase classification accuracy in real-time settings. The development of these improvements is directed by the intention to contribute to improving the system's overall performance. Although these models are quite precise, scaling them up would require the installation of more components, which is not feasible. Because of this, they are unable to be used in real-world applications. A gamification model was suggested in studies that were published in References [34, 35] with the aim of enhancing scalability as well as classification performance in real-time circumstances. In this model, k-Nearest Neighbours (kNN), Support Vector Machines (SVM) , and Random Forest (RF) are all combined. This action is being conducted in an effort to overcome the limitation that was previously specified in the paragraph. The various extensions that may be made to these models are discussed in Reference [36], in which the Test of Mathematical Abilities (TOMA) or the Test of Symbolic and Nonsymbolic Numerical Magnitude Processing, both of which were carried out, assisted in improving the context-specific performance of these models under clinical conditions. This refers to characteristics that improve the performance of machine learning models when they are used in practical clinical contexts.

The majority of these models, however, rely on machine learning approaches, which enhances their applicability in scenarios where the context significantly influences the outcome. Additionally, the characteristics that indicate learning disabilities are concealed inside a black box. Many students may be using e-learning platforms without the required learning abilities. For those who struggle with learning, there are several online resources. However, they fail to take into account and adapt to the unique learning properties. Each student with a learning impairment may have a unique learning disability. For instance, one dyslexic learner could fail to read written text, while another may struggle with letter and number reversals. Many times, the student is unaware that he is facing a particular LD symptom. Sometimes students are reluctant to acknowledge that they experience one or more LD symptoms. To address these concerns, this research then provides a paradigm for the detection of learning disabilities using dynamic learning characteristics using a detection model. Further, this model will also provide statistical modeling of the learning behavior correlative evaluation of distinctive use patterns in students with and without learning problems based on multimodal analysis. Identifying the different traits that are specific to a certain type of learning disorder is important to recognize a learning disability. Determining the features of learning disabilities according to age or grade is the first step towards identification of learning disability. The student will be able to learn in accordance with his or her learning requirements and preferences once the disability has been identified, which might result in improved performance for the learner with LD.

To validate its efficacy, the suggested model's performance was also assessed in the context of several real-time scenarios and compared with existing approaches. The research approach to accomplishing the objectives is covered in Section 4, which presents the design of the proposed correlative assessment of differential usage patterns for students with or without learning disabilities via multimodal analysis. Section 5 validates and hypertunes the model. Section 6 compares the proposed model's performance to that of current approaches in terms of precision, recall, accuracy, and latency metrics across a variety of real-world use cases. The last section of this research offers some concluding thoughts on the suggested paradigm and how it may be improved for therapeutic applications.

## 3 METHODOLOGY OF RESEARCH

The goal of the research is to create a method for identifying a learning disabled person's learning profile. A behavioral analysis engine is created to examine how people with learning disabilities learn. The engine will make an effort to determine the learner's preferences to try to record the learner's behavior when they are learning. All of this student-related data will be included into a learner model that will be created. Throughout the learner's learning process, the analytics engine will dynamically update the learner model. When given the characteristics and features from the learner's learning pattern, the model would be trained using machine learning to identify the learning disability.

- (1) Creation of a learner model based on the dynamic properties of learning. The students are categorized as LD/NonLD using the machine learning model. Example: Consider a student A, who begins exploiting the adaptive learning platform. On the basis of her quick comprehension and high engagement with the topic, the model first labels her as Non-LD.

- (2) The Behavioral Analysis Engine will update this model to capture the learner's evolving learning features. The student goes through this process as they are learning. Example: The engine observes the student A's learning rate has slowed and her engagement level has fallen as she moves through her curriculum. It makes the appropriate adjustments to her learner model.
- (3) This engine will show the learner the adaptive content, assess how well they did, and update the model if necessary. The modified learner profile will be reflected in the learner model. Example: A's slower learning rate is recognized by the platform, which then provides her with additional practice activities on difficult subjects. The material adjusts to fit her new pace once she has shown improvement.
- (4) The performance evaluator will assess the performance and perform correlative assessment in accordance with the different performance metrics discussed in the text based on the answers to the questions. Example: The system keeps track of A's quiz results, the amount of time she spends on assignments, and how much she interacts with the supplemental resources to determine how well she did. It shows a strong positive correlation between her use of extra resources and her improvement in quiz results.
- (5) The model is validated for robustness and improvements over time. The model is refined continuously for new data and knowledge.

## 4 DESIGN OF THE PROPOSED CORRELATIVE ASSESSMENT OF DIFFERENTIAL USAGE PATTERNS FOR STUDENTS WITH-OR-WITHOUT LEARNING DISABILITIES VIA MULTIMODAL ANALYSIS

Based on the review of existing LD identification techniques, it can be observed that a wide variety of analysis models is proposed by researchers to perform this task, but most of these models use static parameters and are not able to reflect the dynamic learning behavior of a student. These techniques are highly complex and cannot be scaled for multimodal parameter sets. This section discusses the design of a model for multimodal assessment of differential usage patterns among students with and without learning disabilities to address these issues. Figure 1 depicts the model's flow, where it can be seen that the proposed model initially collects real-time inference sets for students with and without LD. These sets include question-specific recorded responses for 'Addition,' 'Carry Propagation,' 'Basic to Advanced Grammar,' 'Direct, Inference and Vocabulary Comprehension,' 'Finding odd-man-out,' 'Sequencing,' and 'Pseudo and Sight Spelling' for a variety of question sets. Answers to these questions and their metadata were processed by a correlative engine that aided in evaluating correctness, time required per question per category, number of skips, number of revisits, and unanswered ratio for various students. This evaluation was combined with a temporal analysis to determine the students' progress by category. Based on this progress, students were either promoted to the next level or given lower-level questions to help them improve their grades incrementally for real-time scenarios. To perform these tasks, the model extracts a series of analytical features from collected data samples. These features include:

- -Correctness (C), which is estimated via Equation (1) and assists in finding total questions that were correctly answered for individual categories.



where N q represents number of questions in the given category, while C a is a flag, which is set to 1, if student has answered the question correctly, else it is 0 for incorrect responses.

- -Time needed per question (T), which is estimated via Equation (2) and is a measure of speedof-answering different question types.

These features are collected for LD and Non-LD students and fed as input to the detection model. The detection model is an ensemble of classifiers (KNN, Random forest, SVM, Linear Regression). The data is collected from LD-certified students and non-LD students from grades 6, 7, and 8.

Once a student has completed an iteration of examination, then the system recommends improvement areas. Based on this above complete process, students are categorized into LD and non-LD types, and their learning performance is continuously improved for real-time scenarios.

Once the child has attempted the questionnaire for various subjects, the detection model will detect in which subjects the child is facing a learning difficulty. The statistical modeling will be used to decide the level of difficulty the child is facing in each subject using the I scorevalue and thereby the amount of improvement needed. Once the child has attempted the lessons multiple times, the learning analytics engine will update the learner model to store the updated learner profile of that child. The learning analytics engine enables to predict the status of the child on his first attempt. If the child is detected as suffering from a learning disability, then the LA engine also recommends the number of re-attempts needed to have a substantial amount of improvement in that child for a particular lesson.

These features are collected for LD and non-LD students and stored to perform a correlation process. Similar features are extracted for new students, and then a statistical measure such as correlation is estimated with LD and non-LD features via Equation (15).



where F and F ( New ) represent features of already stored samples and new student samples. This correlation is estimated for LD and non-LD features under individual question categories. Based on this correlation level, students are having a high chance of falling into category-specific LD and non-LD students via Equation (16).



If the features of new student is highly correlated with features associated with learning disabilities for a specific question type, then the analytical engine runs the detection algorithm to detect the presence/absence of learning difficulty in each subject so accordingly, the difficulty level for that question type is reduced, and students are re-analyzed via the same process.

To validate this performance, the model was evaluated in terms of accuracy of mapping, precision levels, recall levels, and delay needed for mapping under real-time scenarios. This evaluation was done for different use cases in the next section of this text.

## 6 MODEL VALIDATION

Within the framework of our binary classification task, we evaluate the RandomForest (RF) classifier's performance in this section. We use a variety of indicators to conduct a thorough evaluation with the goal of determining how well the classifier can distinguish between the two classes.

To allow LD and non-LD students to participate in the various lessons, the system was made available online. The lessons were made available to the 6th-, 7th-, and 8th-grade LD or non-LD students. The LD students who attempted the classes were identified as having a learning impairment and were connected to special schools or remediation facilities. Of the 220 students that attempted the classes, 137 were non-LD and 83 were LD. This made sure that accurate responses from LD students were captured to create a strong training and testing dataset and, ultimately, a model for more accurately identifying LD in a given subject. The dataset's correctness and reliability were ensured by the students' real responses, including those who had learning problems and those who did not.

A manual dataset was created by collecting the responses of 220 students who participated actively in 13 subject areas. Then, their performance in these subjects was assessed using this dataset. The remediation center was contacted to approach the LD children, since they had received official certification of their condition. The dynamic learning profile was extracted from their responses, and the ensemble algorithm was used to classify them into LD and non-LD groups. To determine the final classification performance, the classified sets were compared with ground-truth information. A total of 2,500 samples were used for classification, and they were split up into a group of 70:30 samples. We employed an RF classifier to classify the children with or without learning disability. Based on this arrangement, 1,750 samples were utilized for training, while the remaining 750 samples were used for testing and validation. Then, using the results for accuracy (A), precision (P), recall (R) , and area under the curve (AUC) , all 2,500 samples were used for the parametric analysis. The total number of correct predictions a model makes may be counted using an evaluation metric called accuracy. In the context of binary classification, a form of machine learning problem where the objective is to categorize instances into one of two classes (positive or negative), words such as TP, FP, TN, and FN are frequently employed. The term true positives (TP) refers to situations where the model properly predicted the positive class. False Positives (FP) are situations where the model predicts the positive class while the true class is really negative. True Negatives (TN) are situations in which the model accurately predicted the negative class. False Negatives (FN) are situations where the model predicts the wrong class, usually a negative one, when the correct class is a positive one. So, despite the model's negative prediction, the actual class was positive. Accuracy, precision, and recall are some of the evaluation metrics for classification models that are frequently calculated using these concepts. By taking into account several features of a classification model's predictions, these metrics assist in evaluating its performance. In Equation (17), the accuracy calculation is displayed.

The accuracy of a model on a dataset is measured by the F-score, also known as the f1-score. It is employed to evaluate binary categorization schemes that label instances as 'positive' or 'negative.' The f1-score formula is shown in Equation (20).

Table 1 presents the performance of the random forest classifier. To boost the model's performance, we implemented a cross-validation technique called RandomizedSearchCV. RandomizedSearchCV is a popular techniques for hyperparameter tuning in machine learning. It is used to systematically search for the best combination of hyperparameters for a machine learning model. With respect to detection of learning disability and the parameters accuracy, recall, and precision, our classifier should have a better recall, because in case of detecting LD, we should have low false negative rate. Thus, we hypertune the parameter with cross-validations to improve the accuracy, precision, and recall score. The hypertuning was done for the parameters 'max\_features' and 'max\_depth.' This technique allowed us to efficiently explore a wide range of hyperparameter combinations, resulting in improved model performance metrics.

## 7 RESULTS ANALYSIS AND COMPARISON

With the hypertuned Random forest model, a total of 2,500 evaluations were performed, out of which 70% were used for training the model, while 30% each were used for testing and validation purposes. Based on this strategy, the model was evaluated in terms of accuracy of detection, precision, recall, and delay compared with RTL [8], LR [9], and HNF [26]. Table 3 presents a comparison of these parameters for all the above-mentioned models with the proposed model.

From Table 3 and Figure 2, it can be observed that the proposed model is able to improve the accuracy of detection by 14.5% when compared with RTL [8], 19.4% when compared with LR [9], and 9.5% when compared with HNF [26] under different use cases. The accuracy is improved due to the use of high-performance evaluation metrics, which assist in improving LD and non-LD identification performance in real-time scenarios. The proposed model is able to improve the precision of detection by 5.9% when compared with RTL [8], 8.3% when compared with LR [9], and 3.5% when compared with HNF [26] under different use cases. This precision is improved due to the use of correlative mappings, which assist in improving LD and non-LD identification performance in real-time scenarios. Similarly, the proposed model is able to improve recall of identification by 5.5% when compared with RTL [8], 6.4% when compared with LR [9], and 2.9% when compared with HNF [26] under different use cases. The recall is improved due to use of high-performance temporal correlative mapping, which assists in improving LD and non-LD identification performance in real-time scenarios. Similarly, the proposed model is able to improve speed of detection by 19.4%

Fig. 2. Performance of the proposed system compared with other model sets.



when compared with RTL [8], 12.5% when compared with LR [9], and 5.9% when compared with HNF [26] under different use cases. The speed is improved due to the use of low-complexity temporal analysis, which assists in improving LD and non-LD identification performance under realtime scenarios. Due to these optimizations, the proposed model is able to improve the correlative analysis performance for multiple use cases and can be deployed under real-time conditions. This model also assists students in improving their performance by incrementally recommending questions as per their LD and non-LD performance levels, thereby boosting their confidence under different types of question categories.

The proposed correlation method initially collects responses from LD and non-LD students and estimates different temporal metrics. These temporal metrics are estimated on a per-category basis and correlated with new student responses. Based on this correlation, students are either upgraded to the next learning levels or given lower-level questions. Thus, this process analyzes individual students, depending on the number of attempts. It is also not necessary that there is always an improvement; there can also be a decrease in performance. The model is tracking it, which is done to inculcate continuous learning capabilities in students for different question types. This is true for both new and old students. But, specifically for new students, the model is also able to analyze:

- -The ability to answer direct, indirect, vocabulary, and title questions;
- -Dependency among the topics and their correlation with LD and non-LD students;
- -Correctness during sequencing operations;
- -Correctness to spell pseudo and sight words;
- -Correctness to provide word meanings;
- -Correctness to pick the odd-man-out from similar entities;
- -Correctness for addition and carry propagation operations;
- -Tendency to skip difficult topics;
- -Too many revisits of a particular topic or set of topics;
- -Time needed for individual question types.

- (2) Efficiency Gains: The model's shorter computation time guarantees real-time flexibility, which makes it appropriate for use in realistic educational contexts. This effectiveness is essential for giving students timely support.
- (3) Continuous Learning: Our results highlight the significance of allowing for both gains and losses in student performance. Regardless of a student's initial level of ability, this inclusive approach creates a possibilty of continuous improvement for all students.
- (4) Targeted remedial measures are required for LD children given the performance gaps between LD and non-LD students that have been found. Multiple attempts and adaptive lessons can help LD children close the skills gap.
- (5) Building Confidence: Students' confidence in answering different question types is increased by incremental recommendations based on LD and non-LD performance levels, which in turn creates a positive learning environment.

- (1) Data Amount and Diversity: The amount and diversity of the data samples for our investigation may be constrained. To establish generalizability, future research should examine the model's performance on larger and more varied datasets.
- (2) Model Complexity: Although the suggested model is effective, it might not be able to handle really complicated circumstances. For such situations, further optimization and scaling considerations may be required.
- (3) Generalization: The model's performance has been assessed across a range of use cases, but it is important to confirm in larger contexts that the model can be applied to all educational environments.
- (4) Real-world Deployment: Despite the model's promise for real-time deployment, real-world educational environment problems and factors such as hardware limitations and data privacy should be taken into account.

- (5) Long-term Effects: The study mainly concentrates on immediate enhancements in learning performance. Future studies should examine how long-term benefits and sustainability of these improvements last.

Despite these drawbacks, our suggested model represents a significant advancement in the field of instructional technology and will help students with learning difficulties learn more effectively. These results can be used as a foundation for future research to improve and enhance the model's capabilities.

## 9 CONCLUSION AND FUTURE SCOPE

The proposed correlation method initially collects responses from students with LD and students without LD and estimates various temporal metrics. These temporal metrics are estimated per category and correlated with responses from new students. Based on this correlation, students are either promoted to higher learning levels or given questions of a lower difficulty. Consequently, this procedure analyzes each student according to their number of attempts. Also not required is an improvement; a decline in performance is also possible. The model is tracking it to instill in students the capacity for continuous learning for various question types. This is true for both new and returning students. In terms of accuracy levels, it was observed that the proposed model can improve the accuracy of correlative analysis by 14.5% when compared to RTL [8], 19.4% when compared to LR [9], and 9.0% when compared to HNF [26] for various use cases. This accuracy is enhanced as a result of the utilization of high-performance evaluation metrics, which contribute to the enhancement of LD and non-LD identification performance in real-time scenarios. In terms of consistency levels, it was observed that the proposed model improves the precision of correlative analysis by 5.9% when compared to RTL [8], 8.3% when compared to LR [9], and 3.5% when compared to HNF [26] across a variety of use cases. Correlative mappings, which aid in enhancing LD and non-LD identification performance in real-time scenarios, enhance this precision. When evaluated in terms of specificity levels, it was found that the proposed model improves recall of correlative analysis by 5.5% when compared to RTL [8], 6.4% when compared to LR [9], and 2.9% when compared to HNF [26] for various use cases. Utilizing high-performance temporal correlative mapping helps improve LD and non-LD identification performance in real-time scenarios, thereby enhancing recall. In terms of computational delay, it was found that the proposed model can improve the speed of correlative analysis by 19.4% when compared to RTL [8], 12.5% when compared to LR [9], and 5.9% when compared to HNF [26] for various use cases.

With respect to multiple attempts and correlative assessment, the performance of LD students is 55% less than the non-LD students. The skipping tendency of LD students is 22% higher than non-LD students. The number of revisits for non-LD is 220, which is far greater than mere 25 for LD students. LD students take more than double the time, around 130% more than that needed by non-LD students. This indicates that the LD students need remediation in this regard so they can attempt the questionnaires faster than before. The multiple attempts for a subject in which an LD student faces difficulty will help the student in improving his skills in that subject, thereby leading to improvement. Finally, the percentage of LD students who have achieved improvement from the provided adaptive lessons is more than that of non-LD. An average of 73% LD students has achieved an average of 33% of improvement after having multiple attempts of the adaptive lessons.

Utilizing low complexity temporal analysis aids in enhancing LD and non-LD identification performance in real-time scenarios, thereby enhancing the speed. Due to these enhancements, the proposed model can improve the performance of correlative analysis for multiple use cases and can be deployed in real-time. This model also helps students improve their performance by incrementally recommending questions based on their LD and non-LD performance levels, thereby boosting their confidence in various question types.

Important conclusions from our study that have a big impact on educational technology and how learning for kids with learning difficulties goes are as follows:

- (1) Better Learning Results: The suggested model's improved correlative analytical accuracy, precision, and specificity translate to better learning results. It gives teachers the ability to personalize learning routes for each student by adjusting educational content.
- (2) Efficiency Gains: The model's shorter computation time guarantees real-time flexibility, which makes it appropriate for use in realistic educational contexts. This effectiveness is essential for giving pupils timely support.
- (3) Continuous Learning: Our results highlight the significance of allowing for both gains and losses in student performance. Regardless of a student's starting ability level, this inclusive approach promotes a culture of ongoing learning for all students.
- (4) Remediation for Students with LD: The observed performance gaps between LD and non-LD children highlight the necessity of individualized remedial plans. Multiple tries and adaptive lessons can help LD kids close the skills gap.
- (5) Building Confidence: Students' confidence in answering different question types is increased by incremental recommendations based on LD and non-LD performance levels, which ultimately fosters a positive learning environment.

Our suggested paradigm has a lot of scope for implementation in real-world settings. It can be included into educational platforms and adaptive learning systems, giving teachers insightful information and allowing them to give students the support they need. Real-time adaptation also guarantees that pupils get timely interventions when they require them. The model has potential for further validation and improvement on larger datasets as well as for integration with cutting-edge techniques to improve the educational experience of students in various learning environments.

In the future, the performance of this model must be validated on larger data samples, and it can be enhanced through the integration of Q-Learning and Auto-encoders, which will contribute to the incremental improvement of classification performance under real-time conditions. In addition, this performance can be enhanced through the incorporation of hybrid bio-inspired models, which facilitate context-based evaluation for clinical use cases.

## ABSTRACT

Dyslexia and dysgraphia are two common learning disabilities that affect children's ability to read, write, and spell accurately. These disabilities can significantly impede a child's academic performance, leading to lack of self-confidence, anxiety, and frustration. Traditional approaches to address these disabilities often involve one-on-one sessions with a tutor or special education teacher, which can be time-consuming and expensive. Artificial intelligence (AI) language learning models have shown tremendous potential in assisting children with dyslexia and dysgraphia. These models can provide real-time feedback and personalized instruction to help children overcome learning difficulties. This chapter highlights the importance of addressing these challenges and proposes a solution that leverages AI language learning models to assist children with dyslexia and dysgraphia. By embracing AI language learning models, educators and parents can empower children with dyslexia and dysgraphia, providing them with the necessary tools and support to overcome their learning challenges.

## BACKGROUND

The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in language learning has become increasingly popular in recent years. This is particularly relevant for children with dyslexia and dysgraphia, who face unique challenges when it comes to language acquisition. By leveraging AI technologies, educators and researchers are exploring new ways to support these children and enhance their language skills. In this chapter, we review the current state of research on AI-based language learning for dyslexic and dysgraphia children, with a focus on the benefits and challenges of these technologies. The study conducted by (Gkeka, 2019) discusses the use of techniques supported by AI technologies in the diagnosis and treatment of language disorders, including dyslexia, aphasia, and developmental language disorder. The article emphasizes the importance of early diagnosis and intervention in improving language outcomes for individuals with language disorders. The authors highlight several techniques that can be used in the diagnosis and treatment of language disorders, including computer-based assessments, natural language processing, and AI technologies. The article also discusses the potential of AI-based chatbots and virtual assistants in supporting language learning and communication for individuals with language disorders. The authors conclude that AI techniques have the potential to enhance the accuracy of diagnosis and improve the effectiveness of treatment for individuals with language disorders, and that further research is needed to fully explore the potential benefits of these technologies in language learning and communication (Gkeka, 2019). The work by (Zingoni A, 2021) discusses a proof-of-concept study of a virtual reality (VR) platform that aims to support dyslexic university students. The study investigated the issues and needs of students with dyslexia and how the AI-VR platform can address those needs. The platform includes features such as a text-to-speech system, an AI-powered personalized learning assistant, and a VR environment for immersive learning experiences. The study involved a small group of dyslexic students who used the platform for a period of time and provided feedback on its effectiveness. Preliminary results indicate that the platform has the potential to improve the learning outcomes and confidence of dyslexic students. The authors suggest that further research is needed to refine and improve the platform in order to explore its potential for wider use. Overall, the study highlights the potential of AI and VR technologies to support dyslexic students in higher education settings (Zingoni A, 2021).

In the research article (S. Thelijjagoda, 2019), the authors propose a mobile solution called 'The Hope'' which is designed to help individuals with dyslexia overcome their writing, reading, and speaking weaknesses. The solution incorporates several interactive features, such as speech recognition and textto-speech technology, to assist dyslexic users in their daily activities. Users can dictate texts and have them converted to written words, and vice versa, with the app reading the written texts aloud. Additionally, the app provides personalized feedback on grammar and spelling errors, and includes exercises to improve reading speed and comprehension. The article highlights the potential of such mobile solutions in addressing the challenges faced by dyslexic individuals and the need for further research to evaluate their effectiveness. The Hope offers a promising tool for dyslexic individuals to overcome their communication difficulties and increase their confidence in everyday tasks. A study by (Minoofam, 2022), focuses on the development of an adaptive reinforcement learning framework called RALF to support the teaching of dyslexic students. The article notes that dyslexic students often struggle with language learning, and that traditional teaching methods may not be sufficient to meet their needs. The RALF framework is designed to adapt to the individual learning needs of each dyslexic student, using a reinforcement learning algorithm to adjust the difficulty level of tasks based on the student's performance. The article describes a pilot study in which RALF was used to teach dyslexic students English language skills. The results of the study suggest that RALF can be an effective tool for teaching dyslexic students, with improvements in both accuracy and response times observed over the course of the study. The article concludes that RALF has the potential to be a valuable tool for supporting language learning in dyslexic students, and that further research is needed to fully explore its potential benefits (Minoofam, 2022).

The article (Patra, 2020) explores some possibilities related to the ways AI can be used as a medium or tool to address the discussed challenges for creating a better accessible, inclusive learning environment for all, i.e., Optical character recognition, Speech recognition, Individualization of learning, Language learning, Virtual learning and Universal Design of Learning. The study (Patra, 2020), explores the potential of AI in improving the education of children with disabilities. The authors argue that AI can be used to create personalized learning experiences for children with disabilities, based on their individual strengths and needs. They discuss various AI-based tools and technologies that can be used for this purpose, such as intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning algorithms, and virtual assistants. The authors also discuss the potential benefits of AI for teachers, such as automating routine tasks, providing real-time feedback to students, and generating insights into student learning. Finally, the article highlights some of the challenges and limitations of using AI in education, such as the need for adequate training and support for teachers and the potential for biases in AI algorithms. Overall, the article suggests that AI has the potential to transform the education of children with disabilities and improve their learning outcomes (Patra, 2020). The study by (Lakshmanan, 2022), proposes a novel approach for dyslexic reading assistance using language processing algorithms. The authors explain that dyslexia is a learning disability that affects an individual's ability to read and process written language, as the existing reading assistance technologies have limitations in their effectiveness. To address this problem, the authors propose a new algorithmic approach that leverages natural language processing and machine learning techniques to identify and highlight difficult words or phrases for dyslexic readers. The system provides real-time assistance by providing the reader with definitions, synonyms, and pronunciation guides for difficult words. The authors also provide an evaluation of the system's effectiveness in improving reading comprehension for dyslexic readers, and the results show a significant improvement in their reading comprehension scores. The authors conclude that this approach has the potential to improve the reading abilities of dyslexic readers and provide a more accessible and effective reading assistance tool (Lakshmanan, 2022). The study by (Ahmed, n.d.), discusses the use of AI in developing reading and writing skills for kindergarten children with learning disabilities. While the focus of the article is on reading and writing skills development, it does touch on the broader topic of language learning as these skills are essential components of language learning. The authors explain how AI-based tools can be used to provide personalized and engaging learning experiences that improve reading and writing skills, which are essential components of language learning. The article includes a discussion of the potential benefits of AI-based tools in language learning, such as providing individualized support, improving engagement, and increasing motivation. Overall, the article suggests that AI-based tools have the potential to improve language learning outcomes for kindergarten children with learning disabilities (Ahmed, n.d.).

In the research article (Ikermane, 2023), proposes a method for detecting dysgraphia in children using digital handwriting analysis and Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs). The authors explain that dysgraphia is a learning disability that affects handwriting, and early detection is crucial for successful intervention. The article describes a study in which digital handwriting characteristics were analyzed from a group of children, some of whom had been diagnosed with dysgraphia. The authors used ANNs to analyze the data and identify patterns and characteristics that were indicative of dysgraphia. The results of the study showed that ANNs were able to accurately classify children with and without dysgraphia based on their

digital handwriting characteristics. The authors suggest that this method has the potential to provide dysgraphia diagnosis by improving the speed and accuracy. The article concludes that digital handwriting analysis using ANNs can be an effective tool for dysgraphia detection, which can lead to early intervention and improved outcomes for children with dysgraphia (Ikermane, 2023). The article (Wang, 2021), discusses how AI based augmentative alternative communication (AAC) can assist dyslexic students in their learning process. Dyslexia is a learning disorder that affects reading, writing, and spelling skills, and can make it difficult for students to communicate effectively. The authors propose a smart AAC system that uses machine learning algorithms to recognize the speech and convert it into text, which can be helpful for dyslexic students. The system also includes a speech synthesizer that can read the text out loud to the students. The article provides a detailed description of the proposed system and how it can be used to improve the communication and learning abilities of dyslexic students. The authors conclude that the smart AAC system can be a valuable tool in assisting dyslexic students in their education and daily life (Wang, 2021). The study by (Lerga, 2021), focuses on assistive technologies that can support language learning in students with dyslexia. The article notes that dyslexic students may struggle with reading, writing, and other language skills, and that assistive technologies can help to mitigate these difficulties. The article reviews a range of assistive technologies, including text-to-speech software, screen readers, speech recognition tools, as well as technologies that use AI and machine learning to personalize learning for dyslexic students. The article also discusses the importance of considering individual needs and preferences when selecting and implementing assistive technologies for dyslexic students. Overall, the article highlights the potential benefits of assistive technologies for supporting language learning in dyslexic students, and suggests that continued research and development in this area is needed to fully realize their potential (Lerga, 2021).

The study by (Maskati, 2021), explores the use of technology to support students with dyslexia and learning disabilities. Data collection involved questionnaires and unstructured interviews with specialists to identify system requirements and user needs. The results revealed that a majority of teachers recognized the effectiveness of using technology in education and identified reading, writing, and mathematics as significant challenges for students with dyslexia. Interviews with specialists highlighted specific difficulties faced by students with dyslexia and autism. To assess the effectiveness of the proposed application, an experiment was conducted with 10 children aged 6-7 years, randomly assigned to two groups. The experiment compared the proposed application (version 1) with traditional learning (version 2) for Arabic language lessons. The findings indicated that students found the app's explanation and demonstration clear, overcame initial difficulties, and enjoyed the experience. They understood the app's icons and displayed positive emotions, focus, and interest. The results underscore the potential of technology-based interventions for students with dyslexia and learning disabilities. The research contributes valuable insights into the preferences and needs of teachers, parents, and specialists, highlighting the importance of innovative approaches to address students' challenges. Further research and development are needed to explore technical details and evaluate the application's effectiveness fully. Overall, this study supports the use of technology in education as a promising tool to enhance learning experiences and support skill development for students with dyslexia and learning disabilities. The study by (Bhatti, 2020), examines the effectiveness of augmented reality (AR) applications in special education, focusing on individuals with special needs. Sixteen single-subject design studies were analyzed to determine the overall effect of AR on social, living, learning, and physical skills acquisition. The findings reveal a large effect of AR across the studies, with the highest impact observed in learning skills, followed by social, physical, and living skills. The results support the potential of AR to support individuals with special needs and provide valuable insights for decision-makers in special education. The use of AR facilitates meaningful interaction, enhances processing skills, and increases learning motivation. AR applications have been successful in promoting social behaviors, improving vocational and daily life skills, and enhancing physical skills through location-based learning. Future research should explore the effectiveness of AR in other skill domains and consider a larger population of individuals with diverse disabilities. This metaanalysis underscores the role of AR in promoting the acquisition of various skills in special education, contributing to the independence and quality of life of individuals with special needs.

Augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) have shown great importance and potential in supporting individuals  with  special  needs  (Papanastasiou,  2019).  For  individuals  with  disabilities,  AR  and  VR allow for personalized and individualized learning, accommodating different learning styles and pacing. They offer opportunities for repetition, reinforcement, and scaffolding, facilitating skill acquisition and retention. AR and VR have the potential to improve engagement, motivation, and learning outcomes for individuals with special needs, empowering them to overcome challenges and reach their full potential.

AI has gained popularity in language learning, particularly in supporting children with dyslexia and dysgraphia. Research has been conducted to explore the benefits and challenges of AI-based language learning for dyslexic and dysgraphia children, including the use of computer-based assessments, natural language processing, and AI-based chatbots and virtual assistants (Sharma &amp; Dash, 2023). AI has also been used to develop solutions such as mobile apps and adaptive reinforcement learning frameworks to improve language outcomes for individuals with language disorders. AI has the potential to create personalized learning experiences for children with disabilities, such as dyslexia, by automating routine tasks, providing real-time feedback, and generating insights into student learning. However, there are also challenges and limitations associated with the use of AI in education, including the need for adequate training and support for teachers and the potential for biases in AI algorithms. AI has the potential to transform the education of children with disabilities and improve their learning outcomes.

Incorporating (Shapley Additive Explanations) SHAP values within the student performance prediction framework empowers educators to recognize students at risk and provide timely interventions based on the prediction and explanations generated by the model (Sahlaoui, Alaoui, Nayyar, Agoujil, &amp; Jaber, 2021). This research paper presents an approach that not only improves student performance prediction but also offers explanations for the predicted scores. By combining advanced machine learning techniques, effective class balancing strategies, hyperparameter optimization, and the visualization of influential factors, educators can proactively identify students who require support and provide appropriate guidance in a timely manner.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has the potential to greatly enhance virtual reality (VR) experiences in several ways (Huang, 2021). Firstly, AI algorithms can enable real-time object recognition and tracking, allowing AR and VR applications adapt to user movements and actions. This enhances the sense of immersion and interactivity within the virtual environment. Secondly, AI-powered computer vision enables image recognition and tracking, enabling VR systems to respond dynamically to the user's real-world surroundings, seamlessly integrating virtual elements. Thirdly, Natural Language Processing (NLP) can be employed to incorporate voice commands in VR environments, simplifying user interactions and enhancing user convenience. Additionally, AI's predictive analytics capabilities can anticipate user behavior, resulting in more personalized and proactive VR experiences. By analyzing usage data and user feedback, businesses can optimize their AR/VR services, leading to improved customer satisfaction. Finally, AI can analyze user behavior and preferences to create personalized experiences in VR, tailoring content and interactions to meet individual needs. This customization enhances user immersion and engagement.

## INTRODUCTION

In today's globalized world, language learning has become more pertinent than ever before. Language learning refers to the process of acquiring the ability to communicate in a new language. It involves gaining proficiency in understanding, speaking, reading, and writing in a language other than one's native language. Language learning can take place in a formal setting, such as a classroom or language school, or informally through self-study, immersion, or interaction with native speakers. It requires developing skills in grammar, vocabulary, pronunciation, and cultural understanding, as well as being able to use these skills effectively in real-life situations. With the increasing interconnectedness of the world, the ability to communicate effectively in multiple languages has become a key asset in both personal and professional settings. This has led to the development of language learning models, which are designed to help people learn new languages and improve their skills in existing ones. These models utilize advanced technologies and innovative methodologies to provide effective language learning experiences to learners of all ages and backgrounds. The importance of language learning models in modern communication and education cannot be overstated, as they play a vital role in facilitating cross-cultural communication and fostering understanding between individuals from different linguistic and cultural backgrounds. Language learning models are designed to help people learn new languages or improve their existing language skills. These models can take many forms, such as textbooks, online courses, language exchange programs, or language learning apps. They are based on the principles of language acquisition, which involve exposure to the language, practice, and feedback.

Special learning disorders refer to a broad category of conditions that affect an individual's ability to learn and perform specific tasks. These disorders can manifest in different ways, such as difficulty with reading, writing, speaking, or processing information. Some common examples of special disorders include dyslexia, dysgraphia, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder(ADHD), autism spectrum disorder(ASD), and intellectual disability. Dyslexia and dysgraphia are two common learning disabilities that affect children's ability to read, write, and spell accurately. These disabilities can significantly impede a child's academic performance, leading to a lack of self-confidence, anxiety, and frustration. Traditional approaches to address these disabilities often involve one-on-one sessions with a tutor or special education teacher, which can be time-consuming and expensive. In recent years, AI language learning models have shown tremendous potential in assisting children with dyslexia and dysgraphia. These AI models can provide real-time feedback and personalized instruction to help children overcome learning difficulties. Special disorders can have a significant impact on an individual's ability to learn and function in everyday life. For example, individuals with dyslexia may have trouble decoding and recognizing words, which can make reading and writing challenging. Those with dysgraphia may struggle with the generation of written language, such as forming letters and organizing ideas. ADHD can lead to difficulty with attention and focus, making it hard to concentrate in a classroom or complete tasks. Individuals with ASD may have problems with social communication and interaction, making it challenging to form relationships or navigate social situations. Intellectual disability can result in a range of cognitive deficits, such as difficulty with memory, attention, and problem-solving skills. These challenges can have a significant impact on an individual's educational and career opportunities. There are various types of special disorders that affect individuals in different ways. Below are some common examples and their characteristics (Gururanjan &amp; et.al., 2022):

1. Dyslexia: Dyslexia is a learning disorder that affects reading skills. Individuals with dyslexia may struggle with phonological processing, which means they have difficulty recognizing and decoding words. They may also have difficulty with reading comprehension and spelling. Some common characteristics of dyslexia include difficulty reading aloud, slow reading speed, difficulty with letter and sound recognition, and poor spelling.
2. Dysgraphia: Dysgraphia is a learning disorder that affects writing skills.  Individuals  with  dysgraphia may have difficulty with handwriting, spelling, and organizing their thoughts in writing. They may also struggle with fine motor skills, which can make it hard to form letters and write legibly. Common characteristics of dysgraphia include poor handwriting, difficulty with letter formation, and difficulty with spelling and grammar.
3. Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD): ADHD is a neurodevelopmental disorder that affects attention and impulse control. Individuals with ADHD may have difficulty with organization, focus, and completing tasks. They may also struggle with hyperactivity or impulsivity, which can make it hard to sit still or control their behavior. Some common characteristics of ADHD include difficulty with attention and focus, forgetfulness, impulsivity, and hyperactivity.
4. Autism spectrum disorder (ASD): ASD is a neurodevelopmental disorder that affects social communication and interaction. Individuals with ASD may have difficulty with social cues and may struggle to form relationships or understand social norms. They may also exhibit repetitive behaviors or have narrow interests. Some common characteristics of ASD include difficulty with social interaction, repetitive behaviors, intense interests in specific topics, and difficulty with verbal and nonverbal communication.
5. Intellectual  disability:  Intellectual  disability  is  a  condition  that  affects  cognitive  functioning. Individuals with intellectual disability may have difficulty with memory, problem-solving, and adaptive skills. They may also struggle with language and communication. Common characteristics of intellectual disability include difficulty with learning and problem-solving, delays in language development, and difficulty with self-care and independent living skills.

According to a study published in the Indian Paediatrics journal (Goel, 2021), the incidence of dyslexia among primary school children in India was reported to be 18%, while the incidence of dysgraphia was 14%. Dyslexia and dysgraphia are learning disorders that can make language learning particularly challenging for individuals who experience them. In this chapter, the main focus is on Dyslexia and dysgraphia. Dyslexia affects reading skills, while dysgraphia affects writing skills. For individuals with dyslexia,  language  learning  can  be  challenging  because  they  may  have  difficulty  decoding  and  recognizing words. This can make it hard for them to read instructions, vocabulary lists, and other language learning materials. They may also struggle with reading comprehension, making it challenging to understand the meaning of a passage or a sentence. Additionally, individuals with dyslexia may experience difficulty with spelling, which can make it hard for them to write in a new language.

On the other hand, individuals with dysgraphia may find language learning challenging because they may struggle with writing skills. They may have difficulty forming letters, which can make writing in a new language challenging. Dysgraphia can also affect fine motor skills, making it hard to write legibly. This can make it challenging to practice handwriting and develop fluency in a new language. Both dyslexia and dysgraphia can also impact an individual's confidence and self-esteem. Struggling with reading or writing can make individuals feel frustrated and embarrassed, making them avoid language learning activities. This avoidance can further impede their progress in learning a new language. To address these challenges, language learning models should incorporate strategies that support individuals with dyslexia and dysgraphia.

There is no cure for dysgraphia, but there are several strategies and accommodations that can help individuals with dysgraphia improve their writing skills. These may include the use of assistive technology, such as speech-to-text software or word processing programs with spell-checking and grammarchecking features, as well as specialized writing programs that help individuals with dysgraphia learn to write more efficiently and effectively.
