## 3.3    Support Vector Machine (SVM)

In the present study SVM, classifies Dysgraphia and Dyscalculia features such as motor skills, spatial knowledge, spellings, legibility, visual-spatial response, sentence word structure, reasoning and word formation. SVM, which is utilized extensively for classification, regression, and density estimation. SVM methodology creates a hyperplane w. x + b = 0 , xi ϵ R. n to segregate the data elements   x i (the data elements that resides on the same side of the generated hyperplane) that correspond to a given decision g ( x ) = sign ( w . x + b )



In the hyperplane generation task, the distance to the closest data element is maximized to minimize the risk of incorrectly classifying the raw data. The SVM approach aims to find out the classifier of the form given in Eq. 9:

Classification models have been implemented using Python's scikit-learn package (version 0.21) (version 3.6.3). Each classification method is compared with all classification model  performances.  Additionally,  the  features  considered  for  the  classification  process were extended to include cognitive aspects. Responses obtained from the learners' questionnaires  were  integrated  to  assess  their  cognitive  strengths  and  learning  preferences. This  assessment  was  conducted  using  the  Analytic  Hierarchy  Process  (AHP)  technique. This comprehensive approach allows for a thorough examination of both the linguistic and cognitive  dimensions,  enhancing  the  discrimination  and  identification  of  these  learning challenges.

## 3.4    Analytical Hierarchical Process (AHP)

The Analytical Hierarchical Process (AHP) is developed to generate decisions based on multiple criteria. Satty, in the 1980s, has proposed a strong and helpful mathematical tool for the management of qualitative and quantitative criterion elements involving the decision  process  [33].  The  first  step  in  AHP  is  to  construct  a  hierarchy  of  the  problem;  the second is to assign the nominal value to each level of this hierarchy and create a matrix for the pair-wise comparison judgment. There are three steps in the AHP model methodology: structuring the problem, paired comparison, and priority analysis.



Fig. 3 Representation of a separating hyperplane for a 2-D training set



## 3.4.1    AHP process for ranking the Learning disorders

## Step1 Structuring the problem

At the top level of the hierarchy is considered level1 and is the objective of the model's decision process. Directly below is level 2 of the model, related to level 1 of the model. In level 2, the criteria are essential in the learning disability ranking process. The criteria that influence the overall AHP decision process model are Reflective learning, Visual learning, and Active Learning (as discussed above). For clarity, the evaluation of these criteria is based on the more important criteria. In level 3, the sub-criteria are used as a direct reference for evaluating the defined decision alternatives. The sub-criteria in level 3 is utilised as the base for evaluating each decision alternative, as given in Fig. 4. For this study, specific learning preferences/styles for learners with learning disabilities (LD) have been identified, including story-based learning (slides), video-based learning, game-based learning, and practice sets.

Once all the criteria  and  sub-criteria  are  structured  according  to  the  hierarchical  tree structure,  the  second  phase is  a  pair-wise  comparison of these predefined criteria of the structured tree.

## Step2 Paired Comparisons

In  this  stage  of  the  AHP  mathematical  model,  the  paired-wise  comparison  will  be conducted within the sub-criteria of the same level. The pre-judgment scale is used for comparison and to determine the preference of each element. The comparison matrix generated  for  the  sub-criteria:  Dyslexia,  Dysgraphia  and  Dyscalculia  as  shown  in Tables 1, 2 and 3.



Fig. 4 The hierarchical structure of the criteria



Table  1  represents  the  pairwise  comparisons  for  the  Reflective  sub-criteria  (C1)Story/slides, Video based, and Game/practice set. The values in the matrices indicate the strength of preference or importance, and the comparisons are done with respect to a certain criterion.

Story/slides to Video based: Story/slides is considered to be 5 times more important than Video based.

Video  based  to  Game/practice  set:  Video  based  is  considered  to  be  0.2  times  as important as Game/practice set.

Story/slides  to  Game/practice  set:  Story/slides  is  considered  to  be  2  times  more important than Game/practice set.

This Table 2 represents the pairwise comparisons for the Reflective sub-criteria (C2).

Video based to Story/slides: Video based is considered to be 6 times more important than Story/slides.

Game/practice set to Story/slides: Game/practice set is considered to be 7 times more important than Story/slides.

Game/practice set to Video based: Game/practice set is considered to be 0.2 times as important as Video based.

## Step3 Priority Analysis

In this step of the AHP process, these comparisons are standardised after the pairedwise  comparison  has  been  constructed.  The  one  standardisation  process  which  is  frequently used is to divide each number in a column of the paired wise comparison table with the total sum value of the particular column. Afterward, the arithmetic mean of each line is calculated for the standardised matrix, and the respective priorities for each criterion are obtained. Table 4 represents the matrix for the Reading Skill sub-criteria in % (Tables 5 and 6).

## 3.5    Model development

The two cascading models in which one LSTM performs the data reduction part and SVM classifies the learning disabilities. The data predicted correctly by the first model is used as input in the second model for later classification. Moreover, AHP has been incorporated with this cascading model for the additional profile details such as Learning Style (LS), Cognitive Strength (CS), and Problematic Skills (PS). The AHP model has been selected for the optimal selection from the presented Learning styles, Cognitive strengths, and Problematic  skills  as  the  intermediate  output.  Figure  5  demonstrates  the  combination  of  the overall model process.

## 3.5.1    SVM, LSTM and AHP Integration within the ITS framework

Support Vector Machine (SVM), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), and Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) Integration within the framework involves orchestrating these models for a cohesive and comprehensive learning disability classification system. The steps involved in the process are:

Data  Preprocessing:  Speech  and  writing  features  were  preprocessed  using  advanced techniques for high-quality data analysis. Specifically, Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCC) were used for speech feature extraction [34], and the Histogram of Oriented Gradients (HOG) technique was applied for writing feature extraction [35]. These methods provide robust feature representations, ideal for subsequent classification using Long  Short-Term  Memory  (LSTM)  networks.  The  LSTM  classified  audio  data  from surveys,  distinguishing  between  "Learning  Disabled"  and  "Non-Learning  Disabled," with instances labeled as "Non-Learning Disabled" excluded from the final analysis.

Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP) Integration: Apply AHP to evaluate factors related to learning disabilities and assign weights within the defined hierarchy. Conduct comparisons among alternatives (Dyslexia, Dysgraphia, Dyscalculia) using AHP, calculating probabilities for each alternative's impact on learning outcomes.

Learning Disability Ranking: Rank disabilities based on Severity, Learning Preferences/

Style, Cognitive Strength, and Problematic Skills using AHP-calculated probabilities. Framework Integration: Integrate SVM, LSTM, and AHP models into the ITS framework. Design ITS module, ensuring fluid data transitions.

Classification: Execute the classification task on the reduced dataset using the integrated SVM model. Assign learning or non-learning-disabled labels using SVM method and determine the disability category/severity based on AHP rankings.



Fig. 5 A classifier combined with another classifier with intermediate AHP output



The study is based on cascading the LSTM and SVM learning model; the former in this module will reduce the audio data collected through surveys of children (with or without) learning disabilities. The LSTM generates classification results under two classification labels, "Learning Disabled" or "Non- Learning Disabled" all data with the label "Nonlearning disabled" will then be eliminated from the database. Here, AHP will eliminate the incorrect and inconsistent leaner data from the dataset. The AHP transforms the comparison; the weight of each factor related to the disability allows the assessment of each feature inside the defined hierarchy. Further, a comparison is being made, the probability related to each alternative (Dyslexia, Dysgraphia, Dyscalculia) will be calculated. This probability determines the possibility of the alternative to affect the learning outcomes of the learning disabled. If higher is the probability, higher is the rank of the predefined alternative. This assessment will rank the disability in terms of its Severity, Learning Preferences/Style (LS), Cognitive Strength (CS), and Problematic Skills (PS). The final task is to classify the reduced dataset into learning or non-learning-disabled labels and the category/severity of learning disability that the integrated AHP model has already ranked.

## 4    Result and discussion

Research Question 1: To design and develop an Intelligent Tutoring System for the learning disabled (MIRACLE) for learning disabilities prediction, profile, and content generation

The ITS (MIRACLE) has been implemented and integrated utilising Long Short Term Memory  (LSTM),  Support  Vector  Machine  (SVM),  and  Analytical  Hierarchy  Process (AHP)  techniques.  The  ITS  (MIRACLE)  for  the  LDs  is  based  on  the  cascading  model architecture where the output from one learning model has served as the input to another model. This has effectively reduced the cluttered data at the beginning of the module development. Moreover, the AHP mathematical model has added the benefits of ranking the disabilities in terms of Severity, Learning Style, cognitive strength, and Problematic Skills of the learner. Figure 6 shows the developed ITS (MIRACLE) for LDs. Figure 7 represents the learner details obtained from the ITS (MIRACLE).

This  profiling  system  is  dynamic  and  presents  detailed  information  expected  from an  ITS  system.  The  proposed  model  provides  the  following  advantages  over  the  existed models:

1. De-cluttered the ambiguous and unwanted data at the initial stage through LSTM classification process. This has improved the data quality significantly for further classification.
2. Incorporation of the AHP process has added the advantage of a detailed learner profile consisting of LD with category, LD subtype, Learning Style (LS), Cognitive Strength (CS), Problematic Skill (PS).
3. This ITS (MIRACLE) can present learner-specific content according to the generated learner profile details.
4. The performance of this proposed model in the detailed learner profiling task of Learning Disabled is significantly effective.

Research Question 2: ITS (MIRACLE) Evaluation The features selected from the dataset include questionnaires related to Literacy skills, Phonological Awareness, Word Formation, Sentence Structure, Counting Numbers, Calculation,  Reasoning,  Visual-spatial  Response,  Rhyming,  Numeracy  skills,  Handwriting Skills,  Word  Fluency,  Copying  Skills,  Loudness.  These  data  points  are  trained  over  the proposed model.

## 4.1    Performance evaluation of the proposed model

Figure 8 depicts the values of evaluation metrics obtained in this experiment. The data is trained  and  tested  with  a  ratio  of  8:2.  The  results  obtained  through  the  proposed  model are compared with the output of the similar study conducted by ANN, SVM, and LSTM on evaluation metrics of precision, recall, accuracy, and F-1 score. The combined model LSTM and SVM evaluation is based on evaluation matrices Precision, Recall, Accuracy, and F1 score. Moreover, the AHP features have been combined to evaluate the learner's performance to present the optimal selected profile content and other required details. The classification model has been selected based on its comparison with other machine learning models on performance metrics (Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1-score). The accuracy is used as a performance indicator given as Eq. 1, true positive- correctly predicted positive samples  and  false  positive-incorrectly  predicted  positive  samples,  false  negative-  incorrectly predicted negative samples, and true negative- correctly predicted negative instances are used to calculate these performance indicators.

Precision is the total positive predicted samples out of the predicted samples; Eq. 2 is the precision formula.



Recall is the fraction of the positive samples that are correctly classified; the formula is given in Eq. 3.



The metric F-1 score represents the harmonic mean of the recall and precision values. Equation 4 represents F- measure metric.



The  proposed  Model  for  LDs  identification  and  discrimination  from  other  disabilities  generates  promising  results. The accuracy  of  the  proposed  model  is  the  highest,  with  a  98%  score  value.  The  algorithms, ANN, LSTM, and SVM have obtained 96%, 91%, and 97% accuracy. The F-1 score of these algorithms is compared, and the proposed algorithm yielded the highest among the entire algorithm's scores. Therefore, it is evident from the results that the proposed model has outperformed other algorithms in this experiment.

## 4.2    Pretest and Post-test evaluation of the proposed ITS (MIRACLE)

In Fig. 9, the pretest without utilizing proposed ITS to identify a learner as LD (Learning Disabled) or NLD (Non-Learning Disabled) is quite significant but not influential compared with the proposed model post-test results. There are improvements in classifications  values  shown  as  the  result  line  of  the  post-test  using  the  proposed  model. The report  generated  using  the  proposed  model  can  categorise  the  profile  of  learners with disability into the respective category along with their Learning Style/Preference (LS),  Cognitive  Strength  (CS),  and  related  Problematic  Skills  (PS)  because  the  Proposed Model classification for learner profiling provides category range (Extreme, High, Low, and Nil). The category Nil represents the learner who does not have symptoms of the related disability; the severity of the learning difficulties decreases from extreme to nil categories in a profile. The output range is precise and flexible (can be extended or reduced) according to need.

ANOVA (One-Way) test is applied on the data obtained through the proposed Learner module in the ITS of the LD. The ANOVA (One-Way) is conducted on pretest result of the learner module in ITS assuming the samples have equal variance. The ANOVA (One-Way) is selected for evaluation as more than two samples results of the population was used in the pre-test for analysis.



Fig. 9 Pretest and post-test analysis graph of implemented the ITS



Hypothesis There is no significant difference present in the mean of each sample, in the learner module of the implemented ITS of LD.

In Table 7 the alpha value (0.05) is more than P value (0.006108), so the null hypothesis remains unaccepted. Hence, it is concluded that the implemented algorithms for the development of the learner module in the ITS of LDs identification was significant and improves learner specific profiling. Therefore, the proposed method to create learner module is significant and difference in effectiveness found in the methods utilized.

However, it is unknown that which of the specific sample differed and is significant. The Posthoc test is generally preferred test to determine the differed sample group on ANOVA (One-Way). Table 8 is the post hoc test analysis and the alpha-value obtained in post hoc test is (0.0125). The alpha value when compared with the P-value obtained in the post hoc test  the  difference  between  the  proposed  sample  group  mean  is  found  to  be  statistically significant. This post hoc analysis revealed that the proposed method for learner module development in the ITS of LD has obtained significant results.

The above test results proved that the learning outcomes in Learner Model has significantly improved than the existing ITS Learner Models. This improvement in the learning is due to the integration of LSTM and AHP modelling introduced in the Learner Model into the ITS. Hence, it is concluded that integrating the proposed Learner Modelling methodology in the ITS model is significant and improves learning for LD and NLD learner.

The main contribution of this study is the development of an ITS (MIRACLE) for learning disabilities identification and learner profile generation. Moreover, based on the generated learner profile, the content is generated for educated learners. The limitation of the proposed work is:

1. A limited amount of data has been utilised to develop the proposed model. However, the data would increase quality and quantity in future studies.
2. The research focused on a specific context or educational environment. It is important to acknowledge that the effectiveness of the MIRACLE framework might vary when applied to different educational contexts, institutions, or countries.
3. The identification of learning disabilities was based on a pretest and non-invasive tools. The accuracy and validity of these tools in capturing the full spectrum of learning disabilities may be a limitation, as the diagnosis of learning disabilities often requires comprehensive assessments.
4. The success of the MIRACLE framework heavily relies on the chosen machine learning models (LSTM, SVM, and AHP). Limitations or biases inherent in these models may impact the accuracy of learning disability identification.

## 5    Conclusion and future direction

This study has implemented an ITS (MIRACLE) to profile learners with disability and generate learner-specific content. The study classified learners with disability and their learning preferences, cognitive strength, and problematic skills as profile details. Moreover, in this  study,  the  results  in  profile  are  improved  by  classifying  the  subtype  of  the  learning disabilities.  This  framework is a cascading module developed combining the advantages from machine learning models (LSTM + SVM) and mathematical model Analytical Hierarchical Process (AHP). This module can outperform the other implemented architectures for the learning disabled and proves to be a better profiling system. In the future, studies will improve the existing ITS (MIRACLE) performance by incorporating the EEG device dataset for LDs profiling. The data has a significant role in improving the overall accuracies of the developed model. Thus, the focus is to improve the existing dataset to increase the ITS (MIRACLE) efficacy. Additionally, the proposed ITS can be integrated into vocational training programs to simulate real-world scenarios, enhancing practical skills. This could facilitate flexible learning schedules, allowing students to improve their learning outcomes. It provides personalized support for individuals with varying levels of prior knowledge.

## An Intelligent Math E-Tutoring System for Students with Specific Learning Disabilities

Zikai Alex Wen Computer Science, Cornell Tech, United States

[zw385@cornell.edu](mailto:zw385@cornell.edu)

## Erica O Silverstein

Information Science, Cornell Tech, United States es2223@cornell.edu

## ABSTRACT

Students with specific learning disabilities (SLDs) often experience negative emotions when solving math problems, which they have difficulty managing. This is one reason that current math e-learning tools, which elicit these negative emotions, are not effective for these students. We designed an intelligent math e-tutoring system that aims to reduce students' negative emotional behaviors. The system automatically detects possible negative emotional behaviors by analyzing gaze, inputs on the touchscreen, and response time. It then uses one of four intervention methods (e.g., hints or brain breaks) to prevent students from being upset. To form this design, we conducted a formative study with five teachers for students with SLDs. The teachers thought that the design of four intervention methods would help students with SLDs. Among the four intervention methods, providing brain breaks is new and particularly useful for the students. The teachers also suggested that the system should personalize the detection of negative emotional behaviors to help students who have more severe learning disabilities.

## 1 INTRODUCTION AND BACKGROUND

Many math e-learning tools (e.g., Khan Academy [6], ST Math [8]) have been developed to provide independent math practice exercises. However, the commonly used math e-learning tools were not designed for students with specific learning disabilities (SLDs). As a result, our prior research study [15] showed that these students had difficulties in using math e-learning tools. For example, the students struggle with reading problems, hints, and solutions that are presented in text form. The students may also struggle when they have to solve a problem that is beyond their math abilities. As the students struggle in practicing math exercises, they build up feelings of frustration and irritation, which leads up to exhibiting negative emotional behaviors (e.g., randomly guessing answers or even damaging the e-learning device).

Therefore, we worked together with a teacher for students with SLDs to design an intelligent e-tutoring system (as shown in Figure 1) that reduces students' negative emotional behaviors. First, the teacher summarized her students' negative emotional behaviors: (1) staring at the problem without trying, (2) being distracted away from the screen, (3) tapping the screen agitatedly, and (4) showing negative facial expressions. Then, we studied previous work that had tried to automatically detect these behaviors, but we did not find a solution that we can use. Prior work [3, 9] has focused on using machine learning to detect negative facial expressions for students with special needs. Although these systems can detect obvious facial expressions (e.g., crying), they did poorly in distinguishing subtle facial expressions (e.g., mind-wandering compared

Recent research on math e-learning tools for students with SLDs [1, 5, 12] has mainly focused on helping students overcome text processing difficulty by designing interactable manipulatives that can represent text-based math problems. For example, Calcularis [5] challenges students to compare the size of two quantities by positioning two numbers on a number line from 0 to 100. French National Institute of Health and Medical Research designed two games, The Number Race [16] and Number Catcher [17], for the students. These games present Arabic, verbal, and visual representations of numbers together to help students compare which whole number is larger and which is smaller. However, if students struggle in using these e-learning tools, they can only receive two types of help: feedback for wrong answers or step-by-step hints, which were ineffective in preventing students from exhibiting negative emotional behaviors [15].

Figure 1: An overview of the intelligent math e-tutoring system for students with SLDs. Zone 1 presents the problem in text form (and highlights the sentence that the system is reading). Zone 2 illustrates how students slice their fi nger across the pizza to make half pizza slices. Zone 3 presents the dialogue system that asks the students about their emotional state.



with active thinking). So, these systems do not work for students with SLDs because the students already need help before they start crying [10].

After detecting a negative emotional behavior, our system confirms the student's emotional state through dialogue. Our system, like what teachers do, is speculating about the negative feelings of the students, so it is necessary to confirm with the students before deciding how to intervene.

Instead of using facial expression detection technology, analyzing gaze was found to be effective in detecting students who do not know how to solve a math problem [7]. Nonetheless, the existing studies of gaze analysis for learning [4, 7] did not consider students with SLDs. The teacher on our team suggested that analyzing gaze may also be useful for students with SLDs because it is possible for teachers to speculate whether the student is focusing on solving a problem. She also suggested that the system should combine gaze with other student behaviors to predict negative emotions, especially the behaviors that teachers have been observing. For example, teachers pay attention to students who do not attempt a problem for a long time or students who keep tapping the screen. The teachers in our prior research study [15] also mentioned these student behaviors when they talked about observing negative emotional behaviors. Therefore, our system combines eye-tracking data, inputs on the touchscreen, and response time to model the student behaviors.

The existing math e-learning tools for SLDs [1, 5, 12] only provide two intervention methods (i.e., hints or feedback for wrong answers), which is not effective in lightening a student's mood. So, we designed four intervention methods based on the teacher's tutoring experience. To prevent students from getting upset when they don't have the ability to solve the problem, our system provides hints or to switch to a simpler problem. To calm students who have been experiencing negative emotions (i.e., just ok, tired, or angry), our system sends personalized encouraging messages or provides brain breaks.

To form our design, we conducted a formative study with five special education teachers. The study was conducted virtually through video conferencing. During the study, we demonstrated our design prototype to the participants. We then asked teachers to provide feedback about the system design based on their teaching experience. The teachers thought it was necessary for e-learning tools to check in with students' emotional status. They reported that our design of e-tutoring intervention methods would effectively reduce the students' negative emotions. Teachers also suggested that we should personalize the detection of negative emotional behaviors for students who have more severe learning disabilities.

We present an intelligent e-tutoring system for students with SLDs that can reduce the students' negative emotional behaviors. We designed this system together with teachers for SLDs and conducted a formative study with teachers. In the future, we will conduct studies with students to get feedback from them. Our work will inspire e-learning tool designers and developers to design inclusive e-learning tools for students with SLDs.

## 2 SYSTEM DESIGN

## 2.1 System Prototype

We developed a math game prototype that uses the intelligent etutoring system to manage students' negative emotional behaviors. This prototype helps students practice fraction problems. Students practice fraction skills by manipulating pizza in two ways: cutting a pizza into different slices and moving the correct amount of pizza slices onto different plates (as shown in Figure 1, Highlight Zone 2).

The prototype runs in Windows 10 operating system on a Windows Surface Pro 7 tablet. Students use the touchscreen to play the game. A Tobii Eye Tracker 5 is stuck to the bottom of the tablet to detect where the student gazes at the screen. The game prototype processes the eye-gazing data stream to identify the in-game elements that the student gazes at, including texts, fraction numbers, pizza slices, plates, and UI buttons. The game prototype also logs the running time and touchscreen inputs.

## 2.2 Triggering Intervention in Outstanding Behaviors

Many students with SLDs are reluctant to seek help when they were exhausted or agitated, but they show specific negative emotional behaviors [15]. Therefore, our system actively detects three types of negative emotional behaviors. First, students are distracted away from the screen if their eyes have not gazed on the screen for more than one minute. Second, students are touching the screen agitatedly if they repeatedly pressed the screen more than three times within 0.1 seconds. Third, students are hesitating to solve the puzzle if they have not touched the screen for more than two minutes and they have spent more than 70% of the time gazing at UI buttons and interactable but useless manipulatives. After detecting that a student is exhibiting one of the three behaviors, the system will confirm the student's emotional state through dialogue.

## 2.3 Interventions for Learning Difficulties

Students with SLDs build up frustration and irritation in using math e-learning tools for two main reasons [15]. One main reason is that students have to solve a math problem that is too difficult to solve. The other reason is that students cannot manage their negative emotions when they feel exhausted or angry.

Reducing the difficulty level of exercises, however, may not help students recover from exhaustion or anger. Many students with SLDs, due to cognitive differences, feel exhausted or angry quicker than general education students [2]. Inspired by the guidelines for tutoring students with SLDs [11, 13, 14], we designed two methods to help the students maintain or restore a good emotion: praising for a correct problem-solving behavior or providing brain breaks. The behavior-specific praise describes the approval of correct student inputs (e.g., 'Nice work slicing your finger across the whole pizza! You made half pizza slices!'). The genuine approval is more effective in encouraging students with SLDs than generic encouragement (e.g., 'you are doing awesome!') [14]. Nevertheless, students would need brain breaks instead of encouragement when they reach the tipping point of negative emotions [13]. A brain break is a break from the current learning task that students are working on. Students can rest their eyes or take a physical exercise during a brain break. Therefore, we designed a kind of brain break that temporarily hides all e-learning interfaces and guides students to play a kinesthetic game (i.e., a body dancing game that gets the student moving and grooving).

To help students who do not know how to solve a problem, we designed two methods: providing hints or switching to a simpler problem. Providing hints is a traditional method to point the students in the direction of the correct answer. Nevertheless, if the students cannot comprehend the hint due to weak math abilities, switching to a simpler problem that matches their math ability is more useful than providing new hints.

We mapped the e-tutoring interventions in exercises to three negative emotional states (just OK, tired, and angry). If the students feel just ok, they will receive behavior-specific praise. If the students feel confused, they may choose to get a hint or to try a simpler problem. If the students feel tired, they can try a simpler problem or take a brain break. If the students feel angry, they will take a brain break then continue to a simpler problem.

## 3 FORMATIVE STUDY: TEACHER FEEDBACK

To form our design, we conducted a formative study with teachers for students with SLDs (3 females, 2 males, between 0.5 and 7 years of experience in teaching students with SLDs in grades 3-6). We started from interviewing teachers because they have been designing and practicing interventions in tutoring the students. We anticipated that teachers would be able to use their teaching experience to offer valuate insights in our current design. During the study, we demonstrated our prototype to the participants. We asked them to give feedback on the design of e-tutoring intervention methods and the specifications to detect negative emotional behaviors. We screen recorded then transcribed all interviews. We coded the transcriptions and found two main themes that were summarized from the teacher feedback.

Three teachers commented that the detection of negative emotional behaviors may not work for students who have more severe learning disabilities. These students may take significantly longer time to decode information and comprehend the problem. As a result, the current system may initiate chats with these students too early, and thus interrupt the students' thinking. To detect whether students are struggling, teachers had been providing the students both non-math exercises and math exercises to compare the differences of student performance (e.g., response time and body gestures). Teachers will intervene when the students behave much slower or agitatedly in math exercises. However, there is no known way to automate this detection approach.

All five teachers mentioned that e-learning tools should intervene in exercises when the student is experiencing negative emotions. One teacher explained, 'I know how important the emotional status affects these students' ability to learn. Like, if they are frustrated, or if they are stressed, their thinking brain is not [turned] on.' They liked the design of our e-tutoring intervention methods, especially providing brain breaks for students with SLDs. One teacher said, 'there are kids who might be on a computer for a little while and they might get, you know, overwhelmed or zoned-out [ . . . ] For example, I have a kid who works for like 10 or 15 minutes and then gets to break. That's part of their IEP [Individualized Education Program].' Therefore, our design provides an important accommodation for the students as they practice math exercises independently.

## 4 CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK

We presented the design of an intelligent math e-tutoring system for students with SLDs. The system provides four types of intervention methods to reduce negative emotional behaviors. It automatically intervenes in exercises by detecting students' negative emotional behaviors then asking the students about their emotional state to eventually determine which intervention method to use. Teachers in the formative study mentioned that the system meets the needs of students with SLDs. They also suggested that the detection of negative emotional behaviors can be personalized to help students with more severe learning disabilities. In the future, we will explore the personalization of negative emotional behaviors detection. We will also recruit students with SLDs to try our prototype and to provide feedback. Our work provides a starting point for e-learning tool designers and developers to leverage our design to develop e-tutoring systems for students with SLDs.

## ACKNOWLEDGMENTS

The authors would like to thank Bingxin Weng for designing the graphics of the virtual tutor. The authors would also like to thank all teacher participants for providing valuable comments and suggestions.

## Paper Source: ARTIS: a digital interface to promote the rehabiliatation of text comprehension difficulties through Artificial Intelligence

## ARTIS: a digital interface to promote the rehabiliatation of text comprehension difficulties through Artificial Intelligence

Martina Galletti 1,2 , * , † , Eleonora Pasqua 3,2 , † , Manuela Calanca 3,2 , Caterina Marchesi 3 , Donatella Tomaiuoli 3,2,5 and Daniele Nardi 2,4

1 Sony Computer Science Laboratories-Paris (Sony CSL-Paris) - France

2 Sapienza University of Rome - Italy

3 Centro Ricerca e Cura di Roma - Italy

5 Tor Vergata University of Rome, Italy

4 CINI-AIIS - Italy

## Abstract

This study introduces ARTIS, an AI-powered interface aimed at enhancing text comprehension in children with language and learning disorders and deficits. Leveraging neuro-psycholinguistic models, ARTIS offers personalized practice at varying difficulty levels, targeting specific linguistic components of text processing. Through AI algorithms, ARTIS autonomously extracts keywords, associates them with pictograms, identifies complex words, generates semantic networks, and proposes exercises on grammatical components. By automating cognitive processes and providing tailored interventions, ARTIS represents a significant advancement in promoting inclusive hybrid speech and language therapy practices, and improving text comprehension skills in children with special educational needs.

## Keywords

Natural Language Processing, Text comprehension, Language and learning disorders, Speech and Language Therapy

## 1. Introduction

Understanding a text allows us to acquire information, access new content, enrich the knowledge we already possess. Conversely, having difficulty in understanding what one reads is a great limitation to personal growth, and restrict opportunities, not only at school, but also in life. Text comprehension is thus a fascinating but also very complex ability. It requires motivation, attention, memory, but also specific language skills. These can be problematic for children with language and learning disorders. In fact, subjects with poor text comprehension show difficulties related to the processing of syntactic and semantic sentence components [1], the analysis of lexical components of words [2] and deficits in the syntactic representation of words and oral comprehension skills [3]. Moreover, [4] stated that the same subjects report significant deficits in receptive vocabulary and

Ital-IA 2024: 4th National Conference on Artificial Intelligence, organized by CINI, May 29-30, 2024, Naples, Italy

(E. Pasqua); 0000-0001-6606-200X (D. Nardi)

Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0).

semantic processing. Finally, [5] and [6] addressed the issue of grammar, claiming that children and adolescents with problems in text comprehension show difficulties in understanding the role of pronouns within sentences, especially if these are in clitic form.

Artificial intelligence-powered clinical and education tools have the potential to revolutionise learning and speech and language therapy for children with special educational needs and disabilities. It can personalize interventions and adaptive content that meet individual needs, thus promoting a more inclusive and equitable educational experience. Within this context we developed ARTIS - an interface designed to facilitate the rehabilitation and instruction of text comprehension skills through artificial intelligence. Starting from neuropsycholinguistic models of reading comprehension and focusing on the linguistic components of text processing, ARTIS enables personalized practice on texts at different levels. Thanks to AI algorithms, the interface is able to automatically extract pictograms from keywords, identify more complex words, generate semantic networks, and to propose exercises on certain grammatical components. ARTIS is aimed at primary and secondary school children with difficulties in understanding text, but can also be used as support for English as an L2. The output of our contribution is twofold. First, we designed and deployed the interface. Second, we tested whether AI can be a valid support tool for text comprehension from a clinical perspective.

## 2. Pedagogical and Psycho-linguistics Foundations

Over the years researchers in psycho-linguistics had been trying to formalise how people understand connected text. Text comprehension is defined as a complex cognitive task which involves an active process of meaning construction, dependent not only on the information in the text but also on the information possessed by the reader [7]. Researchers in psycho-linguistics have strived to formalize the mechanisms underlying this process. As a result, four main theories emerged as the main ones in the psycho-linguistics landscape:

1. The Simple View of Reading by Gough and Tunmer [8] where the decoding process and language skills are considered central to text comprehension. The key idea of this model is that comprehension, C , is defined as the product of decoding factors, D , defined as fluent word reading and language comprehension, L [8].
2. Structure Building Framework by Gernsbacher [9, 10, 11] where text comprehension is defined with the metaphor of the construction of a building where one's must start from the foundations i.e. from the first element contained in the text, for later one integrating the new information and enriching the departing structure in a cohesive one.
3. Memory-Focus Model of Sanford and Garrod [12, 13] in which is central the process of co-reference resolution. In fact, the key idea of this theory is that when comprehending a text, a reader must first establish a coherent interpretation of the text comprehended so far and must therefore establish whether a given element had been discussed previously or not.
4. Construction-Integration Model of Kintsch and van Dijk [14, 15, 16] focuses on how information from the text, at the granularity level of propositions, is connected to and completed by information stored in the long-term memory of the reader. Besides literal understanding of the words and syntax in the text, it's essential to be able to gather propositions from the text, their concepts and connections, and organise them into interconnected hierarchical structures. It is only with this representation of information, integrated with the reader's preexisting knowledge makes it possible to gain deep access to the content of the text[7, 16, 15]. To reflect this view, Kintsch and van Dijk identified two main levels of processing:

local and global. Local processing involves the understanding of individual sentences and phrases, while global processing focuses on integrating these local meanings into a coherent representation of the entire text. Central to their model is the concept of "coherence," where readers strive to create a cohesive mental representation by linking information within the text and connecting it to their existing knowledge.

Asmuchasthemodelsdescribed may emphasize different components as central to the comprehension process, they all converge on the idea that language skills, along with semantic and inferential skills, participate in linking prior knowledge to new information, creating a coherent and more complex representation of new meanings. In designing our interface, ARTIS, we drew inspiration from these foundational theories in psycho-linguistics.

## 3. Existing Work

In the literature, there is one Italian systems for telerehabilitation targeting specific learning disorders and special educational needs, i.e. RIDInet [17]. RIDInet focuses on text comprehension skills, particularly semantic and syntactic inferential processes. Neberthless, despite the clinical context, RIDInet lacks the integration of Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques. In English, two primary systems are 3D Readers [18] and CACSR [19]. 3D Readers offer users options for verbal or visual strategies to enhance comprehension, with immediate feedback provided. CACSR provides personalized instruction using various techniques like visual images and summarizing strategies, offering real-time feedback. Although these systems enhance reading comprehension, they are primarily used for educational contexts and lack focus on clinical categories. Moreover, Open Book [20] is the only system employing NLP, mainly for children with Autism Spectrum Disorder, focusing on text simplification and customization functions [21]. Its key features include text simplification through NLP techniques and rich customization functions, enabling users to quickly adapt the document presentation (font, font size, line spacing, colors) to their preferences. It also provides assistive tools such as dictionaries and images. However, Open Books was designed for a specific clinical population, and it focused more on improving their decoding skills than reading comprehension per se. Finally, Systems targeting tele-rehabilitation specifically for Dyslexia exist [22, 23, 24, 25], but few focus on reading comprehension skills.

## 4. Target Population of ARTIS

ARTIS targets two distinct target populations: students with specific reading comprehension disorders, and those identified in literature as 'poor comprehenders'.

Reading Comprehension Disorder, identified in the DSM-V[26], delineates difficulty in grasping the meaning of text despite proficient decoding skills. This encompasses understanding word sequences, implicit information (inferences), and the deeper meaning of text content. The distinction between decoding and comprehension abilities is highlighted in the literature [27], which underlines differences in cognitive processes, predictive factors, disorder characteristics, and treatment approaches. The functions involved in text comprehension include lexical skills (vocabulary), inferential skills, working memory, attention, and meta-cognitive control, which are distinct from decoding skills. Even if this disorder therefore often intersects with other conditions such as specific language disorder, decoding disorder (dyslexia), intellectual disability, or memory difficulties, it can be said that specific reading comprehension disorder is somehow independent of specific decoding disorder. Despite complexities in classification, understanding this disorder is crucial, as it often gets conflated with other clinical profiles. This is precisely the reason behind the beginning of this work and the reason why we involved since the beginning of its conception speech and language therapists.

The literature defines 'poor readers' or 'poor comprehenders' students who experience specific problems in comprehension in the face of decoding skills that are instead within the normal range [28],[29], [30]. Distinguishing poor comprehension from a reading or writing learning disability necessitates diagnostic test results. For example, dyslexia manifests as reading effort, characterized by decoding and reading difficulties, error prevalence, and fluency deficits. In contrast, poor readers and writers exhibit milder characteristics, including adequate reading speed with occasional fluency issues. Poor comprehenders' difficulties often stem from factors such as inadequate reading and writing process automation, environmental stimulation deficiencies, cognitive, memory, or attention issues, rather than neurological causes.

## 5. Architecture of ARTIS

ARTIS is an online tool designed to enhance reading comprehension skills. It comprises four distinct levels aimed at fostering a foundational understanding of language. The tool assists users in comprehending the lexical and syntactic aspects of the text, beginning with understanding sentences and progressing to words. Furthermore, the interface aids users in constructing coherent sequences and hierarchical structures within the text through ex- ercises that focus on co-reference structures. Finally, in a preliminary stage, ARTIS endeavors to develop users' ability to construct broader mental models of language by integrating textual information with their existing knowledge [31]. Subsequent sections will delve into the functionalities of each level, providing detailed insights into the underlying algorithms. The initial prototype of the interface was extensively described in [32].

## 5.1. Understanding Sentences

The interface initially presents the text at a sentence level using the Spacy Sentencizer tool 1 ., allowing users to focus on individual sentences. To aid comprehension, users can listen to the text through speech synthesis powered by the Google text-to-speech API, improving accessibility for those with reading difficulties. Keywords from each sentence are extracted and displayed using Picture Communication Symbols (PCS) on the left side of the screen, facilitating comprehension for individuals with literacy challenges. The extraction process involves using a customized version of Keybert [33] and manual verification by speech and language therapists. These keywords are linked to appropriate pictograms through the Arasaac API 2 , replacing real images to ensure suitability for vulnerable audiences.

Figure 1: Section on understanding sentences.



## 5.2. Understanding Words

In a following step, the interface offers a closer examination of the text at the word level. It displays the ten rarest words for each selected text, identified using WordFreq [34], a tool providing frequency estimates across languages. This feature aims to assist individuals with reading comprehension difficulties by addressing their hesitancy towards unfamiliar vocabulary. Upon user selection, the word's definition, along with a PCS representing its meaning and the original sentence context, is provided. Definitions, sourced from the Oxford Dictionary API 3 , are presented in both written and spoken forms through speech synthesis, enhancing accessibility.

## 5.3. Understanding Paragraphs

Based on insights from [6], a co-reference resolution algorithm was incorporated to aid users in grasping the connections between different entities and pronouns within the text. Pronouns were prioritized due to the challenges associated with their recognition. In this level of the interface, sentences are segmented, and grammatical elements such as common nouns, proper nouns, and pronouns are highlighted with distinct colors based on their Part of Speech Tags. This color-coded approach assists in immediate differentiation between elements and suggests the function of each lexical morpheme, guiding the understanding of pronouns by identifying their correct referents. Users are presented with propositions and asked to select the correct referent from four alternatives. One is accurately identified by the co-reference resolution algorithm, while two are intentionally misleading, and the fourth closely resembles the correct answer. Positive feedback is provided upon selecting the correct answer. Spacy part-of-speech tagger 4 was used for parsing, and a fine-tuned version of Coreferee 5 served as the coreference resolution algorithm.

## 5.4. A first attempt for bridging Textual Understanding with Prior Knowledge

As emphasized by [31], text comprehension extends beyond its surface-level representation. To foster deeper understanding, Synset Networks were introduced. Each selected word is presented alongside its associated Synsets from the Merriam Webster thesaurus, facilitating vocabulary expansion and recall. This approach enhances comprehension by elucidating the various meanings a term can encompass within a text and linking it with familiar words, thereby aiding in the integration of new information with existing knowledge. Through the Synset Network, users explore the interconnections of words, fostering a deeper understanding of their multifaceted meanings.

## 6. Empirical Evaluation

A pilot study was conducted at the CRC in Rome, a developmental rehabilitation center, from January to June 2023. The study involved 24 Italian-speaking children from primary 2 to 5, who were assessed using the platform under the guidance of speech therapists from the CRC. Each child had a clinical diagnosis and an updated functional profile, including IQ, language, and learning profiles. The study included children with impairments in text comprehension and language skills, particularly in receptive and expressive vocabulary not aligned with their age reference. The participants comprised children diagnosed with Specific Learning Disorder (7 subjects), Primary Language Disorder (8 subjects), Borderline Intellectual Functioning (7 subjects), and High Functioning Autism (3 subjects).

The children who participated in the feasibility study underwent standardised pre- and post-treatment evaluations, with particular attention in the post-evaluation to data on reading comprehension and language skills. The speech therapists who followed the children in the trial were also asked to fill in a questionnaire (google form) to investigate usability, functionality and the level of perceived effectiveness of ARTIS in its different components, in relation to the different pathologies, with qualitative questions structured according to a five-point likert scale (Very Little, Slightly, Sufficient, Very Much). The data collected focused on the platform usage, work area preferences, exercise types, and their correlation with different clinical profiles. The therapists' feedback regarding exercise functionality, including the need for additional support or information beyond AI-generated content, was also evaluated.

Results indicated that all participants (24 children) utilized the platform to visualize sentences and aid comprehension of selected texts. This feature included displaying relevant images corresponding to individual sentences and the option for speech synthesis reading. No supplementary material or therapist intervention was required for this aspect. Children with more significant language deficits (DPL, FIL, AUTISM) tended to use the vocabulary area (focused on words) more frequently. The inclusion of definitions accompanied by pictures proved highly beneficial. Occasionally, additional information sourced from Google searches was needed to clarify or enhance the meaning of certain words. A small subset of the sample (4 subjects diagnosed with DSA) engaged with the semantic network. Utilizing the semantic network required meta-cognitive and generalization skills, with therapist support in tasks such as image searches, reflection on different word uses, and identification of texts or phrases highlighting semantic distinctions.

The results of the pre and post-treatment evaluations show a significant increase in text comprehension and some language skills with particular reference to receptive and expressive vocabulary.

## 7. Risks and Mitigations

To ensure the development of a trustworthy AI system, extensive involvement of key stakeholders, particularly speech and language pathologists, was maintained throughout the work. Their participation ranged from the initial decision-making phases to the final evaluation of the interface, with continuous exchange of advice and feedback. Moreover, the administration of exercises always occurs under the supervision of practitioners. Before conducting clinical trials involving children, precautionary measures were taken to mitigate risks. Texts were pre-selected and categorized by school age to cater to users' individual levels. Additionally, manual clinical control was implemented to identify and rectify any potentially unsafe pictograms or misleading keywords extracted by the AI models. A stop button was integrated into the interface to prevent exposure to misleading material. Furthermore, certain functionalities, such as the semantic network, are selectively displayed based on individual needs and clinical judgment, ensuring tailored support for each user.

## 8. Conclusions &amp; Future Work

In this paper, we described the development of ARTIS, an AI-powered interface designed to enhance text comprehension in children with language and learning disorders. By leveraging neuro-psycholinguistic models and thanks to the integration of AI algorithms, ARTIS autonomously extracts keywords, associates them with pictograms, identifies complex words, generates semantic networks, and proposes exercises on grammatical components. These features aim to improving text comprehension skills in children with special educational needs by promoting inclusive hybrid speech and language therapy practices.

Looking ahead, future work could focus on several aspects. Firstly, conducting an extensive clinical evaluation is essential to assess the effectiveness of the interface in clinical settings. Additionally, we aim to integrate concept-map-based document summaries, as highlighted in [35], to enhance the bridging between knowledge present in the text read and prior knowledge.

## Audio Signal Recognition Based on Intervals' Numbers (INs) Classification Techniques

Chris Lytridis, Eleni Vrochidou, George Sidiropoulos, George Α . Papakostas, Vassilis G. Kaburlasos Human-Machines Interaction Laboratory (HUMAIN-Lab) International Hellenic University

Kavala, Greece

{ lytridic, evrochid, georsidi, gpapak, vgkabs } @teiemt.gr

Abstract -Speech  is  one  of  the  major  human-machine interaction modalities and it is especially important in the case of  special  education  using  social  robots.  Although  modern speech  recognition  engines  can  effectively  deal  with  normal human-robot  conversations,  there  are  instances  in special education where additional word detection and word comparison capabilities are needed to run in parallel with the typical conversation flow. This paper investigates the efficiency of a word detection method based on intervals' numbers.

Keywords-Speech recognition, Human-machine interaction, Intervals' numbers (IN)

## I. INTRODUCTION

Scientists in the field of socially intelligent robotics focus on developing robots capable of exhibiting natural-appearing social qualities [1]. Beyond the basic capabilities of moving and acting autonomously, social robots need to communicate with humans in a social and engaging manner. Dialogue is the main joint process of communication [2], [3]. Humans employ a variety of linguistic social cues (i.e. words or phrases that reveal sympathy, empathy, encouragement etc.) to regulate a dialogue. These cues would also be effective for controlling human-robot interaction, which is important due to the current robots' perception (e.g. speech processing) limits [4]. Thus, in order to improve the quality of human-robot interaction, it is essential for social robots to be capable of guiding a dialogue towards  specific  directions,  so  as,  for  example,  to  serve specific therapeutic intervention purposes.

Towards this end, the methodology presented in this paper is intended to serve the latter purpose; contribute towards the design of therapeutic interventions for children with learning disabilities or Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) where speech is the basic communication channel of child-robot interaction. More  specifically,  in  this  work  trigger  words  to  regulate  a conversation and guide the therapeutic activities are represented by Interval Numbers (INs). An IN is an established  mathematical  object  [5],  [6]  that  may  represent either  a  fuzzy  interval  or  a  distribution  of  numbers.  A proposed k nearest neighbor (kNN) classification scheme is adopted  to  recognize  the  trigger  words.  This  method  is especially designed to be a computationally inexpensive tool used in conjunction with the robots' build-in speech recognition engine.

The proposed technique falls into Lattice Computing (LC) paradigm.  LC  techniques  are  expected  to  be  beneficial  to human-robot interaction applications, since they can deal with both numerical and non-numerical data (e.g. verbal cues) and facilitate computations with semantics. Moreover, LC techniques  can deal with fuzzy sets,  engage  logic  and reasoning and can process data fast [7], [8].

Speech  recordings  may  result  in  big  data, therefore efficient data representation and processing are essential. The

This research has been co -financed by the European Union and Greek national funds through the Operational Program Competitiveness, Entrepreneurship and Innovation, under the call RESEARCH -CREATE

-

{ kourampa, elpis\_kar } @hotmail.com

engagement  of  INs  in  this  work  provides  significant  data reduction without losing data statistics. No prepossessing or feature extraction takes place; the INs scheme results directly from the raw data (i.e. the speech signal).

The layout of the paper is as follows: Section II briefly outlines the theoretical background of LC and INs. Section III describes  the  proposed  experimental  methods.  Section  IV presents  the  experimental  results.  Section  V  concludes  by discussing  the  contribution  of  the  paper  and  the  related upcoming work.

## II. THEORETICAL BACKGROUND

In  this  section, the  hierarchy  of lattices  from  Level-0 to Level-2, resulting to the lattice of INs [5], [6], [9] is presented.

## A. Application of INs

The  application  of  INs  to  Neural  Networks  (NNs)  and Fuzzy  Inference  Systems  (FIS)  have  been  reported  in  the literature [6], [8], [10]-[12].

In  [6],  an  LC  extension  of  a  fuzzy  neural  classifies  for human  facial  expression  recognition  was  presented.  The reported advantages of working with INs are the incremental real-time  learning  and  generalization  based  on  fuzzy  lattice reasoning (FLR) techniques. The proposed classifier performs efficiently, demonstrating the capability  of  INs to represent partially ordered non-numeric and nonstationary data (i.e. data semantics). The effectiveness of INs in demonstrated in [10]; accommodation of granular data, introduction of tunable nonlinearities and induction of descriptive decision-making knowledge  from  the  data,  are  some  of  the  additionally reported  advantages  of  INs  application  in  three  different benchmark problems. In [11] INs represent a distribution of image features for the recognition of  image patterns. An FLR classifier is developed to learn distributions of INs, and four well-known benchmark image pattern recognition applications  are  demonstrated.  In  [12]  novel  schemes  for tunable fuzzy rule interpolation and extrapolation are presented, based on INs. Preliminary application involves the reconstruction of partially occluded human facial expressions based on a NN.

In all aforementioned applications of INs, the algorithm CALCIN  is  used  for  inducing  an  IN  from  a  distribution. Despite its proven performance, CALCIN has been met with criticism because of the fact that the induced IN does not retain a  clear  statistical  interpretation.  An  extension  of  CALCIN, namely algorithm distrIN, was proposed in response, in order to provide a straightforward, statistical interpretation [8]. The pilot  application  of  distrIN  that  was  presented  in  [8],  uses electroencephalography  (EEG)  signals  with  significant  data reduction  without  losing  the  statistical  features  of  the  data. The kNN classification scheme was used to demonstrate the effectiveness  of  the  newly  proposed  technique,  resulting  in good  classification  performances  compared  to  alternative state-of-the-art methods in the literature.

## B. Lattice Hierarchy

This section presents a  hierarchy of lattices,  resulting in the lattice of INs. The analytic theory of FLR is presented in [5], [6], [11].

A lattice is a partially ordered set ( L , ⊑ ) with the property that any  two elements x,  y ∈ L have  both  a greatest lower bound (infimum) represented by x ⊓ y and a least upper bound (supremum) represented by x ⊔ y .  If  in a  lattice  ( L , ⊑ ) every pair ( x, y ) satisfies either x ⊑ y or x ⊐ y then the lattice ( L , ⊑ ) is totally-ordered. A lattice ( L , ⊑ ) is called complete if each of its  subsets X has  both an infimum and a supremum in L .  A non-void complete lattice contains both a least element and a greatest element symbolized by o and i , respectively [5].

- 1) Level-0; the lattice ( 𝑅 &amp; , ≤ ) of Real Numbers: Consider the  totally-ordered  complete  lattice  ( 𝑅 &amp; , ≤ ),  where 𝑅 &amp; = 𝑅 ∪ {-∞,+∞} with  least  and  greatest  elements -∞ and +∞ , respectively.  The  corresponding  infimum  and  supremum operations are symbolized by ˄ and ˅ , respectively.
- 2) Level-1; the lattice ( 𝐼, ⊆ ) of Type-1 intervals: Considering a1,a2 ∈ 𝑅 &amp; such that a1 ≤ a2 , a Type-1 interval A = [ a1, a2 ] is defined as [ a1, a2 ] = { x : x ∈ 𝑅 &amp; and a1 ≤ x ≤ a2 }.  The  set  of  Type-1  intervals  in 𝑅 &amp; (including  the  empty interval) is symbolized by I1. The lattice ( 𝐼 1 , ⊆ ) is a complete lattice, where ⊆ is  the  set  theoretic inclusion.  Considering two intervals A = [ a1, a2 ] and B = [ b1,b2 ] in I1 , their infimum ( ∩ ) is given by 𝐴 ∩ 𝐵 = 𝑎 1 ∨ 𝑏 1 , 𝑎 8 ∧ 𝑏 8 , if and only if 𝑎1 ∨ 𝑏1 ≤	𝑎8 ∧ 𝑏 8 , and their supremum ( ∪ ̇ ) is given by 𝐴 ∪ ̇ 𝐵 = 𝑎1 ∧ 𝑏 1 , 𝑎 8 ∨ 𝑏 8 .

Given of (1) a positive valuation function v : L à 𝑅= &gt; , and (2) a dual isomorphic function θ : L à L in lattice ( L , ≤ ), results a  positive  valuation  function v 1: L ´ L à 𝑅= &gt; in  lattice  ( L ´ L , ≥ ´ ≤ ) of generalized intervals , is given by v1 ([ a,b ])= v ( θ ( a ))+ v ( b ).  Therefore, both a metric  function 𝑑1 (. , . ) and two  fuzzy  order  functions 𝜎⊓ (. , . ) and 𝜎⊔ (. , . ) ,  can  be defined. The following three functions are available in ( Ι 1 , ⊑ ).

The  metric  function d1 : I1 ´ I1 à 𝑅= &gt; in  lattice  ( Ι 1 , ⊑ )  is calculated as follows:



The two fuzzy order functions are introduced as 𝜎⊓ (𝑥, 𝑦) = F(G⊓H) F(G) ,  namely σ -meet,  and 𝜎⊔ (𝑥, 𝑦) = F(H) F(G⊔H) , namely σ -join.

Parametric functions ν (.)  and θ (.)  can  be  selected  with various ways  and  may  introduce  tunable  nonlinearities towards optimal classification schemes.

- 3) Level-2;  The  lattice  (F1, ≤ )  of  INs: A  Generalized Intervals' Number (GIN) is defined as a function f : [0,1] à ( 𝑅 &amp; ´ 𝑅 &amp; , ≥ ´ ≤ )  where  ( 𝑅 &amp; ´ 𝑅 &amp; , ≥ ´ ≤ ) is a lattice  of generalized intervals. Assume G the set of GINs. Then, the ( G , ⊑ )  is  a  complete lattice. The interest  is  focused  to the sublattice of IN. An IN, is defined as a function F : [0,1] à I 1, which satisfies the following:
- ℎ1 ≤ ℎ8 ⇒𝐹LM ⊒ 𝐹 LO and
- ∀𝑋 ⊆ [0,1] : ⋂ L∈X 𝐹L = 𝐹 ∨Y

The set F1 of INs is a partially ordered, complete lattice, which is denoted as (F1, ≼ ). An IN is interpreted as a grain of information [5]. It has been shown that the set F1 is a metric lattice with cardinality equal to the infinity ℵ 1 of set R of the real numbers. In other words, there are so many ΙΝ s, as real numbers.

The  proposed  distrIN  algorithm  is  presented  in  Fig.1. Assume a speech signal recording as shown in Fig.1(a). All the different speech signal values of Fig.1(a) can form a set of n +1 sorted real numbers x0 &lt; x1 &lt;…&lt; xn .  i.e.  a  distribution function. An IN, equivalently, can be represented as a set of intervals Fh , h ∈ [0,1],  which  is  the  interval-representation, shown in Fig.1(b), or as a function F(x) = ∨ 𝒉∈[𝟎,𝟏] {𝒉:𝒙 ∈ 𝑭 𝒉 } ,

which is the membership-function-representation, shown in Fig.1(c).  As  expected,  audio  signals  representing  the  same spoken  word  produce  very  similar  distributions,  even  for different  speaker  voices.  However,  different  spoken  words produce audio signals which result in more varied distribution shapes,  and  are  therefore  distinguishable.  Note  that  the membership-function-representation  of  the  induced  IN  is identical to the corresponding distribution function. This is a straightforward representation with a clear statistical interpretation. An IN is represented by L intervals all having the  same end,  where only one of the intervals is trivial  by construction.  In  conclusion,  it  takes  L  real  numbers  to represent  an  IN.  An  IN  also  represents  a  distribution,  i.e. orders of magnitude more than L.

Fig. 1. Induction  of  IN F from  a  speech  signal.  (a)  the  speech  signal corresponds  to  the  recording  of    a  spoken  digit.  (b)  The  membershipfunction-representation of the induced IN F. (c) The interval-representation of IN F for L=32 cuts



## III. EXPERIMENTAL METHODS

The word classification experiments were conducted using the  spoken  digits  open  dataset  found  in  [13].  The  dataset contains 2000 recordings of English utterances of digits 'zero' to 'nine' by four speakers. The audio signals were extracted from the audio files and were converted to INs, each described by 32 cuts, as described in the previous section. This resulted in the creation of 2000 INs, i.e. 200 INs per class.

## A. Classification

For the classification tasks, the kNN classification method was employed with a 'leave-one-out' approach. This approach was selected because of its reliability, given that the amount of our training data was not prohibitively large. Table I shows how the INs are arranged for a classification task.

TABLE I. ARRANGEMENT OF INS FOR THE CLASSIFICATION TASK

|             | List of INs   | List of INs   | Label   |
|-------------|---------------|---------------|---------|
| Subject1    | IN 1,1        | IN 1,32       | ZERO    |
| ⋮           | ⋮             | ⋮             | ⋮       |
| Subject200  | IN 200,1      | IN 200,32     | ZERO    |
| ⋮           | ⋮             | ⋮             | ⋮       |
| Subject1801 | IN 1801,1     | IN 1801,32    | NINE    |
| ⋮           | ⋮             | ⋮             | ⋮       |
| Subject2000 | IN 2000,1     | IN 2000,32    | NINE    |

Initially, a subject IN is selected as the test datum, and the rest of the subjects are marked as training data. The test subject and each of the training subjects are then compared using the distance  metric  or  one  of  the  two  fuzzy  order  functions presented in the previous section. Having selected one of the three metrics, it is used to compare all of the corresponding cuts of the two INs. The mean of these per-cut comparisons, is a representation of the overall relationship between the two INs. The relationships between the test subject and the training subjects are then sorted in order to find the k INs most related to the  test  subject. The  sorting order depends on the  metric used; Training INs that are most related to the test subject are those with the shortest distance (closest to zero) but the highest fuzzy order value (closest to 1). The overall nearest neighbour is then determined using majority voting and the classes of the nearest  neighbour  and  the  test  subject  are  compared  to determine  if  classification  was  successful.  The  process  is repeated until all INs have been classified.

## B. Optimization

The classification rate depends on the parameters chosen for the parametric functions ν ( x ) and θ ( x ). For this purpose, a genetic  algorithm  has  been  implemented.  In  this  GA,  each individual is a set of ν ( x ) and θ ( x ) parameters, as well as the k value used in the kNN classifier.

An initial population of 100 individuals (sets of parameters) is generated. In each generation, every individual's set of parameters are used in a classification task as  described  above,  in  order  to  evaluate  the  parameters' performance. The performance of each individual is described by a vector D ,  which  contains the diagonal elements  of  the resulting  confusion  matrix.  The  cost C of  an  individual  is calculated  using  the  mean  of  vector D ,  subtracted  by  the optimal  performance  of  100%,  i.e. C  =  100-mean(D) .  To improve the speed of evaluation of the individuals, parallel processing techniques were employed.

Evaluation of all  individuals  results  in  a  l  ist  of  costs, used  to rank the individuals'  performance  and  genetic operations are applied. Crossover is applied in every generation  by  exchanging  random  sets  of  genes  between randomly selected individuals. Mutation is applied every five generations  by  modifying  the  values  of  randomly  selected parameters of a predefined number of individuals.

## IV. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS

The  experiments  that  were  carried  out  investigated  the classification  performance  of  the  proposed  method  for  the following sets of classes: a) three classes (spoken digits '0', '5' and '9'), b) five classes (spoken digits '0', '3', '5', '7' and '9') and c) ten classes for all spoken digits. In each case, the distance  metric  and  the  two  fuzzy  order  functions  were evaluated. In addition, the effect in performance of employing the linear and sigmoid functions, with and without parameters, as the ν ( x ) and θ ( x ) parametric functions for the calculation of the relationship between pairs of INs was also investigated.

Initially,  the  classification  experiments  were  carried  out with no parameters for the linear ( v ( x ) = x and θ ( x ) = -x ) and sigmoid ( v (x) = 1/(1 + e -x ) and θ (x) = -1/(1 + e -x )) functions.

For the kNN classifier, an arbitrary value of 4 for k was selected. The classification results for the distance metric and the  two  fuzzy  order  functions  using  the  linear  and  sigmoid functions with default parameters are presented in Table II.

TABLE II. CLASSIFICATION RESULTS WITH NO PARAMETERS

| Metric   | Parametric function   | 3 classes   | 5 classes   | 10 classes   |
|----------|-----------------------|-------------|-------------|--------------|
| Distance | Linear                | 70.5%       | 51.3%       | 34.45%       |
|          | Sigmoid               | 54.5%       | 38.8%       | 24.05%       |
| Join     | Linear                | 64.5%       | 52.7%       | 39.8%        |
| Join     | Sigmoid               | 41.83%      | 23.4%       | 16.85%       |
| Meet     | Linear                | 67.33%      | 55%         | 41.5%        |
| Meet     | Sigmoid               | 41.83%      | 23.4$       | 16.1%        |

Following  the classification results with the default parameters,  the  parameter  optimization  process  took  place. Parameters were then introduced to the parametric equations in order to create tunable distance and fuzzy order functions, which  would  alter  the  comparisons  between  the  INs,  and would in turn lead to different classification accuracies. The positions  of  the  parameters  in  the  parametric  equations  are shown in (3) and (4) for the linear type and in in (5) and (6) for the sigmoid.









For each of the six conditions (the three sets of classes and the two types of parametric functions), a GA was executed. The conditions for the GA was an initial population of 100 individuals and the duration of the algorithm was 10 generations. The classification rate for the best individual and the corresponding parameters were recorded. The classification results are shown in Table III.

| Metric   | Parametric function   | 3 classes   | 5 classes   | 10 classes   |
|----------|-----------------------|-------------|-------------|--------------|
| Distance | Linear                | 81%         | 70.7%       | 54%          |
|          | Sigmoid               | 59.66%      | 40.2%       | 25.7%        |
| Join     | Linear                | 70.16%      | 58.4%       | 43.1%        |
| Join     | Sigmoid               | 60.83%      | 36.9%       | 16.85%       |
| Meet     | Linear                | 70%         | 56.9%       | 41.7%        |
| Meet     | Sigmoid               | 53.66%      | 34%         | 18.85%       |

It can be seen from the experimental results that the use of linear  parametric  functions  is  significantly  better  than  the sigmoid for the particular classification problem. In this case the  nature  of  the  audio  signals,  is  such  that  this  type  of parametric function is more suitable for INs' comparison.

It is also evident that the GA improves the classification performance considerably. It appears that appropriate parameter selection is vital to the effectiveness of the proposed method. These results are a clear indication that more work is needed on the selection of appropriate parametric functions according to the characteristics of the original signal.

## V. DISCUSSION

The experimental results presented in this paper demonstrate the potential of the proposed methodology. The observed classification rates illustrate that spoken words can be distinguished from each other, even though there is no preprocessing  of  the  audio  signals  and  no  feature  extraction techniques are employed, which implies a reduced computational burden and a less complex algorithm. Also, the introduction of tunable non-linearities through the parametric functions v (.) and θ (.) and the subsequent use of a GA for their optimization,  leads  to  significantly  improved  performance. Another major advantage of the method is the compression achieved without the loss of data statistics.  The  main disadvantage of INs is the loss of the time dimension. Future work will consider the preservation of the time dimension by computing INs per time-windows for a time series, as well as and the use of other classification schemes.

The  methodology  presented  in  this  paper  is  intended  to contribute towards the design of therapeutic interventions for children with certain types of learning disabilities and children with ASD as part of the national project titled 'Social Robots as Tools in Special Education', where speech will be a vital component of child-robot interaction. This method is aimed to be  a  computationally  inexpensive  tool  used  in  conjunction with the robots' built-in speech recognition engine to recognize trigger words, as well as a detection mechanism for speech  sound  errors  observed  in  children  with  learning disabilities. The generalization properties of the method allow the investigation of such varied tasks that will be pursued for the purposes of the project.
