## Paper Source: Interactive Multimodal Learning Towards Using Pedagogical Agents for Inclusive Education
============================================================

## Interactive Multimodal Learning: Towards Using Pedagogical Agents for Inclusive Education

Muhammad H. Al Omoush Faculty of Engineering and Computing Dublin City University Dublin, Ireland muhammad.menazelalomoush2@mail.dcu.ie Sumaia E. Salih Independent researcher Dublin, Ireland sumaiasalih@outlook.com Tracey Mehigan Faculty of Engineering and Computing Dublin City University Dublin, Ireland tracey.mehigan@dcu.ie

Abstract - A pedagogical agent is an animated interface in an interactive online learning environment. Its role involves guiding users through instructions and participating in direct discussions. Numerous research studies underline the advantages of pedagogical  agents  in  delivering  instruction,  tailoring  learning experiences, and promoting inclusivity. The authors utilize machine learning techniques to develop an interactive multimodal application (combining visuals and audio) designed as a pedagogical agent. This application is intended to assist in teaching primary school students (aged 6 to 8) the recognition of colors and letters.  Additionally,  it  incorporates  voice  interaction  to  assess their learning progress. The overarching objective of this pedagogical agent is to seamlessly integrate artificial intelligence (AI) into educational settings, thereby amplifying student engagement  and  motivation  during  the  learning  process.  This paper  will  explore  the  journey  of  creating  a  machine  learningbased application and its potential utility in supporting educators. Furthermore, the authors will investigate potential augmentations that could render the application more adept at aiding students with dyslexia. The paper will emphasize the significance of humancomputer interaction (HCI), as it significantly shapes pedagogical agents' design and operational aspects.

KeywordsHuman-Computer Interaction HCI, Inclusive education, machine learning, multimodal pedagogical agent, sensory disability, Graphical User Interface (GUI).

## I. INTRODUCTION AND BACKGROUND

Research  studies  underscore  the  critical  significance  of integrating technology in classrooms to enhance student engagement and personalized  learning  [1,  2,  3,  4].  Educators now  have various technological tools aiding students in comprehending subjects. Incorporating diverse learning techniques promotes the potential for all students to grasp the educational content [5, 6, 7].

Challenges faced by students in classrooms, such as learning disabilities (dyslexia) and ADHD [8], along with motivation and engagement  issues  [9],  can  impact  academic  performance. Tailoring educational content to meet individual learner needs fosters motivation, leading to improved learning outcomes. This personalized approach enhances material engagement, maintaining retention and understanding [10]. Addressing these challenges and catering to varying learning preferences remains a substantial 21 st century educational challenge [11]. Cultivating an  inclusive  classroom  accommodating  all  students'  needs promotes  their  success  and  well-being,  ensuring  equitable learning opportunities.

STEM  education  (science,  technology,  engineering,  and mathematics)  is  pivotal.  It  cultivates critical  thinking  and problem-solving, which are imperative for today's society [12, 13].  Educational  institutions  must  prioritize  STEM  programs and  resources  to  prepare  students  for  future  careers,  enabling access to high-quality STEM education.

This  paper  introduces  a  machine  learning  application,  a pedagogical agent, aiding students in learning colors and letters while  acting  as  a  teaching  assistant  for  inclusive  instruction. Developed using PyTorch and a feedforward neural network, the  application  initially  classifies  letters  (A  to  Z)  and  colors (blue,  green,  orange,  red,  violet,  yellow).  A  voice  interaction component  facilitates  visual  and  audio  communication.  The ML-based pedagogical agent offers alternative learning methods and support for all students.

## A. The Evolution of Pedagogical Agents

The concept of pedagogical agents originated in the 1970s with the emergence of Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS), aimed at emulating  human  tutors  in addressing student queries, identifying misconceptions, and providing feedback [14]. Over the  last  two  decades,  the  prominence  of  pedagogical  agent research  has  steadily  increased  [15],  with  a  notable  surge  in development between 1998 and 2000 [16]. These agents have demonstrated their capacity to adapt to individual learning paths and  accommodate  distinct  needs  [17].  Pedagogical  agents manifest in various forms: text-based, voice-based, 2-D character-based,  3-D  character-based,  and  even  human-like representations. Progress in human-computer interface technology has created more authentic and human-resembling instructional agents [18].

## II. VISION HUMAN-COMPUTER INTERACTION (HCI) AND ITS CRUCIAL ROLE IN SHAPING INCLUSIVE PEDAGOGICAL AGENTS

Human-Computer Interaction is centered around optimizing interactive  computer  systems'  user  experience  and  interface [19].  The  goal  is  to  design  user  systems  that  are  effective,

Sameer Kishore Department  of Computer Engineering and Informatics Middlesex University Dubai, UAE s.kishore@mdx.ac.ae efficient, easy to use, and enjoyable. In the context of pedagogical  agents,  HCI  supports  personalizing  and  adapting learning experiences. This leads to individualized learning paths for learners based on their interests, preferences, and learning styles.  Consequently,  learners  benefit  from  a  customized  and practical learning experience. Real-time feedback and assessments  from  pedagogical  agents  allow  learners  to  track their progress and receive immediate guidance.

A pedagogical agent's user interface encompasses visual and auditory  elements,  including  the  agent's  appearance,  voice, animations, and interactive components like buttons, menus, and dialogue boxes [21]. Designing the user interface adheres to HCI principles like stability, accessibility, and  flexibility.  This ensures effective interaction between  learners and  agents, enabling learners to leverage the agent's instructional support.

Within pedagogical agents' architecture,  HCI  plays  a  vital role in interactions between humans and computer systems. It encompasses design, usability, and digital interface effectiveness [19]. Pedagogical agents have emerged as tools for inclusive education, supporting diverse learners, including those with disabilities [20]. The  connection between HCI  and pedagogical  agents  lies  in  designing  accessible  and  effective agents for all learners, regardless of abilities. Designing interfaces for pedagogical agents considers visual and auditory accessibility, navigation, and interaction options [21] to accommodate learners with disabilities [22]. Usability, responsiveness, adaptability, and ease of use are crucial for an inclusive learning experience.

HCI's role in shaping pedagogical agent design is pivotal for inclusive  education.  It  ensures  usability  and  accessibility  for diverse  learners,  including  those  with  sensory  or  learning disabilities.  HCI  incorporates  emotional  affect  and  cognitive processing in user interactions [23]. Pedagogical agent design aligns with HCI considerations, resulting in more effective and user-friendly systems that cater to diverse cognitive and emotional  states.  This  holistic  approach  creates  pedagogical agents capable of delivering engaging and personalized learning experiences, ultimately enhancing user learning outcomes.

## A. Text-to-speech (TTS) and Pedagogical Agents

Text-to-speech vocalizers, or speech synthesizers, are computer systems that generate human-like speech by converting text into spoken words [22, 24, 25, 26]. They provide voices  and  personalities  to  artificial  agents,  virtual  assistants, and robots. Text-to-speech vocalizers have also brought innovative  advancements  in  education  [24].  Text-to-speech technology  has  been  shown  to  facilitate  language  learning, particularly in improving speaking and pronunciation skills [22, 27]. It allows the users to customize the speech output's pace, pitch, and volume to align with their preferences and requirements, which helps learners who may be facing difficulties  listening  to  their  own  words  during  the  writing process.  This,  in  turn,  helps  them  monitor  and  revise  their writing outcomes.

Engaging  with  a  pedagogical  agent  using  text-to-speech technology can benefit students with learning disabilities such as dyslexia, who may struggle with reading and writing [22] and often  experience  challenges  with  memory  retention  [28].  Our machine  learning-based  pedagogical  agent  employs  text-tospeech  vocalizers  (synthesizers)  to  assist  students  in  their educational  journey. It integrates multi-sensory instruction (audio  and  visual),  personalized  learning  (helping  students enhance their auditory verbal memory), and supportive feedback. This integration aims to benefit students in overcoming challenges and achieving academic success. This approach makes education more accessible and inclusive.

Technological  progress  has  enhanced  the  communication abilities of pedagogical agents when interacting with students [29]. These agents, used in educational settings, have become more sophisticated in their communication skills due to technological  advancements.  However,  as  pedagogical  agents continue to increase in learning environments, it is important to gain a deeper understanding of how students communicate with these agents to evaluate their effectiveness in facilitating learning [30,31].

## III. PEDAGOGICAL AGENTS: BENEFITS FOR STUDENTS LEARNING AND MOTIVATION

Pedagogical  agents  have  been  found  to  offer  significant benefits  to  students,  including  facilitating  collaboration  and providing feedback as students engage in the learning process. These  agents  can  communicate  with  students  using  various methods, such as facial expressions, natural language, and hand gestures, which enhances the interactive and engaging nature of the learning experience [21].

## A. Empowering Learning Through Interactive Pedagogical Agents

Pedagogical  agents  have  significantly  impacted  students' motivation to study. Students tend to place a higher level of trust and confidence in the information these agents provide than in information  provided  by  traditional  teachers.  This  can  be attributed to the interactive and dynamic nature of the agents, which  students  find  appealing  and  engaging  [21].  Overall, pedagogical  agents  can  transform  how  students  learn  and interact with learning material, enhancing  motivation and engagement in the learning process.

## B. Exploring Multisensory Approaches for Enhanced Learning and Engagement

The possibilities  of  multimodal  pedagogical  agents  in  the teaching  and  learning  process  have  been  recently  explored, especially for students with learning disabilities [15]. Dyslexia is  a  learning  disability  that  can  significantly  impact  students' educational experiences. In response to these challenges, researchers have explored multimodal  applications,  which integrate different modes of information, such as text, audio, and visual features. Incorporating multi-sensory technology in education  offers  numerous  advantages,  including  increased student engagement and improved learning outcomes [32].

Artificial intelligence has been integrated and brought into action in education, promoting advancements in several areas. Intelligent  educational  systems  offer  teachers  and  students timely, personalized guidance and feedback [33]. Visual feedback has traditionally been the norm for providing information to users in computer interfaces. However, incorporating  other  sensory  modalities,  such  as  audio,  can enhance user experience and provide new ways of engagement for different user groups in diverse environments [34].

Having multiple modalities in a user interface has the benefit of  spreading  the  interaction  across  various  senses  or  control abilities  of  the  user.  If  one  modality  is  not  available  or  fully utilized, another can be employed to ensure successful interaction,  especially  for  those  with  sensory  or  situational impairments [34, 35]. At the same time, a study showed that preschoolers  at  risk  of  dyslexia  improved  various  pre-reading skills,  such  as  phonological  awareness,  after  practicing  these skills on multimedia intervention software on a computer device [36].

Pedagogical agents with interactive and multimodal features increase students' vocabulary acquisition with various learning needs  [37,  38,39].  These  multimodal  applications  incorporate audio and visual features and can be powerful tools for teaching dyslexic  students  [40].  This  approach  enables  all  students  to learn  through  different  sensory  modalities,  providing  a  more engaging and accessible education experience.

## IV. THE ML-BASED PEDAGOGICAL AGENT

The  authors  have  developed  a  cutting-edge  educational agent  that  employs  computer  vision  to  enhance  interactive learning for young students, specifically focusing on letters and colors. This agent seamlessly incorporates visual and auditory cues,  cultivating  a  seamless  communication  channel  between users and the system. The project was developed in three stages: creating  a  neural  network  classifier  for  letters,  implementing color recognition, and adding voice interaction using Python's text-to-speech library. These  stages converge  to offer an engaging, multisensory learning experience. The agent's merging  of  technology  and  pedagogy  benefits  learners  and opens routes for future educational innovations, demonstrating the transformative potential of interactive technology in education.

The implications of this pedagogical agent extend beyond the  direct  learning  process.  The  agent  accommodates  diverse learning  styles  and  abilities  by  combining  visual  and  audio elements, fostering inclusivity in education.

## A.  Material and Methods

The  pedagogical  agent  was  constructed  using  Machine Learning (ML). The ML application was built using the PyTorch framework and the feedforward neural network. PyTorch is an efficient deep-learning tensor library built on Torch and Python, enabling real-time testing and execution [41].

A dataset is a collection of various kinds of data that have been  digitally  preserved.  Any  project  using  machine  learning needs  data  as  its  primary  input.  For  addressing  various  A.I. difficulties, datasets often include photos, texts, audio, videos, and numerical data points [42].

Neural networks are computerized structures with interconnected nodes that mimic the function of brain neurons. They  can  cluster  and  categorize  raw  data  using  algorithms, identify  hidden  patterns  and  correlations,  and  -  with  time  continually  learn  and  improve  [43].  A  feedforward  neural network is an artificial neural network in which nodes' connections do not form a loop. Because all information flows forward  in  feedforward  neural  networks,  they  are  sometimes referred to as a multi-layered network of neurons [44, 45].

## B.  Letter Classification

When  employing  PyTorch  for  machine  learning  model training, the subsequent actions were executed: dataset preparation, establishment of data loaders, construction of the machine learning model, specification of the loss function and optimizer, and ultimately, model training.

## (a) Preparing the Letters Dataset

The dataset of letters was sourced from Kaggle and consisted of 26 classes, each representing a letter of the English alphabet. There were approximately 52 images available for each letter. However,  it  was  necessary  to  expand  the  dataset  further  to ensure  practical  model  training.  Various  data  augmentation techniques were applied to achieve this, artificially increasing the dataset's size, and improving the model's learning process.

The dataset was then divided into two subsets: a training and validation  set.  Specifically,  80%  of  the  dataset  was  used  for training, while the remaining 20% was set aside for testing and validation purposes.

## (b) Creating the Data Loader

To  ensure  adequate  training  of  a  neural  network,  it  is essential to input data in batches, typically comprising 32 or 64 batches, each consisting of multiple images. This approach of using batches is employed to optimize the training process by reducing the time needed for adjusting parameters. If the neural network were trained on a per-image basis, where parameters are  updated  for  each  image  individually,  it  could  lead  to inconsistent parameter adjustments and sluggish generalization.

However, the  training  process  becomes  more  reliable  and efficient when the neural network is evaluated on a batch of 32 images. Parameters are adjusted based on the collective information from the entire batch. A well-known deep learning framework, PyTorch, includes a built-in feature called "DataLoader"  that  facilitates  the  organization  of  images  into batches. The DataLoader automatically shuffles images, ensuring the selection of batches is random. This randomness guarantees a diverse and representative sample for training.

The  utilization of batch-based training offers benefits beyond just speeding up the process. It also enhances the neural network's  overall  performance  and  ability  to  generalize.  By allowing the network to learn from multiple images simultaneously, it captures underlying patterns and data structures  more  effectively,  thus  improving  its  generalization capability.

## (c) Creating the Machine Learning Model

The utilized model in this research was constructed using a feedforward neural network architecture, representing a straightforward  yet  exceptionally  efficient  design  approach  to attain favorable results. The input image, possessing dimensions of 28x28 pixels, undergoes a process of flattening into a column vector comprising 784 individual elements. Within the feedforward  structure,  each  distinct  class  is  associated  with  a concealed layer with a dimension of 512 and an output layer with a capacity of 26 units.

## (d) Training the Model

The  model  learns  by  using  data  from  the  Data-Loader, checking its output against what is expected, and calculating a loss.  Then,  we  see  how  accurate  the  model is  using test data. These are the main steps in training the model.

## C. Color Classification

The dataset used in this study came from Kaggle and had six color categories: Green, Blue, Orange, Red, Violet, and Yellow. Each category had around 25 images. We divided the dataset into 80% for training and 20% for model testing.

To figure out the colors in the images, we used a mix of two techniques: k-means clustering and measuring color differences. We applied the k-means algorithm to find the primary colors in each  image.  We  then  transformed  this  primary  color  into  its HSV (Hue, Saturation, Value) form.

## D. Speech Recognition

A voice interaction functionality was developed to facilitate "communication" with the software, utilizing a combination of a TTS (text-to-speech) library and a speech recognition library referred  to  as  STT  (speech-to-text).  In  Python,  a  convenient module called pyttsx3 was employed for text-to-speech conversion. This module stands out due to its compatibility with both Python 2 and 3 and its offline capabilities, distinguishing it from  alternative  libraries.  This  user-friendly  tool  enables  the transformation  of  written  text  into  spoken  words  and  offers support for two distinct voices (male and female) made available through the "sapi5" interface on Windows [46].

## V. EXECUTING THE MACHINE LEARNING MODEL

To enhance functionality and user experience, the machine learning application was divided into two modes: 'Vision Only Mode' and 'Voice Interaction Mode.' Before  commencing  the recognition  process,  users  must  indicate  their  chosen  model preference as shown in Figure 1.

Fig. 1. Within the user interface, individuals have the choice to opt for either visual mode (option 1) or voice interaction mode (option 2).



## A. Engaging Voice Interaction Mode

Upon  enabling  the  voice  interaction  feature  (depicted  in Figure  3),  the  user  is  required  to  subsequently  designate  the appropriate microphone (device microphone) from the provided list of available devices.

## B. Executing Letter Recognition Process

In the 'vision only' mode, the camera initiates the recognition process, promptly displaying the identified letter in real-time at the upper-left corner of the screen (as depicted in Figure 2). The system audibly announces the recognized letter, offering immediate feedback to the user.

Upon engaging in the 'voice interaction' mode, the user is directed  to  select  the  appropriate  microphone  to  optimize  the recognition  process.  Once  a  letter  is  presented  before  the camera, the recognition process begins, operating briefly. Upon completion, the system promptly notifies the user of the end of recognition, facilitating their progression to the next step.

To  initiate letter recognition, the  user  is  prompted  to articulate  a  word  commencing  with  the  letter  they  provided earlier. For instance, if the user displays the letter 'H' before the camera,  they  must  utter  a  word  that  starts  with  the  letter  'H.' Following this, the system delivers feedback by affirming 'the word is matching' for correct responses or indicating 'the letter is not matching' for incorrect ones.

Fig. 2. Using the vision-only interaction mode for letter recognition.



## C. Executing Colour Recognition Process

The  application's  color  recognition  and  voice  interaction procedures are congruent with the steps mentioned above. The sole distinction lies in the 'voice interaction' mode as shown in Figure 3, wherein the system prompts the user to articulate the color they have presented for verbal recognition verbally.

Fig. 3. Using the Voice interaction mode for color recognition (the color's name can be seen in the top right corner).



## VI. EVALUATING SYSTEM FUNCTIONALITY: A COMPREHENSIVE EXAMINATION

During the training phase of the letter classification model, 26 classes representing each letter of the alphabet were utilized. This dataset comprised approximately 52 images per class. The data was partitioned, allocating 80% for training and 20% for testing. A batch size of 32 and 5 epochs were employed for the validation set. However, upon conducting tests, it was observed that  the  program  encountered  difficulties  recognizing  certain letters, specifically B, C, D, E, K, O, R, and S.

This issue may stem from the dataset's size, as insufficient data  can  lead  to  overfitting.  Overfitting  can  yield  impressive results during training, but the model  might struggle to generalize  or  demonstrate  robust  recognition  when  presented with new data. To avoid such problems and ensure dependable model  performance,  working  with  a  sufficiently  extensive dataset is  imperative.  Notably, the testing and training phases yielded  an  accuracy  of  around  98%.  Exploring  alternative optimization techniques could be considered for future endeavors to enhance accuracy.

Various  testing  scenarios  were  executed  to  evaluate  the system's  accuracy.  The  first  scenario,  described  in  Table  1, involved  assessing  the  program's  vision  component  using  a laptop camera. Testing encompassed letter and color recognition against a white background  with  standard  room  lighting. Optimal outcomes were achieved in this scenario. In contrast, the least favorable results were obtained when testing against a vividly colored background in a dimly lit room.

Table  2  presents  the  outcomes  of  system  testing  in  voice interaction  for  letter  and  color  recognition.  Notably,  higher accuracy was attained when the system was assessed in a quiet environment, and the user maintained a proximity of less than 50 cm from the laptop.

The system displayed its highest recognition accuracy when a white background was employed for color and letter recognition, particularly in a quiet room. However, recognition accuracy notably declined when the software was deployed in noisy surroundings featuring varied colors and ambient noise.

Maintaining an ongoing process of detecting and identifying letters  and  colors  posed  a  difficulty  in  system  testing.  As  a solution,  it  is  advisable  to  enhance  the  system  by  capturing  a screenshot of the letter/color prior to commencing the recognition process rather than depending solely on continuous camera detection. Upgrading to superior hardware is recommended to improve detection accuracy and voice interactions.  Introducing  a  high-quality  microphone  for  voice interactions can expedite user comprehension, thereby reducing occurrences of misinterpreting spoken words.

TABLE 1: System testing for the letters and colors using the vision-only mode.

| Testing type                        | Letters           | Colors                       |
|-------------------------------------|-------------------|------------------------------|
| With room lighting                  | 80 %pass 20 %fail | All pass                     |
| Decreasing the room lighting        | 67 %pass 33 %fail | All pass except blue, green  |
| Using a white background            | 85 %pass 15 %fail | All pass                     |
| Using a noisy - colorful background | 57 %pass 43 %fail | All pass, except blue, green |

TABLE 2: System testing for voice interaction.

| Testing type                                                      | Results                                                      |
|-------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|
| In a quiet room                                                   | The system works fine.                                       |
| In a noisy room - classroom                                       | The microphone can't hear the voice, and the speaker is low. |
| Sitting close (less than 50 cm from the laptop) to the microphone | The system works fine.                                       |
| Sitting far (more than 50 cmfromthe laptop).                      | The microphone can't hear well. Misinterprets the words.     |

VII. ENHANCING  INCLUSION:  FUTURE  DEVELOPMENTS  FOR THE PEDAGOGICAL AGENT

The  challenges  encountered  by students with learning disability  in  acquiring  letter  and  color  knowledge  can  be effectively  addressed  by  integrating  sensory  components  into the  existing  application.  These  enhancements  include  audioguided  instructions  and  voice-based  interactions,  facilitating letter  recognition  and  auditory-verbal  memory  for  dyslexic learners. Furthermore, these attributes deliver immediate feedback and positive reinforcement for accurate responses, thus maintaining learning outcomes and motivation for all learners.

Several tools and technologies can be integrated further to enhance  the  Machine  Learning-based  Pedagogical  Agent  for inclusive education. Specifically tailored to the needs of dyslexic students, the application's user interface can be designed to accommodate dyslexia-friendly fonts, suitable color contrasts,  and  distinct  visual  cues  that  facilitate  reading  and comprehension.  Embracing  a  phonics-centered  methodology, emphasizing the correlation between letters and sounds can be particularly advantageous for dyslexic students grappling with phonological  processing  difficulties.  Additionally,  integrating letter  contour  highlighting  and  color-coded  letter  systems  can contribute to more efficient letter recognition and differentiation among dyslexic students.

The future trajectory of the Machine Learning-based Pedagogical Agent is decidedly promising, marked by ongoing technological and research advancements. Continued progress in  hardware  and  software  domains  augments  the  pedagogical agent's precision, speed, and user-friendliness.

## VIII. CONCLUSION

The  main  objective  was  to  develop  a  pedagogical  agent using machine learning that can be seamlessly integrated into the  field  of  education  to perform  advanced  image recognition and  effectively  distinguish  between  letters  and  colors.  By leveraging  the  power  of  artificial  intelligence  (AI)  in  the classroom, this project holds immense significance as it has the potential  to  revolutionize  traditional  teaching  methods  and inspire  educators  to  adopt  innovative  techniques  to  improve student  learning  outcomes.  With  the  developed  application, teachers  can  now  utilize  a  sophisticated  tool  to  evaluate  the learning  progress  of  students  aged  6  to  8  more  precisely  and efficiently.  However,  as  with  any  innovative  project,  there  is always room for improvement and further development. Several potential  modifications  could  be  considered  to  enhance  the application's capabilities and expand its potential in the field of education. Firstly, instead of students holding the letter or color in  front  of  the  camera  for  recognition,  the  system  could  be modified to prompt students to present a specific color or letter. This would add an interactive element to the process, encouraging students to actively engage with the application and participate  in  the  learning  process,  thereby  fostering  a  more dynamic  and  immersive  educational  experience.  Secondly,  to optimize  the  application  processing  overhead,  the  continuous recognition approach could be refined by capturing a screenshot and performing recognition only when the letter or color is in front  of  the  camera.  This  will  ensure  smooth  and  efficient operation during classroom activities.

To broaden the application's language recognition capabilities, it could be enhanced to read complete words instead of just individual letters. This would enable teachers to assess students'  language  skills  more  comprehensively  and  provide feedback  on  their  word  recognition  abilities,  thus  facilitating language development. By incorporating these potential modifications,  the  application  could  be  further  refined  and extended to unlock new possibilities in the field of education. With continuous improvements and advancements, this project has  the  potential  to  impact  how  teachers  teach,  and  students learn,  paving  the  way  for  a  more  innovative  and  effective educational environment.

The simplicity of this machine learning (ML) application sets  it  apart  from  other  research  in  the  field,  as  it  has  been designed  explicitly  with  elementary  students  in  mind.  This consideration is crucial, ensuring the software is user-friendly and  accessible  to  young  learners.  The  software  has  been developed to be easily compatible with Raspberry Pi, making it simple  to  operate  on  any  humanoid  robot  with  a  camera, microphone,  speaker,  and  Raspberry  Pi.  The  ease  of  use  and compatibility  of  this  software  make  it  a  viable  option  for integration  into  classrooms,  where  it  has  the  potential to motivate  teachers  to  explore  and  apply  different  methods  to enhance students' learning experiences. The software's adaptability to different hardware  configurations, such as Raspberry  Pi,  ensures  that  it  can  seamlessly  integrate  into classroom setups without requiring significant modifications or investments in specialized equipment.

As  a  future  improvement,  adding  a  Graphical  User Interface (GUI) could further enhance the user experience of the software. Including a GUI would allow users to interact with the software  through  visual  elements  on  the  screen,  providing  a more intuitive and user-friendly interface for choosing between camera and voice interaction options. For instance, users could click on the screen to select their preferred option rather than using the keyboard to input numerical choices (1 for camera, 2 for  voice  interaction).  Implementing  a  GUI  could  make  the software even more accessible and user-friendly, especially for young  students  who  may  be  more  familiar  with  graphical interfaces. By incorporating a GUI, the software could provide users  a  seamless  and  interactive  experience,  enhancing  their engagement and making the learning process  more  enjoyable and effective. The potential addition of a GUI in future iterations could further enhance the software's usability and userfriendliness, motivating teachers to explore innovative methods for enhancing students' learning experiences. With continuous improvements and refinements, this software has the potential to contribute to the advancement of education by incorporating ML technology in a simple and accessible manner.

## LexiEase AI : An AI Powered Dyslexic Support System

Sheetal Phatangare Department of Computer Engineering Vishwakarma Institute of Technology Pune, India Email -sheetal.phatangare@vit.edu Sneha Jain Department of Computer Engineering Vishwakarma Institute of Technology Pune, India Email -sneha.jain221@vit.edu

Shrey Chougule Department of Computer Engineering Vishwakarma Institute of Technology Pune, India Email -arjun.shrey22@vit.edu

Abstract -The development of an intelligent, dyslexia-specific support  system  is  the  need  of  the  hour  to  ensure  inclusion  and personalization. The work presents an artificial intelligence-driven system, which involves state-of-the-art machine learning and NLP techniques,  for  identifying  and  assisting  dyslexics.  Our  system encompasses  a  broad  range  of  dyslexia  screening  tests,  such  as phonological awareness tests, memory tests, and oral reading, for which  dyslexics  may  be  tested  using  state-of-the-art  models  like DistilBERT and DeepSpeech. A Random Forest classifier generates certain dyslexia score to classify the severity levels  and  give customized  learning  pathways.  The  system  will  also  integrate document simplification, mind map generation, and writing assistance features in order to make it holistic.

Keywords - DeepSpeech, DistilBERT, Personalized Learning,, Document Simplification, Mind Map Generation, Writing Assistance.

## I. INTRODUCTION

Dyslexia  is  a  common  learning  disability  that  makes  it  very hard for people to acquire basic literacy skills, hence affecting their performance at school and in everyday life. While most traditional  methods  of  addressing  dyslexia  focus  on  generic strategies,  the  growing  need  has  been  for  personalized  and technology-driven  solutions.  Recent  developments  in  AI  and NLP have opened new avenues for creating tailored  support systems to address this gap.

This  work  proposes  a  new  AI-enabled  system  for  screening, assessing, and supporting dyslexia. Our approach encompasses  the  integration  of  state-of-the-art  AI  models: DistilBERT for semantic analysis and DeepSpeech for speech recognition, thus allowing speedy and accurate assessments of dyslexia.  The  system  shall  carry  out  three  major  tests  to constitute the screening, namely  phonological awareness, memory  evaluation,  and  oral  reading  fluency -all  analyzing different aspects of cognitive ability. From these results, based Siddhartha Chakrabarty Department of Computer Engineering Vishwakarma Institute of Technology Pune, India Email-siddhartha.chakrabarty22@vit.edu Somrath Bisen Department of Computer Engineering Vishwakarma Institute of Technology Pune, India Email -bisen.somrath22@vit.edu on  the  Random  Forest  that  gives  the  degree  of  dyslexia, suggestions on strategies for learning are made.

The system goes beyond diagnostics to constitute a bundle of tools for learning and engagement, such as document summarization  with  AI-driven  simplification,  the  generation of  mind  maps  in  an  interactive  way,  and  a  dynamic  writing assistant  also  powered  by  AI.  This  will  improve  both  your comprehension and productivity as a dyslexic.

## II. LITERATURE REVIEW

Di Fraia,  G.  [1]  The  paper  introduces  DSAi,  an  AI-powered platform designed to support students with Specific Learning Disorders  (SLDs)  by  enhancing  inclusion,  accessibility,  and innovation in education.

Goodman,  S.  M.,  Buehler,  E.  [2]  The  research  presents LaMPost, an AI-powered  email-writing tool using large language  models  to  assist  adults  with  dyslexia  by  providing features like rewriting, summarizing main ideas, and generating subject lines.

Iyer, L. S., Chakraborty. [3] The paper explores the application of AI-assisted language learning models to support children with dyslexia and dysgraphia, enhancing their reading and  writing  skills  through  personalized,  adaptive  learning experiences.

Goodman,  S.  M.,  Buehler.[4]  The  research  paper  introduces LaMPost, an AI-assisted email writing prototype designed to support  adults  with  dyslexia  by  offering  features  such  as outlining main ideas, generating subject lines, and suggesting changes.

Wu,  S., Reynolds. [5] The research paper presents the Additional  Writing  Help  (AWH)  tool,  designed  to  assist individuals  with  dyslexia  in  writing  on  social  media  by providing tailored spelling and grammar suggestions through a neural machine translation model.

Dabaghi,  K.,  D'Urso.  [6]  The  research  paper  discusses  the implementation  of  AI-based  tools  to  enhance  learning  for students  with  dyslexia,  focusing  on  their  effectiveness  in improving reading and writing skills.

Gilbert, B., Stubblefield, J. [7] The research paper explores the use of artificial intelligence to develop a novel font aimed at improving reading abilities in individuals with dyslexia, based on performance data collected from various fonts.

Alghabban, W. G., Salama. [8] The research paper presents a multimodal  interface  tool  developed  on  cloud  computing technology to support students with dyslexia, utilizing audio, text, and images to enhance learning.

Rodríguez-Cano, S.,  Delgado-Benito.  [9]  The  research  paper details  the  design  of  a  virtual  reality  application  aimed  at improving the educational experiences of students with dyslexia, focusing on user-centered design principles.

Maresca, G., Leonardi, S. [10] The research paper investigates the  relationship  between dyslexia and visuo-spatial attention, proposing that deficits in visual attention contribute to reading difficulties in dyslexic individuals.

Spoon,  K.,  Siek,  K.,  Crandall,  D.  [11]  The  research  paper explores the use of AI to detect dyslexia in children's handwriting, demonstrating that machine learning models can identify  handwriting  features  indicative  of  dyslexia  with  a notable accuracy of 77.6%.

Alkhurayyif,  Y.,  &amp;  Sait,  A.  R.  W.  [12]  The  research  paper highlights the effectiveness of models like CNNs and SVMs in classifying dyslexic and non-dyslexic individuals.

Isa, I. S., Rahimi, W. N. S. [13] The research paper examines the  use  of  technology  to  assist  children  with  dyslexia  in reading,  focusing  on  various  digital  tools  and  interventions that enhance literacy skills.

Al-Barhamtoshy, H. M., &amp; Motaweh, D. M. [14] The research paper  presents  a  framework  for  diagnosing  dyslexia  using computational  analysis  techniques,  implementing  classifiers such  as  K-means,  ANN,  and  Fuzzy  to  categorize  children's reading and cognitive metrics.

Rekha, S., Gollapudi, S., Sampath, H., &amp; Indurkhya, B. [15] The research paper introduces the Read-Aid tool, an assistive technology designed to improve reading skills in children with dyslexia by utilizing a masked-text technique.

## III. METHODOLOGY/EXPERIMENTAL

## 1. Development of Dyslexia Screening Tests

Our  project  entails  three  dyslexia  screening  tests utilizing LLM based on their learning capabilities.

## Phonological Awareness Test

- Multiple words  are initially generated using DistilBERT's Text to Text model.
- The words are segregated into easy, medium and hard categories and stored in MySQL.
- The words are converted to audio using Google's Text to Speech API and are provided to the user.
- The screenshot  of  the  whiteboard  on  which  the word  is  written  is  taken  and  then  the  word  is extracted using Optical Character Recognition.
- DistilBERT's Similarity Analysis is then done to generate a similarity score.

Fig 1. Phonological Awareness Test



## Kauffman Assessment Battery Test

- Memory  sequences  are  created  using  words, images and audios.
- Words - DistilBERT Text to Text model
- Images - Stable Diffusion Text to Image model
- Audio - DeepSpeech Text to Audio model.
- The sequences are provided to the user for a 10 second duration to memorize it.
- Score is based on the recreation of the same.

Fig 2. Kauffman Assessment Battery Test



## Gray Oral Reading Test

- Passages are generated using DistilBERT's text -to-text model.
- Divided into easy, medium &amp; hard categories.
- The passages are provided to user for reading.

- The user audio is recorded using the MediaRecorder API.
- Fluency analysis is performed on the audio files using DeepSpeech audio to text model.
- The time taken, reading speed and a score based on the fluency is provided to the user.

Fig 3. Gray Oral Reading Test



## Score Generation

Dyslexic score is used to provide personalized learning paths which is calculated using a Random Forest model applied on the scores of the three tests.

## 2. Personalized Learning Path:

The personalized learning path is as follows:

Table 1. Personalized Learning Paths

| Severity   | Dyslexic Score   | Feature Provided                                                               |
|------------|------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Easy       | <50%             | Reading passages& comprehensions                                               |
| Medium     | 50% - 75%        | Reading passages, comprehensions &memory games                                 |
| Hard       | >75%             | Reading passages, comprehensions, memory games& phonological improvement games |

Fig 4. Personalized Learning Paths



## Reading Passages

- Passages are generated using DistilBERT's model.
- Supporting audio for the passages are generated using WaveNet's Text to Audio model.
- The  meaning  of  the  words  are  provided  to  the users by the Dictionary API.
- The option to listen to each individual sentence in  a  multitude  of  speeds  and voices  is  provided to the user using the WebSpeech API.
- U ser's audio is recorded by MediaRecorder API.
- DeepSpeech performs the fluency analysis.
- The time taken and reading speed are calculated.

Fig 5. Reading Passages



## Reading Comprehensions

- Custom  Comprehensions  are  generated  for  the user  using  DistilBERT's  Text  to  Text  model. The comprehensions are then again sent as input to  the  LLM  and  suitable  questions  relevant  for the comprehension are generated.
- Supporting Audio's generated using WaveNet's Text  to  Audio  model  as  well  as  GIFs  for  the same are provided to the user.
- The  answers  to  the  questions  are  recorded  and then  compared  to  the  answers  generated  by  the DistilBERT  model  to  generate  a  score  for  the same  which  is  stored  in  the  MySQL  based database.

Fig 6. Reading Comprehensions



## Memory Games

- Images  for  the  cards  are  generated  using  the Stable Diffusion Text to Image model.
- Each card is to be matched with its corresponding pair.

Fig 7. Memory Games



## Phonological Improvement Assistant

- A udio  is  generated  using  WaveNet's  Text  to Audio model.
- Puzzle  Grid  consisting  of  a  shuffled  word  is initialized  and  user  needs  to  swap  the  tiles  to create the word in the proper order.

Fig 8. Phonological Improvement Assistant



## 3. AI Powered Document Simplification

- DistilBERT  is  applied  on  the  text  is  extracted using PyPDF2 from the files uploaded.
- Further,  DistilBERT  identifies  important  words from the summarized text which are then higlighted using Dynamic CSS.
- Finally, summarized PDF is generated with keywords highlighted and entire text summarized.

Fig 9. AI Powered Document Simplification



## 4. AI Driven Mind Map Generation

- DistilBERT is applied on the text is extracted using PyPDF2 from the files uploaded.
- Important  points  generated  using  DistilBERT  are used to create a mind map using reactflow library.
- The  model  generates  important  words  which  are highlighted using dynamic CSS.

Fig 10. AI Powered Document Simplification



## 5. AI Powered Writing Assistant

- Identifies mistakes and improves the text.
- Text is corrected using fine-tuned DistilBERT.
- Image is corrected using fine-tuned OCR  and DistilBERT on dyslexic handwriting styles.

Fig 11. AI Powered Writing Assistant



## 6. AI Chatbot

- Input is in the form of Text, Audio and Images.

Table 2. LLM model used for various inputs

| Input   | Model used              |
|---------|-------------------------|
| Text    | DistilBERT              |
| Audio   | DeepSpeech + DistilBERT |
| Image   | OCR + DistilBERT        |

Fig 12. AI Chatbot



## 7. Integration of Frontend and Backend

- All  the  above  features  are  integrated  using  react  for the frontend and flask for the backend.
- Axios is used to connect the frontend to the backend.
- Multiple hugging face models are used in the course of this project to bring the above features to life.

## Paper Source: Nexia Tutor: An AI-Powered Language Personalized Learning System for Kids with Dyslexia and Reading Challenges

## Nexia Tutor: An AI-Powered Language Personalized Learning System for Kids with Dyslexia and Reading Challenges

Nancy Hany 1 , ∗ , Ramez Sherif 2 , Kirollos Emad 3 , Amr Emad 4 , Maha Elsayed 5 , Hossam Abdelrahman 6

Faculty of Computer Science

Misr International University, Cairo, Egypt

{ nancy2010755 1 , ramez2003170 2 , kirollos2010269 3 , amr2006223 4 , maha.sayed 5 , hossam.csc0225 6 } @miuegypt.edu.eg

Abstract -This research introduces Nexia Tutor, an AI-driven, microservices-based personalized language learning system designed for children with dyslexia. The system comprises three main services: a screening service for dyslexia identification, a report generation service for customized feedback, and an educational, game-based tutoring service tailored to individual needs. The screening service utilizes Random Forest algorithms, achieving an accuracy of 89.2%, to effectively diagnose learning difficulties. Personalized reports analyze dyslexia subtypes, identifying specific weaknesses and providing actionable guidance for parents. The tutoring service, powered by the BERT model, customizes games that target cognitive skills, such as visual memory and phonological awareness, and integrates Google Voice technology for auditory reinforcement. Findings indicate that the system's personalized approach enhances critical language skills in dyslexic children. Assessment data demonstrate improvements in comprehension, retention, and phonological awareness among users. The system's use of Natural Language Processing (NLP) and image generation technologies, such as BERT and DALLE, further enriches the learning experience, making it interactive and accessible. Overall, this research underscores the potential of Nexia Tutor to offer timely, individualized interventions, aiding children with dyslexia in overcoming specific language challenges

Keywords: Dyslexia, ITS, Personalized Tutoring, NLP, BERT, Random Forest

## I. INTRODUCTION

Reading disorders significantly impact individuals, with early language delays, speech challenges, and language difficulties strongly linked to reading disabilities [1]. Children with dyslexia face unique challenges beyond reading, including learning difficulties, hyperactivity, and compromised psychosocial functioning, affecting productivity and well-being in educational and workplace settings [2]. These individual challenges vary widely, with specific deficits in areas such as phonological processing, visual processing, working memory, and attentional control, all of which require tailored intervention approaches.

Targeted interventions can address specific difficulties and enhance related skills. For instance, phonics-based interventions have significantly improved reading skills in students with intellectual disabilities by strengthening phonological awareness [3], while visual-attentional interventions have en-

979-8-3503-6777-5/24/$31.00 ©2024 IEEE

hanced reading abilities in both dyslexic and neurotypical children by targeting visual processing skills [4]. However, current interventions often lack personalization and regular progress tracking, leading parents to seek assistance from centers that may overlook the educational needs of children with dyslexia [5].

Language learning challenges impact reading, spelling, and memorization for individuals with dyslexia and other learning disabilities. These reading disorders frequently co-occur with additional language, attention, and learning disorders, underscoring the crucial role of oral language skills in literacy development [6]. Without targeted support, deficits in these areas can lead to broader educational and social difficulties, ultimately affecting productivity in both academic and workplace settings. Thus, early intervention is essential for improved developmental outcomes [7].

Addressing these complex needs in children with learning disabilities (LD) requires pinpointing individual areas of difficulty, such as phonological processing deficits, which interfere with sound recognition, or visual processing challenges that impact reading fluency. Comprehensive screening combined with personalized tutoring can effectively tackle these specific challenges, ensuring a more productive and adaptive learning experience [8, 9]. Despite the prevalence of language learning applications, there remains a lack of platforms that integrate comprehensive screening with tailored language learning services capable of addressing the nuanced needs of individuals.

AI systems have demonstrated potential in dyslexia diagnosis, using tools like eye tracking and machine learning with high predictive accuracy [10, 11]. However, these systems often provide only binary classifications, which lack the granularity required to inform individualized interventions. Similarly, while AI-driven tutoring advancements have led to game-based educational experiences, these approaches frequently lack the specificity needed to target individual cognitive and learning challenges in dyslexia, thus limiting their effectiveness for personalized interventions [12].

Our solution bridges these gaps by integrating comprehensive screening with personalized tutoring. This approach advances through stages like categorizing specific learning difficulties, generating detailed PDF reports, implementing keyword extraction using BERT transformers, and creating educational games tailored to individual needs. By addressing the individual challenges faced by children with dyslexia, our contributions include a game-based screening service, sophisticated report generation, keyword extraction for enhanced textual analysis, and personalized educational games that cater to each child's unique learning profile. Data and functions traverse our system via message brokers and gateway services, facilitated by a centralized database, ensuring a seamless and responsive user experience.

## II. RELATED WORK

## A. Large Language Models in Education

Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in educational tools to process language and provide personalized feedback. For example, Amira is an AI-driven system offering reading tutoring, oral fluency assessment, and dyslexia screening through speech recognition [13]. While effective for general assessments, Amira's broad approach may lack the specificity required for children with dyslexia, and its reliance on quiet environments limits flexibility.

Our system builds on Amira's approach, utilizing BERT for real-time keyword extraction to deliver targeted, game-based interventions tailored to dyslexic learners. Unlike Amira's generalized feedback, our system focuses on precise, individualized support.

Similarly, BITS, a Bayesian-based tutoring system, customizes learning goals for general programming but lacks metrics and applicability to dyslexia [14]. Our framework instead provides measurable, dyslexia-specific interventions, bridging gaps in existing LLM-based educational tools.

## B. Machine Learning for Dyslexia Screening and Intervention

Machine learning approaches have shown promise in dyslexia research for improving diagnostic accuracy and intervention. For instance, Rauschenberger et al. developed a web-based game for dyslexia detection, achieving accuracies of 74% for German and 69% for Spanish [15]. However, this model's binary output limits its ability to provide detailed insights into individual learning challenges, which is essential for tailored interventions.

Our approach goes beyond binary classification, using ML for in-depth analysis of individual learning patterns. Through BERT-based keyword extraction and customizable game interventions, we provide specific, actionable insights for educators, enabling personalized dyslexia interventions beyond simple diagnostic output.

Rello et al. also developed a gamified dyslexia test that achieved 89.2% accuracy in detecting dyslexic traits in children aged 7-17 [16]. Despite its high accuracy, the model's binary nature restricts its usability for individualized interventions, limiting its application in educational contexts that require fine-grained data on each child's learning profile.

Unlike Rello's model, our system generates nuanced, datadriven feedback for each learner, focusing on personalized support that addresses individual difficulties encountered by dyslexic students.

## C. Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) and Special Education

Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) have also been developed to support learners with special educational needs, providing adaptable learning solutions. Dutt et al. designed an ITS based on fuzzy neural networks for students with learning disabilities, but the system lacks detailed information on dataset size and performance metrics, which limits its realworld applicability [17].

Our system enhances adaptability through deep learning and LLMs, which dynamically respond to learners' evolving needs. Unlike Dutt's ITS, we employ real-time tracking and logging to ensure consistent, measurable intervention, enhancing the efficacy of our dyslexia-focused tutoring approach.

BITS also offers ITS capabilities, utilizing Bayesian networks to recommend learning sequences but failing to address dyslexia or other specific learning disabilities [14]. Our research builds on ITS concepts by integrating specific dyslexia interventions, using adaptive strategies that target unique challenges faced by children with dyslexia, ensuring our system remains relevant and effective in supporting special education needs.

## D. Summary of Comparative Analysis and Strengths of Our Research

In each area reviewed, our research addresses critical limitations in existing systems. LLM-based systems like Amira provide general assessments but lack dyslexia-focused support; our system's personalized interventions fill this gap through targeted, real-time support. Machine learning models for dyslexia screening offer high diagnostic accuracy but are limited by binary outputs; our approach provides detailed, actionable insights for tailored support. Intelligent Tutoring Systems like BITS and those using fuzzy neural networks are adaptable but often lack specific application for dyslexia; we address this by combining deep learning adaptability with precise, real-time tracking.

Our system bridges gaps across LLM, ML, and ITS methods by combining dynamic analysis and specific interventions, offering comprehensive support for dyslexic learners that addresses individual needs.

## III. METHODOLOGY

## A. Research Design

This study employed a descriptive research design to evaluate a comprehensive dyslexia screening and tutoring system, which included three services: screening for early identification and dyslexia classification, personalized report generation, and keyword-based game tutoring.

## B. Participants

Participants were recruited through dyslexia associations and centers, and included 392 dyslexic individuals (45.2% female, 54.8% male) and 3,252 non-dyslexic individuals (49.7% female, 50.3% male). All participants were native Spanish speakers. The focus was on the 9-11 age group due to their highest classification accuracy I).

## C. Screening Service

The screening service used a gamified test based on the 'Predicting Risk of Dyslexia -PLOS ONE' dataset. Traditional methods, including metrics like reading speed and errors, were combined with machine learning to simplify the process. The predictive model utilized Random Forests for their adaptability and interpretability, ensuring a balanced analysis with weighted attributes to account for class imbalances. A trivial classifier achieved an accuracy of 89.2%, as this percentage of participants did not have dyslexia.

Report Generation Personalized reports were generated, calculating the average score for each dyslexia subtype. Scores below the average indicated weaknesses, and the reports provided actionable advice for parents.

## D. Personalized Tutoring Service

The personalized tutoring service utilized the BERT model to analyze learning materials uploaded by participants, extracting keywords and concepts to generate customized educational games. These games included visual memory enhancement exercises using DALL-E-generated images and a rhyming game crafted from web-scraped keywords. Google Voice technology provided auditory reinforcement, and remote accessibility enabled participants to learn at their own pace. The service's effectiveness was evaluated through pre- and post-assessments, alongside participant feedback.

1) Image Generation Evaluation: We primarily focused on confirming that DALL-E-generated images met minimal quality and relevance standards to support the tutoring system, rather than achieving rigorous metric benchmarks.

Sample Size and Evaluation Scope: The evaluation was conducted on a limited sample of images directly tied to a handful of specific educational prompts. This small sample size and narrow scope limit the generalizability of the Fr´ echet Inception Distance (FID) with score of 25%, Inception Score (IS) with score of 75%, and Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP) scoring 85%, all scores to the overall performance of DALL-E within the tutoring application. The results, therefore, provide only a rough indication of image quality and alignment with educational goals.

Learning Outcomes : Significant improvements were noted in phonological awareness and visual memory retention, indicating the tutoring module's success in supporting dyslexic learners.

## D. Classification Model

The Random Forest model was selected as the primary classifier for dyslexia screening due to its robustness, interpretability, and suitability for high-dimensional, imbalanced datasets. Dyslexia diagnosis requires accounting for a wide range of cognitive and demographic factors, which introduces complexity in the data. Random Forest offers several key advantages in this context. Its ensemble-based approach aggregates multiple decision trees, providing stability and reducing the risk of overfitting, especially valuable for our high-dimensional data. Additionally, Random Forest models are inherently interpretable, allowing us to analyze feature importance, which aids in identifying the most influential variables contributing to dyslexia risk assessment. These characteristics make Random Forest a compelling choice for building a reliable dyslexia screening model tailored to learning difficulties in children.

We considered alternative models, including Support Vector Machines (SVM) and neural networks, during the initial model selection process. SVMs, known for their effective margin maximization in classification tasks, lack the interpretability Random Forest provides-an essential attribute for educational and clinical applications, where understanding feature contributions is critical for guiding targeted interventions. Neural networks, while powerful in complex pattern recognition, require larger datasets and significant computational resources, making them less practical for our application, where interpretability and computational efficiency are prioritized. Moreover, prior studies have validated the effectiveness of Random Forest in dyslexia screening, achieving high classification accuracy and interpretability, as demonstrated in [15, 16].

In our study, the Random Forest model achieved an accuracy of 89.2%, effectively balancing sensitivity and specificity. We further optimized the decision threshold to prioritize recall for the dyslexia class, reducing the likelihood of false negatives-a critical consideration for early diagnosis and intervention. To validate the model's robustness.

We employed a 10-fold cross-validation approach, which yielded consistent results, underscoring the model's reliability. Table IX presents the confusion matrix for the final model, highlighting its performance across diverse participant profiles and further confirming its suitability for this application.

## E. Tutoring Service Implementation

A tutoring service module was added, allowing users to upload content in PDF format. BERT was used to extract keywords, with pre-processing steps ensuring accuracy. The preprocessing steps included removing newline characters, handling Unicode, cleaning bullet points, removing stop words, identifying and removing code-related content, and partial stemming implementation.

## V. FUTURE WORK

While this study establishes a solid foundation for AI-driven dyslexia intervention, several areas for future exploration could further enhance the Nexia Tutor system's effectiveness and adaptability. This section outlines targeted research directions that align with reviewer feedback.

## A. Longitudinal Impact Assessment

To evaluate the long-term effects of Nexia Tutor on reading and language development, future studies should incorporate longitudinal data, including follow-up assessments. Tracking students' progress over extended periods would enable researchers to gauge the system's capacity for sustained literacy improvement, providing a comprehensive understanding of its impact on students' educational trajectories.

## B. Expanded Dataset for Robust Evaluation

Future work should expand the dataset, incorporating historical data to allow for more comprehensive analyses of Nexia Tutor's effectiveness across diverse populations. Additionally, randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing Nexia Tutor to traditional interventions would provide valuable, data-driven insights, validating the system's efficacy in improving language skills for children with dyslexia.

## C. Ethical Considerations in Data Privacy

Given the sensitivity of handling children's personal information, future iterations of Nexia Tutor should prioritize stringent data privacy protocols. Implementing encrypted storage, consent mechanisms, and robust access controls is essential to align the system with ethical standards and to protect user data, particularly in educational settings.

## D. Scalability and Cost-Effectiveness

Ensuring scalability is key to Nexia Tutor's broader applicability. Future research should focus on optimizing computational efficiency and minimizing operational costs, allowing the system to function across various hardware environments. These strategies will make Nexia Tutor accessible to a wide range of educational institutions, supporting widespread adoption.

## VI. CONCLUSION

This study presents Nexia Tutor, an AI-driven system offering a comprehensive and personalized approach to dyslexia diagnosis and intervention. By combining natural language processing, machine learning, and game-based tutoring, Nexia Tutor addresses the specific cognitive and linguistic needs of children with dyslexia. The system comprises three main services: a screening module for dyslexia identification, a report generation service that provides personalized insights, and an educational tutoring service designed to reinforce critical language skills through engaging, adaptive games.

The screening service achieves a notable accuracy rate of 89.2% in dyslexia diagnosis using Random Forest classifiers, enabling early identification and targeted intervention. The report generation service empowers parents, educators, and clinicians with actionable feedback tailored to each child's dyslexia subtype, facilitating the creation of customized intervention plans. Meanwhile, the tutoring component, supported by BERT for natural language understanding, DALL-E for image generation, and Google Voice for auditory reinforcement, enhances skills such as phonological awareness, visual memory, and comprehension within an accessible and interactive environment.

The encouraging outcomes of Nexia Tutor highlight its potential to improve language and reading capabilities in children with dyslexia, with demonstrated advancements in comprehension, retention, and phonological awareness. However, to fully realize the system's impact, future work should focus on expanding the dataset and conducting randomized controlled trials to rigorously assess its efficacy compared to traditional methods. Additionally, robust data privacy protocols and scalability strategies are essential to support safe, widespread adoption.

This research establishes a foundation for Nexia Tutor as a versatile and cost-effective tool, addressing ethical considerations while advancing AI-driven education. Nexia Tutor contributes to the broader mission of inclusive education, providing innovative, impactful resources that support the diverse learning needs of children with dyslexia.

## Personalized Educational Assistant for Students with Learning Disabilities

Koduri Lakshmi Vinugna 1 ⋆ , Amara Pranav 1 , Joshika Somisetty 1 , and Pooja Gowda 2

Abstract. Students  with  learning  disabilities  often  tend  to  struggle  with  attention  and  information  retention during  regular  lessons.  Although  note-taking  and  attention  tracking  would  bridge  these  gaps,  actual  learning necessitates  continuous  assistance  based  on individual needs. Through the implementation of real-time content processing, de- tection of distractions, this research seeks to facilitate easier and more individualized learning by keeping them attentive and noting key points. It introduces the development of a Virtual Educational Assistant for Students with learning disabilities, such as dyslexia, aimed at improving learning opportunities for them through real-time feedback  on  attention and  understanding.  The  system  incorporates  two  major  functionalities Distraction Detection and Speech Processing. The Distraction Detection module uses computer vision techniques, such as face detection and Eye Aspect Ratio (EAR) calculation, to monitor the attention levels of the students. If any distraction is detected, a voice based alert is given to gain the focus of the student. The Speech Processing module  transcribes  audio  content  in  real-time  or  audio  file  using  automatic  speech  recognition  and  then summarizes the text for easier understanding. The integration of both modules offers a comprehensive tool that can significantly improve the learning experience for students with learning disabilities by ensuring they remain attentive  and  improve  in  academics.With  multithread-  ing  the  system  output  was  returned in 25 seconds, and without  multithreading  it  consumed  a  lot  of  processing  time.  Multithreading  was  used  to  ensure  that  the communication between both modules has been in sync for a smooth and faster execution.

Keywords: Learning Disabilities, Personalized Education, Operating Systems, Real-Time Processing, Distraction detection, Speech Processing

## 1 Introduction

Learning disabilities like Dyslexia [Zingoni et al., 2024], affects some portion of the student population globally, leading to various challenges in academic environments. Students with learning disabilities often struggle to stay focused during lectures, understand complex concepts, and understand the information presented. In traditional educational environments, where attention and focus were crucial for learning, these students faced greater difficulties in keeping up with the pace of instructions. As a result, their academic performance tends to decline, leading to a sense of  dis-  sapointment  and  frustration.  The  need  for  adaptive  technologies  that  can  support  these students in real-time has become more relevant, as existing methods may not provide that much flexibility or support required to meet their needs.

⋆ Corresponding author: Department of Artificial Intelligence Amrita School of Artificial Intelligence, Kasavanahalli, Bengaluru 560035, bl.en.u4aid23026@bl.students.amrita.edu

The recognition of the fact that traditional teaching [Zhang and Zhang, 2024] methods were not al-  ways  effective  for  students  with  learning  disabilities,  especially  those  who  struggle  with attention difficulty, motivated towards this respective research. In the common classroom, these students  could  find  it  challenging  to  maintain  focus  during  long  lectures,  and  without  proper support,  they  may  miss  critical  information.  Additionally,  the  lack  of  real-time  assistance  can prevent  these  stu-  dents  from  actively  engaging  with  the  material.  Most  existing  tools  for learning disabilities  focus  on  post-session  support,  such as recorded lectures or textbook-based interventions, but they do not offer the level of real-time interaction needed to prevent students from losing focus in the first place.

Addressing this issue required a system that not only helps students stay engaged or attentive during lessons but also needed immediate support when distractions are detected. This study is motivated  by  the  belief  that  a  combination  of  real-time  distraction  detection  and  speech processing can provide an adaptive solution for  students  with  attention  difficulties.  By integrating these tech- nologies, the proposed system will allow for a continuous monitoring of students attention, making the learning experience more effective and personalized [Sajja et al., 2024a].

The conventional methods such as taped lectures and extra tutoring [Gutjahr et al., 2017], offer less  help,  mostly  after  the  lecture  has  occurred.  Such  resources  fail  to  provide  real-time, immediate support needed to help students maintain focus in classrooms. Such methods also fail to  meet  individual  needs  during  learning,  which  is  vital  in  students  with  attention  difficulty. There exists a gap in solutions on the market that this study aims to fill by offering a system to monitor and improve student interest during lessons in real-time.

This  study  suggests  a  virtual  learning  [Essel  et  al.,  2022]  aid  designed  to  assist  students  with learn-  ing  disabilities  by  tracking  their  level  of  attention  and  giving  instant  feedback  when distraction  is  sensed.  The  system  is  composed  of  two main modules: the Distraction Detection module  and  the  Speech  Processing  module.  The  Distraction  Detection  module  monitors  a student's involve- ment based on behavioral data, while the Speech Processing module converts class  discussions  into  text,gives  live  summaries  and  important  points.  These  are  designed  to collaborate and keep the students interested in the lesson and that they can be able to retrieve and

## access relevant infor- mation.

The  key  objectives  of  the  proposed  system are to develop a distraction detection system that monitors a student's attention during lessons, provide real-time transcription of classroomdiscussions, offer summaries and key takeaways from the lesson. These objectives aim to create a more effec- tive learning environment by providing personalized support [Chiu et al., 2024] for students with learning disabilities in real-time.

The primary contribution of this study is the combination of distraction detection and speech processing technologies to offer real-time assistance to students with learning disabilities [D'Urso and Sciarrone, 2024]. As compared to the traditional tools that hardly offer any post-session intervention,  this  system  provides  constant  guidance,  allowing  students  to  remain  engaged and alert throughout the lesson. With a mix of attention-tracking and speech-to-text technology, this publica- tion adds to more flexible and individualized learning for students with difficulties with attention.
