## Design and Implementation

## System Overview

The primary objective of ReadSmart is to support students with dyslexia by providing an integrated educational platform that leverages both Augmented Reality (AR) and Generative AI (GenAI) technologies. ReadSmart, is designed to enhance the learning experience by making it more interactive and personalized, addressing the unique challenges faced by dyslexic learners. The core functionalities of ReadSmart include capturing text from realworld environments using AR devices, processing the captured text using Optical Character Recognition (OCR), summarizing and generating educational content with GenAI, and displaying this content in an interactive AR environment. Additionally, ReadSmart allows users to interact with it through gestures and voice commands, ensuring a highly engaging and tailored learning experience.

ReadSmart's architecture is designed to facilitate seamless interaction between its various components, ensuring efficient data flow and processing. The architecture comprises the following key modules:

1. Text Capture Module: This module utilizes AR devices to capture text from real-world environments. The captured images are then sent to the Text Recognition Module for processing.
2. Text Recognition Module: This module uses OCR technology to convert the captured images into editable text. The OCR service, such as Azure OCR, can recognize both printed and handwritten text, ensuring high accuracy and versatility.
3. Content Generation Module: Leveraging the capabilities of Generative AI models like GPT-4, this module generates personalized educational content based on the recognized text. The content generated

includes text summaries, explanations, and visual aids tailored to the needs of dyslexic students.

4. Content Display Module: This module presents the generated content within an AR environment. By overlaying digital information onto the real world, it enhances the learning experience through interactive and immersive visuals.
5. User Interaction Module: Facilitating interaction through gestures and voice commands, this module ensures  that  users  can  navigate  and  engage  with  ReadSmart  intuitively.  The  immediate  feedback provided by this module enhances the usability and accessibility of the platform.

Figure 2. ReadSmart's Interaction Workflow



ReadSmart interaction flow (Fig. 2) illustrates how users interact with ReadSmart. Users can capture text from the real world using the AR device, which is then processed by the OCR service to extract the text. The extracted text  is  sent  to  the  GenAI  model  for  content  generation,  which  produces  personalized  educational  materials. ReadSmart then displays the generated content in the AR environment, allowing users to interact with it through gestures and voice commands. This interactive and personalized learning experience aims to support dyslexic students in overcoming their reading challenges and enhancing their academic performance.

## Technology Stack

The selection of appropriate technologies and tools is critical to the performance and usability of ReadSmart. The chosen technologies include:

-  Hardware:  The  Microsoft  HoloLens  2  is  selected  for  its  advanced  capabilities  in  capturing  and processing real-world images with high precision. Its robust computational power and integration with AR applications make it ideal for this project.

- Software: Unity3D, combined with the Mixed Reality Toolkit (MRTK2), is used for developing the AR environment. Unity3D's versatility and MRTK2's specialized features for AR development ensure a seamless and interactive user experience.
- Programming Language: C is used for the development of ReadSmart due to its strong compatibility with Unity and Azure services. It facilitates the implementation of various functionalities, including user interface design, interaction handling, and integration with cloud services.
- OCR Technology: Azure OCR services are employed for text recognition due to their high accuracy and  ability  to  process  various  text  formats,  including  handwritten  text.  This  ensures  reliable  text extraction from diverse sources.
-  Generative  AI  Model:  OpenAI's  GPT-4  model  is  utilized  for  generating  personalized  educational content. GPT-4's advanced natural language processing capabilities enable it to produce high-quality, contextually relevant educational materials tailored to the needs of dyslexic students.

By integrating these technologies, ReadSmart is designed to provide an effective, engaging, and personalized learning tool for students with dyslexia. The combination of AR and GenAI technologies allows for a seamless blend of real-world interaction and digital enhancement, offering a novel approach to educational support.

## User Interaction Design

The design of the user interaction within ReadSmart focuses on creating an intuitive and engaging experience for dyslexic students. Central to this design is the hand menu (handmenu) that follows the user's palm movements, providing an accessible interface for interacting with ReadSmart's functionalities.

Figure 3. Handmenu Interface Design



The handmenu (Fig. 3) is designed to appear on the inner side of the user's palm when it is within the field of view. As the user moves their palm, the handmenu follows, ensuring that it remains easily accessible. When the user's palm moves out of the field of view, the handmenu stays fixed in its last position using spatial computing techniques, effectively anchoring it in the real world. Additionally, users can drag the handmenu to place it at any desired location within their environment, providing flexibility in interaction.

The handmenu contains four main buttons, each providing a specific functionality, as well as several display areas for showing text, images, and captured content. The key features of the handmenu include:

- Text Display Area: On the left side of the handmenu, there is a text display area that shows either the recognized text or the summarized text, depending on the user's selection. This area also includes two additional buttons for navigating through the history of captured texts. Users can switch to the previous or next text, with ReadSmart supporting a history of up to five recent captures. This feature allows users to review and compare different texts and their summaries. During TTS playback, the text is highlighted in sync with the audio narration, providing a synchronized visual aid.

- Image Display Area: The right side of the handmenu is dedicated to displaying the images generated by ReadSmart based on the summarized text. This visual representation aids in the comprehension of complex concepts, providing a multi-sensory learning experience. The images are updated in sync with the text navigation, ensuring that the visual aids correspond to the selected text.

- Captured Image Preview: A specific area within the handmenu shows a preview of the captured image. This allows users to confirm that they have successfully captured the desired text area before proceeding with text recognition and processing.

-  Capture  Button:  Allows  users  to  capture  text  from  real-world  environments  using  the  HoloLens  2 cameras. The captured text is then processed by ReadSmart for further analysis and content generation.

- Play/Pause Audio Button: Enables users to play or pause the audio narration of the recognized text or generated summaries. This feature leverages ReadSmart's TTS capability to provide auditory support.

- Stop Audio Button: Allows users to stop the audio playback, giving them control over the listening experience.

- Toggle Original/Summary Text Button: Enables users to switch between the original recognized text and the summarized version generated by ReadSmart, providing flexibility in content presentation.

- History Navigation Buttons: Enable users to switch to the previous or next text, supporting a history of up to five recent captures. This feature allows users to review and compare different texts and their summaries.

The interaction mechanics are designed to be user-friendly and responsive to ensure that students can focus on learning rather than navigating the interface. The handmenu's ability to follow the user's palm and remain within easy reach reduces the need for extensive hand movements, minimizing physical strain. The spatial anchoring of the handmenu when the palm moves out of view ensures that users do not lose track of the interface, maintaining a seamless interaction flow.

By combining visual, auditory, and tactile interaction methods, ReadSmart accommodates various learning styles and preferences. This multimodal approach ensures that dyslexic students can engage with the educational content in a way that best suits their individual needs, ultimately enhancing their learning experience.

## Evaluation and Testing

The evaluation and testing phase is critical to ensure that the AR and GenAI system effectively supports dyslexic students and meets the project's objectives. Given the current constraints, testing primarily involves self-testing and  feedback  from  peers,  focusing  on  functionality,  performance,  usability,  and  ReadSmart's  ability  to  save reading time.

The performance testing was conducted in two main phases. In the first phase, ReadSmart was subjected to 50 tests using the same set of text data. This phase focused on assessing ReadSmart's response time, content accuracy, and the quality of generated images. Key metrics, such as average processing time per task and accuracy rates in text recognition and summarization, were meticulously recorded.

In the second phase, ReadSmart's robustness was tested using a diverse set of 50 text samples, including various fonts and handwritten texts. This phase aimed to evaluate ReadSmart's adaptability and accuracy across different types of input, simulating real-world usage conditions. The testing included measuring the time taken to process each type of text and the accuracy of the output, particularly focusing on how well ReadSmart handled more challenging inputs, such as poorly legible handwriting.

To evaluate ReadSmart's usability and overall user experience, a comprehensive online user testing approach was adopted. Participants, including individuals with backgrounds in education, such as students and professors, as well  as those  from  other  industries,  were  invited  to  participate in the online  survey.  A  total  of  45 professors/teachers and 258 students participated in the survey. The demonstration video provided a first-person perspective on ReadSmart's functionalities, including text capture, summary generation, image creation, and the TTS feature.

After watching the video, participants were asked to complete a standardized survey designed to gather both qualitative  and  quantitative  feedback.  The  survey  included  questions  aimed  at  assessing  the  ease  of  use, intuitiveness of navigation, and overall user interface design. Participants were prompted to rate their agreement with statements regarding the clarity and user-friendliness of the interface, as well as any points of confusion or difficulty they perceived.

Additionally, the survey collected feedback on the quality and relevance of the generated summaries and images. Participants evaluated how well these outputs aligned with the original content and whether they found the visual aids helpful in understanding the material. The effectiveness of the TTS feature was also reviewed, focusing on the clarity of the synthesized voice, the pace of speech, and its overall utility in enhancing the learning experience. The insights gathered from this online user testing approach are invaluable in identifying ReadSmart's strengths and areas for improvement. These insights are crucial for guiding future iterations of ReadSmart, ensuring that it meets the needs of its intended users and provides a seamless and supportive learning experience. Based on the feedback and data collected from these evaluations, ReadSmart undergoes iterative refinement. Adjustments are made to address identified issues, enhance functionalities, and improve the overall user experience. This iterative approach ensures that ReadSmart evolves based on practical feedback and continues to meet the educational needs of dyslexic students effectively. Although direct testing with dyslexic students was not feasible, the evaluation and testing phase involving detailed peer feedback is essential for validating ReadSmart's technical performance and  user  experience.  This  approach  ensures  that  the  project  delivers  a  robust,  user-friendly,  and  effective educational tool that can significantly enhance the learning experience for dyslexic students.

## Results

## System Performance Evaluation

ReadSmart's performance evaluation focuses on assessing the functionality and efficiency of the AR and GenAI system  based  on  extensive  testing  across  various  components,  including  OCR  accuracy,  text  processing  and generation speed, overall response time, and system stability.

Figure 4. OCR Accuracy Test Result



The OCR component demonstrated high accuracy over a total of 100 tests conducted under different lighting conditions  and  with  various  text  types.  In  bright  scenes,  the  OCR  accuracy  for  common  print  fonts  was exceptionally high at 99.99%, representing the best performance of ReadSmart. When processing more ornate print  fonts,  the  accuracy  slightly  decreased  to  99.32%.  For  easily  readable  handwritten  texts,  the  accuracy remained robust at 98.25%, but it dropped to 89.75% when handling difficult-to-read handwriting.

As the chart shows, the OCR performance exhibits a slight decline under darker lighting conditions, with the average accuracy dropping by 4-5% for all text types. Despite the lower accuracy rates in certain challenging scenarios, such as difficult handwriting and low-light conditions, these situations had a minimal impact on the overall testing process. This is because ReadSmart is primarily designed to handle common printed text, which constitutes most use cases. Thus, the overall reliability and practicality of ReadSmart remain intact for its intended applications.

In terms of average response time, a cycle of text capture, processing, and content generation took an average of 5.5 seconds, with image generation processing accounting for most of the time. The capture and OCR components were highly efficient, taking only 2 seconds on average, while the GenAI model processing time varied depending on the complexity of the text and the length of the summary generated. About 64% of the total processing time was spent on text and image generation, indicating potential areas for optimization in this component.

Figure 5. Average Processing Time for Each System Component



Based  on  self-testing  and  peer  feedback,  the  reading  time  was  significantly  reduced  when  using  ReadSmart compared to traditional reading methods. It took approximately 3-5 minutes to read and understand a 500-word text before using ReadSmart, whereas using ReadSmart reduced the time to 1-2 minutes. This reduction in reading time was attributed to ReadSmart's summarization and image generation features, which provided concise and visually engaging content that facilitated quicker comprehension.

Regarding system stability, the platform demonstrated robust performance throughout the testing phase. Earlier issues related to performance degradation and occasional crashes were addressed through targeted optimizations, resulting  in  a  stable  operational  environment.  The  absence  of  recent  performance  issues  highlights  the effectiveness of these optimizations, ensuring reliable system performance under typical usage conditions.

## User Feedback

During the testing phase, user feedback was collected from over 40 participants, including 4 professors/teachers, 25 students, and 13 professionals from non-education fields, through an online survey that included a detailed video demonstration of the AR system. The primary feedback revolved around the user interface, interaction experience, and overall system functionality.

The user testing phase involved a detailed survey designed to gather both quantitative and qualitative feedback on ReadSmart's  usability,  user  interface,  content  generation,  and  TTS  features.  Participants  provided  ratings  on various aspects of ReadSmart, and their comments offered deeper insights into their experiences. After collecting the survey responses, the data was analyzed to identify key trends and patterns in the feedback. The weighted mean for each question and the standard deviation were calculated to assess the overall user satisfaction and identify areas of consensus and divergence.

Quantitative data from the survey revealed that ReadSmart received an overall satisfaction rating of 3.9 out of 5

from users, indicating a generally positive reception. The standard deviation for this question was 0.63, suggesting that user feedback was relatively consistent, with most users providing scores close to the mean. This low standard deviation  reflects  a  consensus  on  ReadSmart's  overall  effectiveness,  with  few  outliers  indicating  significant dissatisfaction.

The TTS feature received a high mean score of 4.1, reflecting that most users found this feature beneficial for aiding comprehension. However, the standard deviation for this feature was 0.85, indicating some variability in user experiences. This suggests that while many users rated the TTS feature highly, there were differing opinions, possibly due to individual preferences or variability in how the feature performed across different scenarios.

For  OCR  accuracy,  ReadSmart  achieved  a  mean  rating  of  4.0.  This  score  suggests  that  users  generally  felt ReadSmart met their expectations in accurately recognizing and processing text, which is crucial for dyslexic students who rely on precise text interpretation. The standard deviation here was 0.82, showing that while most users  had  similar  positive  experiences  with  the  OCR  functionality,  there  was  some  level  of  disagreement, potentially pointing to occasional inconsistencies in text recognition.

The user interface (UI) was rated at 3.7, indicating that while users found the interface somewhat intuitive, there is room for improvement. The standard deviation for the UI rating was 0.86, which is relatively high, suggesting that user opinions varied significantly. Some users may have found the interface easy to use, while others may have encountered difficulties, highlighting a need for further refinement in UI design to achieve a more universally positive user experience.

Navigation within ReadSmart also received a rating of 3.7, with a standard deviation of 0.82. The mean score suggests that users generally found the navigation functional, though not without some challenges. The standard deviation indicates that user experiences with navigation were somewhat inconsistent, which might point to areas where the flow or layout could be optimized to improve overall usability. ReadSmart's response time had a mean rating of 3.7, reflecting that users generally found ReadSmart's performance satisfactory, though not exceptional.

The standard deviation was 0.85, indicating that some users experienced delays that negatively impacted their experience, suggesting that improving response time could enhance user satisfaction.

In terms of visual content, users provided a mean rating of 3.9, suggesting that they found the visual aids helpful in supporting learning. The standard deviation for this feature was 0.79, indicating a moderate level of agreement among users, though some may have found the visual content less effective or relevant, which could indicate an area for potential improvement. Finally, the clear understanding from the demo was rated highly, with a mean score  of  4.1,  reflecting  that  the  demonstration  effectively  conveyed  ReadSmart's  functionalities  to  users.  The standard deviation for this aspect was 0.67, indicating a strong consensus among users that the demo provided a clear and understandable overview of ReadSmart.

Qualitative feedback from the open-ended question of the survey complemented these ratings, with many users expressing satisfaction with the project's goals and the innovative integration of AR and GenAI technologies. One participant noted, "The TTS feature is very clear and significantly aids in understanding the text," while another appreciated  the  OCR  functionality  for  its  accuracy.  However,  significant  criticism  was  directed  at  the  user interface,  with  comments  such  as  "The  UI  is  cluttered  and  complex"  and  "Navigation  needs  to  be  more straightforward."  Users  also  highlighted  the  need  for  a  more  streamlined  and  aesthetically  pleasing  design, suggesting improvements in user interaction mechanisms and overall visual appeal.

## Conclusion and Future Work

## Conclusions

The results of this project confirm that the research questions have been effectively addressed. By integrating AR and GenAI technologies, ReadSmart has demonstrated its potential to create an educational platform that supports dyslexic students in a meaningful way. The evaluation indicates that ReadSmart not only meets its intended goals but also offers valuable insights into usability and functionality, which will inform future improvements. These findings underscore ReadSmart's capacity to contribute to more inclusive and effective learning environments while also highlighting areas for ongoing refinement.

ReadSmart  successfully  integrated  key  technologies,  including  Microsoft  HoloLens  2  for  augmented  reality, Unity3D and MRTK2 for development, Azure Cognitive Services for OCR, and OpenAI's GPT-4 for content generation.  The  inclusion  of  a  dynamic  handmenu  provided  a  unique  interface  for  users  to  interact  with ReadSmart, capturing text, receiving summaries, and accessing visual aids. The TTS functionality further enriched ReadSmart by offering an auditory learning component, which was particularly well-received by users. Through testing  and  feedback,  ReadSmart  demonstrated  high  accuracy  in  text  recognition  and  efficient  processing capabilities.  Users  appreciated  the  quality  of  the  generated  summaries  and  images,  noting  that  these  features significantly aided their understanding of complex texts. The positive reception of the TTS feature highlighted its importance in providing accessible content, further validating ReadSmart's design choices.

However, the feedback also revealed areas where the user experience could be improved, particularly in the intuitiveness of the interface and the physical ergonomics of using the handmenu. These insights are crucial for guiding future iterations of ReadSmart, emphasizing the need for more user-friendly interaction mechanisms and better  onboarding  processes.  This  project  has  developed  an  innovative  tool  that  meets  the  specific  needs  of dyslexic students by integrating advanced technologies. ReadSmart's ability to provide real-time text processing, summaries, and multimodal content delivery represents a significant advancement in educational technology for individuals with learning disabilities. This work lays a strong foundation for future research and development, offering valuable lessons and clear pathways for enhancement.

## Limitations

The  AR  and  GenAI  system  for  supporting  dyslexic  students,  while  innovative  and  promising,  has  several limitations that were identified during the development and testing phases. These limitations highlight areas for improvement  and  provide  directions  for  future  development.  One  of  the  primary  limitations  lies  in  the  user experience and interface design. Feedback from users indicated that finding and operating the handmenu was initially  challenging,  particularly  due  to  the  lack  of  intuitive  guidance  and  clarity  in  on-screen  prompts.  This suggests that the current interface design may not be sufficiently user-friendly, especially for first-time users. Additionally, the reliance on hand gestures for interacting with ReadSmart led to physical discomfort and fatigue, particularly during extended use. This ergonomic issue points to a need for more diverse interaction methods that reduce physical strain.

Technically, while ReadSmart's OCR functionality generally performed well, it struggled with certain inputs, such as poorly handwritten text or text captured in low-light conditions. These scenarios led to decreased accuracy and reliability, indicating a limitation in handling diverse and less-than-ideal input conditions. Similarly, although the TTS feature received positive feedback, its naturalness was rated as moderate, which may affect user engagement and satisfaction during prolonged use.ReadSmart's dependency on advanced hardware, such as the Microsoft HoloLens  2,  also  presents  a  significant  limitation.  The  high  cost  and  accessibility  of  such  devices  limit ReadSmart's  potential  user  base,  making  it  less  feasible  for  widespread  adoption,  particularly  in  resourceconstrained educational environments.

Moreover, the current testing scope was limited to a small group of users who provided feedback based on an online demonstration, primarily consisting of non-target users. The absence of direct interaction with dyslexic students,  the  primary  target  audience,  limits  a  comprehensive  evaluation  of  ReadSmart's  effectiveness  and usability in real-world educational settings. This limitation highlights the need for future testing with a broader and more representative user base, including hands-on trials with dyslexic students.

Additionally, while ReadSmart demonstrates strong capabilities in text processing and content generation, its overall functionality remains relatively constrained. The lack of support for voice commands or remote control limits the flexibility and accessibility of user interactions. Furthermore, ReadSmart does not yet fully leverage machine learning for personalized learning experiences, which could adapt to individual users' needs and learning styles over time. These limitations provide a roadmap for future enhancements and refinements. Addressing these issues will be crucial in improving ReadSmart's usability, accessibility, and overall effectiveness, thereby better serving the educational needs of dyslexic students and potentially broader user groups.

## Future Research Directions

The future research directions for the AR and GenAI system are focused on enhancing user experience, expanding functionality,  and  increasing  accessibility  across  various  augmented  reality  hardware  platforms.  As  AR technology continues to evolve, ReadSmart aims to adapt and improve in several key areas.

Firstly,  enhancing  user  experience  and  interaction  methods  remains  a  priority.  The  introduction  of  voice commands and remote-control devices, such as handheld controllers, could significantly reduce the reliance on hand gestures, thereby alleviating physical fatigue associated with prolonged use. This development would offer users  more  flexible  and  accessible  interaction  options,  catering  to  different  user  preferences  and  physical capabilities. Additionally, refining the user interface to be more intuitive and user-friendly is crucial. This could involve more comprehensive onboarding instructions, interactive tutorials, or even an AR virtual assistant to guide users through ReadSmart's features, particularly for first-time users.

Secondly, in terms of technical performance, there is a need to optimize the OCR and TTS technologies. While the  current  system  performs  well,  further  improvements  in  the  accuracy  of  OCR,  especially  in  challenging conditions such as handwritten text or low-light environments, would enhance reliability. Similarly, increasing the naturalness and quality of TTS output would improve the overall user experience, making the auditory aspect of ReadSmart more engaging and easier to understand. Incorporating machine learning algorithms could also enable  personalized  learning  experiences,  allowing  ReadSmart  to  adapt  content  presentation  and  interaction methods based on user feedback and interaction patterns, thus better meeting the diverse needs of individual learners.

Expanding ReadSmart's functionality and application scope is another critical direction. Supporting a broader range of AR glasses beyond the Microsoft HoloLens 2 would make ReadSmart more accessible as AR technology becomes more widespread and affordable. This would involve ensuring compatibility with different AR hardware, thus  expanding  the  potential  user  base  and  applicability  of  ReadSmart.  Additionally,  extending  ReadSmart's capabilities to support multiple languages, including OCR, TTS, and content generation, would cater to a more diverse, multilingual audience, further broadening ReadSmart's reach and utility.These future research directions are aimed at addressing current limitations, enhancing user satisfaction, and ensuring that ReadSmart remains at the forefront of educational technology for dyslexic students and potentially other user groups. By continually evolving and incorporating cutting-edge advancements, ReadSmart can better serve its users and adapt to the changing landscape of AR and educational technologies.

## Paper Source: Real-Time Assistive Reader Pen for Arabic Language

## Real-time Assistive Reader Pen for Arabic Language

## MOHAMMADA. ALZUBAIDI, MWAFFAQ OTOOM, and NOURAN S. AHMAD,

Yarmouk University

Disability is an impairment affecting an individual's livelihood and independence. Assistive technology enables the disabled cohort of the community to break the barriers to learning, access information, contribute to the community, and live independently. This article proposes an assistive device to enable people with visual disabilities and learning disabilities to access printed Arabic material in real-time, and to help them participate in the education system and the professional workforce.

This proposed assistive device employs Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and Text To Speech (TTS) conversion, using concatenation synthesis. OCR is achieved using image processing, character extraction, and classification, while Arabic speech synthesis is achieved through concatenation synthesis, followed by Multi Band Re-synthesis Overlap-Add (MBROLA). Waveform generation in the second phase produces vocal output for the disabled user to hear. OCR character and word accuracy tests were conducted for nine Arabic fonts. The results show that six fonts were recognized with over 60% character accuracy and two fonts were recognized with over 88% accuracy. A Mean Opinion Score (MOS) test for speech quality was conducted. The results showed an overall MOS score of 3.53/5 and indicated that users were able to understand the speech. A real-time usability testing was conducted with 10 subjects. The results showed an overall average of agreements scores of 3.9/5 and indicated that the proposed Arabic reader pen meets the real-time constraints and is pleasant and satisfying to use and can contribute to make printed Arabic material accessible to visually impaired persons and people with learning disabilities.

CCS Concepts: · Human-centered computing → Accessibility ; Accessibility technologies ; · Computer systems organization → Embedded and cyber-physical systems ; Embedded systems ; Embedded software ;

Additional Key Words and Phrases: Arabic language, assistive embedded systems, optical character recognition, reader pen, real-time systems, text-to-speech

## 1 INTRODUCTION

Disability is an impairment, a complex phenomenon reflecting the interaction between a person and the society in which he or she lives. It can be congenital, or it might be acquired at any stage of an individual's lifetime. It can substantially affect a person's life activities. Impairments

are classified as either cognitive, developmental, intellectual, mental, physical, sensory, or a combination of them [1].

The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that more than a billion people have a disability of some form, which corresponds to about 15% of the global population [2].

Many students with disabilities are unable to attend public schools and are only allowed to attend special-needs schools, where they can receive special education. This keeps them isolated from the society [4]. However, there are 420M people around the world who speak Arabic, and more than 1.5B Muslims who might need to read Arabic.

Assistive technology aims to make the mainstream educational system more accessible to the disabled and enable them to contribute to the community. It also increases their independence by allowing them to carry out tasks that they would otherwise be unable to perform without assistance [5].

A reader pen is a Text-To-Speech assistive device that alleviates learning difficulties associated with visual impairment and learning disabilities by translating input text into speech waveforms. The aim of a universal TTS program is to transform all types of textual input that a human being is able to pronounce, regardless of its complexity [6]. One example of a reader pen is C-Pen, which is designed to scan printed text and then play it as audible speech for the user to hear. It is currently available in languages such as English and Spanish [7].

The current challenges in building an assistive reader device are (1) to meet the necessary realtime constraints and (2) to deliver natural, human-like, accurate speech-especially for less supported languages, such as Arabic. In doing so, certain special requirements for Arabic must be met, such as supporting diacritics and providing correct pronunciation of letters and abbreviations. Ideally, such a device would be implemented within the limited resources available in portable embedded systems and would deliver high-quality Arabic speech to people with visual impairments or learning difficulties.

Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and speech synthesis are the two primary focuses of the research in this article. We employ a traditional approach to OCR (using character extraction and classification) and a novel approach to speech synthesis, which is accomplished through diphone concatenation synthesis, and the MBROLA algorithm.

Previous studies (which will be described in the next section) have concentrated on speech synthesis for languages such as English, French, and Spanish. Only a few speech synthesis frameworks support Arabic, and most of them are implemented to run on a personal computer or a mobile device. These platforms provide much greater resources than a compact embedded device, which has much less memory and more constrained processing power.

The contribution of this research is toward the development of a real-time TTS reader pen for Arabic, implemented using a System on a Chip (SoC). Such a compact device is an essential tool for the visually impaired to access textual content that they encounter moment-by-moment in their daily life.

This article is organized as follows: In Section 2, we explore the related work. The methodology is explained in the next three consecutive sections, where Section 3 describes the Reader System Algorithms, Section 4 describes the hardware implementation, and Section 5 describes the experimental setup. In Section 6, we discuss the results of the conducted experiments. We conclude the article in Section 7.

## 2 LITERATURE REVIEW

In this section, we review the state-of-the-art work on Text-To-Speech (TTS) and Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technologies, including those that support Arabic language. In addition, we review similar assistive reading pen devices that are presented in the literature.

## 2.1 Text-To-Speech (TTS)

2.1.1 Concatenation Synthesis. One popular TTS method is concatenation synthesis. This method strings together previously recorded words and syllables to generate a near-human-like speech stream. However, speech streams generated using this method have noticeable glitches. Therefore, the quality of the generated speech is not as natural as desired to the human ear [8].

Sanaki [9] introduced an embedded real-time TTS apparatus. In this research, an Advanced RISC Machine receives a stream of input text from a keyboard. This text stream is routed to a PIC microcontroller, which is connected to a speakJet IC. The speakJet IC converts the text stream into a speech stream, using concatenation synthesis, and routes the speech stream to a loudspeaker to output the audio. The downside to this approach is that it requires a lot of hardware, which can be costly and bulky. Moreover, the speakJet IC only supports English.

Hamad and Hussain [10] developed a TTS system for Arabic that relies on concatenation synthesis of allophones and diphones. In this research, the software was developed using the Microsoft Speech API, which requires the Microsoft Windows operating system. The system receives text in a phonetic format and generates speech in Arabic with an accuracy of around 75%.

Praveen Kumar Bamini [11] developed an FPGA implementation of a concatenation speech synthesis algorithm. It employed FPGA flip-flops to provide a relatively small in-memory database of audio recordings, called an acoustic library. Each recording represents a word segment consisting of four letters or less. The speech synthesis algorithm receives segmented words and searches the library for a matching phone for each segment. The concatenation of the audio recordings is done using MATLAB.

The study of Tora et al. [12] demonstrates a hardware-based Turkish TTS implementation, using an external voice synthesizer card. The TTS system is built using an RC8660 voice synthesizer chip, which supports English by default. However, it can be configured to generate speech for other languages by adding a phoneme mapping dictionary. The Mean Opinion Score (MOS) of the system is 3.29 out of 5. However, the RC8660 voice synthesizer chip is limited to languages with ASCII characters. Therefore, Arabic is not supported [13].

Chabchoub and Cherif [14] presented an implementation using Time Domain Pitch Synchronous Overlap-Add (TD-PSOLA) tools to enhance the quality of an Arabic TTS system, which was based on Diphone concatenation. The resulting speech was tested by a group of listeners using two tests: the Diagnostic Rhyme Test (DRT) and the Categorical Estimation (CE) test. The test scores showed an enhancement in accuracy and naturalness. However, the TD-PSOLA algorithm is considered computationally intensive.

2.1.2 Unit Selection Synthesis. Unit selection synthesis is another speech synthesis technology that relies on a database of speech recordings. These recordings are segmented before database creation into a large number of waveform combinations. Accordingly, this method stores phones and diphones, plus samples of half-phones, morphemes, syllables, words, phrases, and even full sentences [15].

Bachan and Tokarski [16] researched the creation and evaluation of synthesized speech for Polish using MaryTTS, which is an open source Java framework for speech synthesis. The chosen method for speech synthesis was unit-selection, which is available in MaryTTS. The authors use Python and Praat scripts for text manipulations. According to this research, the accuracy of the speech synthesis for Polish was over 80%, which is relatively high. However, the MarryTTS framework does not yet support Arabic.

Sarathy and Ramakrishnan [17] researched the development of Text-To-Speech for an embedded mobile device. The synthesis method used is unit selection concatenative-based, where a speech unit is selected from the database based on its phonetic context. This article also studies the tradeoff between database size and the quality of synthetic speech in the mobile environment. Several speech compression schemes used in mobile devices are tested and compared, according to their quality. The paper proposes a methodology that uses the existing speech codec in mobile devices to read SMS text messages to the listener.

The research of Vanitha et al. [18] demonstrates real-time TTS hardware, based on a Raspberry Pi. The Clustergen algorithm is the speech synthesis method used in this implementation. It employs a parametric synthesis cluster-based unit selection method. The software in the system is programmed using the C language. It accepts text input from a keyboard that is connected to the Raspberry Pi. and converts that text to corresponding speech. However, the quality of the generated speech was not addressed by the authors.

The study of Rebai and BenAyed [19] presents an efficient Arabic TTS system with a diacritization engine that uses unit selection for speech synthesis. In this work, the authors proposed an implementation using deep neural networks to predict the correct Arabic diacritics. Experimental results indicate high-precision diacritic generation and high-quality synthesized speech with an MOS score between 3.42 and 3.67 out of 5.

In summary, unit selection is capable of achieving the greatest level of output naturalness by relying on a large database. However, such large databases are not practical for embedded, resourceconstrained systems.

2.1.3 Neural Network-based Synthesis. Frontini and Malcangi [20] reported a neural networkbased method for implementing a TTS system and compared it to a rule-based system. The neural network is trained using the back-propagation algorithm with an adaptive learning rate. The authors developed a software tool called NetTalk using MATLAB and Java programming.

Lakshmi et al. [21] implemented TTS conversion using a Raspberry Pi. Their system combines both optical character recognition and TTS synthesis to create a device that scans English text from an image and converts it to its corresponding speech audio. The hardware used is Raspberry Pi 2, along with a Raspberry Pi Camera Module. The software used for OCR is Tesseract, which is an open source OCR engine. For the TTS, the authors used the Google Speech API, which uses neural networks for speech synthesis.

Fogarassy-Neszly and Pribeanu [22] proposed a software module for TTS synthesis supporting multiple languages. In this article, language detection algorithms are used and tested on texts of different languages. The software used for speech synthesis in this article is the Microsoft Speech API (SAPI). The authors developed multiple versions of their software. The commercial version has been used in a screen reader application and in a personal planner application for the visually impaired. The research includes usability and acceptance tests of the applications with visually impaired and blind users.

Tacotron [23], a software engine built using Python language, relies on a single neural network trained from only data to produce linguistic and acoustic features. Tacotron uses the Griffin-Lim algorithm for phase estimation to vocode the magnitude spectrograms. Initially Tacotron only supported English language. Later in 2019, a multilingual update was published [24], but Tacotron users will need to create training data for the chosen language.

2.1.4 Formant Synthesis. Formant Synthesis is a speech synthesis method that does not use prerecorded human speech samples to create a synthesized output. Instead, it uses acoustic modeling and additive synthesis, which takes a stream of fundamental frequency and noise levels as input parameters to generate artificial speech [25].

Lukose and Upadhya [26] presented a Speech Synthesizer based on Formant Synthesis. The synthesis method used is Cascade Formant Synthesis and is implemented for synthesizing English vowels. Although the formant synthesis method produces robotic and unnatural sound, this approach showed high accuracy evaluation results for their implementation. That evaluation was done using Mean Opinion Score (MOS), which is based on how well the listener can clearly understand the output speech.

The artificial voice generated using formant synthesis method is robotic-sounding, which is quite distinguishable from natural speech. However, in systems where a high level of naturalness is not the main goal, formant synthesis can be useful for its reliability and for reducing anomalies in the output when compared to concatenative-based systems. Formant synthesis programs also need less memory than concatenation-based programs, since they do not rely on a large data-store of pre-recorded audio. Accordingly, this method is preferable for embedded devices with limited storage and processing power [6].

2.1.5 TTS for Arabic. Zerrouki et al. [50] structured new voices and defined new TTS conversion rules to mainly tackle diacritization in Arabic for integration with eSpeak. Zangar et al. [51] studied the class-specific modeling approach of the duration in the Arabic sounds to be used for text-to-speech synthesis, and compared it with other modeling approaches such as the HMM-based and the DNN-based modeling. Zine and Meziane [52] proposed a sub-segments-based approach for concatenative Arabic TTS. The authors measured the intelligibility of the synthesized speech using the Diagnostic Rhyme Test (DRT). In a later work, Zine et al. [53] studied the improvement of the Arabic TTS using a sub-segments-based approach by adopting a lemma-based approach for concatenative Arabic TTS.

Amrouche et al. [54] presented a design and implementation of Diacritic Arabic TTS, called GArabic TTS, under MATLAB environment. Abdelali et al. [55] presented automatic diacritization of Maghrebi Arabic dialects, Tunisian and Moroccan, using a character-level deep neural network architecture. Abed et al. [56] studied the effect of diacritics on Arabic speech recognition systems by building and comparing diacritized and nondiacritized models for different corpus sizes. Darwish et al. [57] presented a new Arabic diacritizer that predicts the diacritics of words and then their case endings. A Viterbi decoder was used for diacritics of words and SVM for case endings.

Abdelmalek and Mnasri [58] modified the original unit selection algorithm to be used to design a high-quality Arabic concatenative speech synthesis system, by integrating more phonological, linguistic, and contextual features. Alsaif et al. [59] developed an intelligent Arabic TTS mobile application. They used a set of statistical language models, n-gram for word prediction, and auto-completion for easy typing. For that, a large new Arabic corpus for daily communication in different domains was constructed.

Abdo et al. [60] built a modern standard Arabic audio-visual corpus for TTS. Hadj Ali et al. [61] presented gemination prediction in an Arabic TTS automatic diacritization module using DNNs. Zine et al. [62] developed a web-based assistive platform, based on a TTS API, and used it for learning Arabic language. Rebai and BenAyed [63] presented an Arabic TTS system based on a statistical parametric approach and non-uniform units speech synthesis. It includes a diacritization engine. Fahmy et al. [64] presented an Arabic speech synthesizer using an end-to-end neural deep network architecture called Tacotron 2. It uses a pre-trained English model and a total of 2.41 hours of recorded speech, followed by Wave-Glow to synthesize Arabic speech. Elharati et al. [65] established an automatic Arabic speech recognition system using MATLAB based on MFCC and discrete-observation multivariate HMM and 24 CVCVCV Arabic words.

## 2.2 Optical Character Recognition (OCR) for Arabic

There are a few works on Arabic document layout analysis, such as the work of Bouressace and Csirik [66], in which they applied a convolutional neural network (CNN) to segment an Arabic document image, captured by a smartphone, into its elements. These elements are categorized into 10 classes, including text, author, figure, table, and so on. Eltay et al. [67] explored various deep learning architectures to recognize handwritten Arabic texts offline. That work focused on the issue of having imbalanced datasets for deep learning. Arora et al. [68] presented a text recognition system based on open vocabulary sub-words using the hybrid deep neural network HMM (DNN-HMM) acoustic model used in the automatic speech recognition (ASR). Mohamad et al. [69] recognized printed Arabic letters using their different shapes within words by defining new geometrical features. Mohammad et al. [70] developed a robust offline character segmentation algorithm for printed Arabic text with diacritics based on a contour extraction technique.

Mustafa and Elbashir [71] presented a deep-learning-based method to recognize common Arabic names very quickly, without any segmentation. Qaroush et al. [72] investigated word and character segmentation for printed Arabic text. Word segmentation was performed using a vertical projection and Interquartile Range (IQR) method to differentiate between word gaps and withinword gaps. For character segmentation, a projection profile method was used, along with a set of statistical and topological features that are font-independent. Al-Sheikh et al. [73] reviewed an Arabic OCR dataset of handwritten, printed, and embedded texts. This dataset can be used in different learning algorithms for recognition. The authors also reviewed existing work on Arabic text recognition using various deep learning approaches. Milo and Martínez [74] proposed a new OCR strategy for Arabic using typographic technology based on deep analysis of Arabic script structures.

Darwish and Elzoghaly [75] presented a new offline Arabic OCR model for printed text based on a Genetic Algorithm (GA) and the Fuzzy K-Nearest Neighbor classifier (F-KNN) to enhance the identification accuracy. GA was used as a feature selection algorithm. The F-KNN algorithm was used to classify uncertain data objects. Kadi and Nasri [76] presented a method to extract the features of isolated Arabic characters based on the Hough Transform. Hussein and Hussain [77] proposed a hybrid of a decision tree and an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) for an online Arabic handwriting isolated character recognition system, through the identification of its features and dots.

## 2.3 Similar Assistive Reading Pen Devices

Ok and Rao [78] demonstrated how digital pens can be used to support learning of students with learning disabilities. The authors surveyed existing digital pens such as Reading pens, Optical Character Recognition (OCR) pens, Anybook Readers, and Smart pens. WizCom Tech [79] has developed a reading pen that can be used to scan printed words or lines, record them, and read them. This reader pen also includes a translation function. Examples of OCR pens include C-Pen [80], IRISPen [81], and PenPower WorldPenScan [82]. These are mainly portable scanners the size of a pen. Some of them are Bluetooth-enabled, facilitating the transfer of the recognized text to mobiles or computers, in an editable format. The Anybook readers [78] allow teachers to attach audio notes on the text. Students can then access these audio notes to better understand the text. Smart pens such as Livescribe pens (and its predecessor the FLY Fusion Pen) [83] can be used for taking digital notes from handwritten text, including recording audio and synchronizing it with the handwritten text.

Huang et al. [84] introduced a digital pen named Glissade. Glissade applied haptic feedback on digital pens, called balance shifting feedback, to enhance interactions. There are many studies investigated the benefits of using digital pens in learning. For instance, Chen et al. [85] used the Livescribe smart pen to support paper-based classroom English learning. Chen et al. [86] used the Que-voice digital pen to facilitate oral reading fluency for English learners. The Que-voice contains a built-in speaker and microphone and can read printed text. Tan et al. [87] evaluated the effectiveness of digital pen-based learning for improving the listening comprehension of English learners. Choi et al. [88] evaluated the use digital pens during English picture book reading for increasing a child's interest in learning English. Krish [89] investigated the effectiveness of using audio pen technology to assist in English reading fluency and comprehension and vocabulary skills among preschool children.

Fig. 1. The flowchart of the reader pen algorithm.



## 2.4 Summary

Multiple speech synthesis technologies have been used to generate artificial speech signals, with each technology having its pros and cons, depending on the field of application. The majority of these studies have concentrated on speech synthesis for high-level applications. A few have been implemented using embedded devices. However, those do not support Arabic. Researchers have also been working on several approaches to implement real-time reading systems. Among all the related works mentioned above, there has been little work in real-time reading embedded devices for Arabic, which requires complex processing and more variations in language rules and pronunciation. Some of those embedded systems require phonemes as input, so text-to-phoneme conversion must be done prior to the TTS conversion. Others require manual configuration of a database of recordings. Those that are fully automated do not support Arabic.

Several works have been done on Arabic OCR using different image processing, object recognition, and machine learning approaches. However, none of them has been designed to work with embedded systems in real-time.

Last, a number of similar reading pen assistive devices have been introduced in the literature. Unfortunately, none of them support the use of Arabic language. Moreover, the majority of them are commercial and thus not open source.

With this in mind, this article proposes to answer the following research question:

How could we build a real-time assistive embedded system that serves as a Text-To-Speech reader pen for the Arabic language?

## 3 READER SYSTEM ALGORITHM

In this section, we describe the algorithms that we used for image preprocessing, OCR and speech synthesis. A set of three main processes are executed to get the desired result, as shown in the flowchart in Figure 1. Basic image pre-processing steps are done to reduce the noise of the captured images, convert them to binary images, and normalize and standardize them. Optical Character Recognition (OCR) is then used to convert the pre-processed images to text. Last, Text-To-Speech (TTS) is used to convert the resulting text into speech. We used existing open source tools: Tesseract [29] for OCR and eSpeak NG [46] for TTS, with some tweaking and configurations, as will be explained in the following subsections. The developed programs, tools, and resources will be available (upon request) as open source for developers and researchers.

## 3.1 Image Preprocessing

The purpose of this step is to prepare a stream of images of text captured by a camera to be processed by the OCR engine [28].

There are three pre-processing steps for text images:

- 3.1.1 Noise Reduction. Text images can be noisy. Visual noise is random variation of pixel intensities within an image. Noise reduction is used to remove light and dark spots from the image, making the text easier to classify by an OCR engine in the next step.

There are many filters that could be used for reducing noise. The choice of filter depends on the type of noise within the image. Most digital images have Gaussian noise. To filter Gaussian noise, we use a median filter. This also removes other types of noise.

- 3.1.2 Grayscale to Binary Conversion Using Adaptive Thresholding. The conventional thresholding operation employs a global fixed threshold for all pixels across the image. Adaptive thresholding (which iteratively calculates a local threshold across the image) involves more computation than global thresholding. However, it produces better results with images that have variations in illumination or shadows.

One approach to adaptive thresholding examines the intensity values of the local neighborhood around each pixel and computes the mean value as a sum of the neighboring pixel intensities divided by the neighborhood block size, as shown in Equation (1):



The size of the neighborhood must be large enough to cover enough foreground and background pixels. Otherwise small objects in the image (such as diacritics) might be lost. However, choosing a block size that is too large can produce undesirable results if the image includes significant variations in illumination.

- 3.1.3 Normalizing Images. The reader pen is not always positioned perpendicular to the paper; the user might be tilting their hand when holding the pen. Therefore, words of text might be skewed, and it might be necessary to tilt them upward or downward a few degrees, to make them horizontal.

The de-skewing function expects to receive foreground objects as white pixels and background objects as black pixels. So, after thresholding the image to a binary format, the image is inverted using a bitwise NOT operation.

The calculation of the skew angle is then performed using the minimum bounding box method. A minimum bounding box has the smallest area that encloses all of the white pixels in an object [27]. There are different algorithms for finding the minimum bounding box. For the twodimensional case, we need to find the smallest bounding rectangle.

Rotating calipers is an algorithm designed to solve many computational geometry problems including the bounding box [28]. After finding the bounding box, we calculate the angle of the box, which becomes the skewing angle. We then use a 2D rotation matrix and an affine transformation to normalize the image.

## 3.2 Optical Character Recognition (OCR)

In this section the process of Optical Character Recognition (OCR) is described. After preparing the text images, each binary image produced from previous step is processed by the OCR engine, which converts the images into equivalent text. The OCR software used is Tesseract OCR, which is open source and currently maintained by Google [29]. The OCR process is divided into steps, as shown in the flowchart in Figure 2. Figure 3 shows the pseudo code for our OCR algorithm.

Fig. 2. Flowchart of OCR steps.



Fig. 3. Pseudo code of OCR process.



Fig. 5. Spacing between words in Arabic.



- 3.2.1 Word Segmentation. Arabic script is cursive, where many (but not all) characters in a word are connected together. That is challenging for the word segmenting process, not to mention the dots above and below certain characters, which are also considered part of the character's structure, as shown in Figure 4.

Strings of characters within the cursive script that are connected are called connected components. The first segmentation step finds connected components and stores the outlines of each connected component for the next step. Those outlines are then combined to form blobs, which include isolated characters adjacent to connected components as well as inner outlines or holes within the cursive script.

The blobs are then sequentially organized to represent the lines of the text. Using punctuations as a first delimiter and spacing as a second delimiter, these text lines are broken into words, An example of the spacing between words is shown in Figure 5.

Arabic script includes diacritics and letters with dots. Each of these is initially seen as a connected component with its own bounded box. For proper word segmentation, these boxes must be combined with boxes of the connected components that are above or below them. This is achieved by analyzing the size of the bounding box for each connected component and then sorting and labeling them according to size-as small or large. If a small, connected component exists too close to a large neighboring component, then a bounding box for both the small component and its larger neighbor is constructed. This ensures that the diacritics, and dots, are included within the bounding box containing the word, as shown in Figure 6.

- 3.2.2 Word Recognizer. Figure 7 shows the word recognizer. It includes a Static character classifier, an Adaptive character classifier, and a Character chopper. It uses the Character chopper in a recursive manner when necessary to chop words into characters.

The Character associator attempts to associate each blob with a word by comparing that blob to all the known words stored in the Dictionary. To do so, we used Tesseract OCR software [29], which employs best-first search to find the word with the lowest total distance rating.

If a satisfactory match for the word is not found in the Dictionary, the recognizer uses the Character chopper to iteratively chop the blob into individual characters, finding a first-best match for each character until it reaches the end of the blob. The characters (labeled with their best matches) are also passed to the Adaptive character classifier for training, so character classification results can improve over time.

Fig. 6. Bounding boxes for diacritics, dots, and words.



Fig. 7. Flowchart of word recognizer process.



Once the adaptive classifier has enough samples, it can provide classification results.

- 3.2.3 Character Segmentation. In this step, connected characters are separated using the Character chopper.

The bounding boxes of the connected components are used to construct a projection profile, which is a data structure that stores the number of projected pixels on x and y axes. That profile is then passed to a dynamic programming algorithm that is responsible for choosing the best set of segmentation points by calculating the cost. The cost function is the sum of profile entries at the cut points added to the variance of the spacing between the points.

The variance and the previously combined bounding boxes for small, connected components are combined, as shown in Figure 8.

- 3.2.4 Feature Vector Extraction. The words and characters are stored in the Dictionary as polygons. Thus, their features are extracted using a polygonal approximation method to represent the contours of these objects, as shown in Figure 9. The purpose is to capture the distinctive characteristics of the digitized characters and combine them into feature vectors. The polygonal



Fig. 8. Segmentation points and result.

Fig. 9. A polygonal approximation for an Arabic letter.



Fig. 10. An Arabic character with two different representations.



approximation technique is used in training, because it is invariant to the character size as well as translation and rotation.

In Arabic script, a single character might have up to four different representations, depending on its position within a word, as shown in Figure 10. This means that all these shapes must be mapped to the same classification.

3.2.5 Long Short-Term Memory Neural Network Classification. The method chosen for character classification is a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network, which is a type of Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) [30]. RNNs have the form of a chain of repeating modules-each containing a neural network. In LSTM, each repeating module consists of a memory cell, an input gate, an output gate, and a forget gate.

The memory cell takes an input and stores it for some amount of time, which is similar to applying the identity function ( f ( x ) = x) to the input. The derivative of the identity function is constant; thus, an LSTM network does not have the vanishing gradient problem.

The vanishing gradient problem is a difficulty found in training artificial neural networks with gradient-based learning methods and back propagation. When the neural network's weights receive updates proportional to the partial derivative of the error function, with respect to the current weight, during each iteration of training, each layer calculates the gradient with the effect of the gradient from the previous layer. The problem is that a small gradient will exponentially shrink as it approaches the earlier layers, effectively preventing the weights of those layers from changing value. This completely stops the neural network from further training [30].

Fig. 11. The two main blocks in the TTS engine.



The input gate of the LSTM controls the extent to which a new value flows into the cell. The forget gate controls the extent to which a value remains in the cell [32]. The output gate controls how the memory cell value affects the output of the LSTM unit. Gates are composed of a sigmoid neural net layer and a pointwise multiplication operation.

In this work, we used Tesseract OCR software V4.0.0 [29] that implements the LSTM Neural Network.

3.2.6 Arabic Text Diacritization. After the OCR Engine extracts the text from the scanned images, the resulting text lines are passed to the dicritization engine to enhance the Arabic speech. The engine used is Mishkal dicritization software, which is an open source Python project [31].

## 3.3 Text to Speech Conversion

After the extracted text is diacritized, the resulting text lines are passed to the Text-To-Speech (TTS) engine. For TTS, we used eSpeak NG [46], which is an open source engine that consists of two main units: a Natural Language Processing (NLP) unit and a Digital Signal Processing (DSP) waveform generator.

The NLP unit does the text-to-phoneme conversion, while the DSP unit generates the output speech waveform from the phoneme string. Figure 11 shows the high-level block diagram of the reader pen, highlighting the two main blocks in the TTS engine.

3.3.1 Natural Language Processing (NLP) Unit. The process flowchart of the NLP module is shown in Figure 12, and the NLP process flow is shown as pseudo code in Figure 13.

The NLP unit receives the input text stream from the OCR engine. First, a lexical analysis is performed to break the sentences into tokens by splitting the text at white spaces and punctuation marks-a process known as tokenization. (A token is a discrete element with an identified meaning.)

Aparser then assigns a pronunciation to each token using rule-based analysis, with a dictionary for exceptions. The parser also determines the stress and emphasis positions. The result is then passed to the prosody processor.

The degree of naturalness of the output speech depends on prosodic factors. The Prosody processor determines the required intonation by assigning a proper amplitude and duration to each speech syllable, as well as the duration of pauses. Without prosody the output speech would sound monotonic and non-human like.

Phonetisation is the process of converting the parsed text into its equivalent phonemes. It is also known as grapheme-to-phoneme conversion. A phoneme is the smallest unit of speech sound. It is represented using phonetic notation from the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA), which is an alphabetic system based on the Latin alphabet and is usually written between two slashes. Examples of an Arabic word and its phonetic representation are shown in Figure 14.

Fig. 12. Flowchart of NLP processing components.



Phonemes are stored in a lookup table that contains all the phonemes used by a language, along with their properties, and data for their production, as sounds. Every character in a word is then mapped to its corresponding phoneme, and resulting phonemes are all joined together in a phoneme string. The phoneme string (with its prosody properties) is then passed to the DSP unit, which translates the phoneme string into a speech waveform.

- 3.3.2 The DSP Waveform Generator. The method we chose for speech synthesis is diphone concatenation. A diphone is the transition between two phones. Diphone concatenation puts together a string of previously recorded diphones to generate output speech. This method requires only a minimal speech database, containing one example of each diphone that occurs in

Fig. 13. Pseudocode of the NLP unit.



## /mudaer'risae/

Fig. 14. An Arabic word and its phonetic representation.

a language. Arabic has 38 phones, so the number of diphones is the number of phones squared, which is 1,444 diphones [33].

The DSP waveform generator uses the string of phonemes that it receives from the Text-toSpeech conversion to look up diphones in the Diphone database, as shown in the flowchart in Figure 15.

That diphone stream is then passed to the prosody processing unit, which applies the string of appropriate prosody properties (also received from the NLP unit) to each position within the diphone stream. The resulting diphone string is then passed to the concatenation unit, which produces the speech signal.

The diphone database used in this research was provided by Reference [34]. The database memory size is 6.564 Megabytes. It consists of diphone labels, waveforms, durations, and border positions between phones. The speech used in creating the diphone database must be recorded in a monotonic manner to allow the prosody processor to modulate the intonation of speech as desired.

Diphone synthesis has the advantage of a manageable database size. However, it suffers from sonic glitches, due to discontinuities when concatenating diphone signals. This can result in a robotic-sounding output. To overcome this problem, the 'glitchy' synthesized speech signal is passed through a signal smoothing step, called the Multi-Band Resynthesis OverLap-Add (MBROLA) algorithm.

MBROLA is a time-domain algorithm that works by dividing the speech waveform into small segments and then combining those segments with an overlap-add technique [35]. The OverlapAdd method is an alternative to sinusoidal summation of signals, which is more computationally expensive [36].

Due to limited resources and processing power usually found in embedded devices, this work used the MBROLA light weight method. We used the pre-defined Prosody models and the default values for all input parameters (such as phone duration and F0).

Fig. 15. Flowchart of DSP waveform generator.



## 4 HARDWARE COMPONENTS

This section provides a description of the hardware components that are used in the prototype of the reader pen, as shown in the hardware block diagram of Figure 16.

We chose a Raspberry Pi Zero as a processor for this system, because (1) it can perform complex tasks that involve neural networks, which are needed for optical character classification, and (2) it runs an operating system, so it can execute tasks that require file manipulation.

There are many models and boards available for the Raspberry Pi. We chose to work with Raspberry Pi Zero because of its small chip size and because its hardware specifications meet our system requirements. Moreover, the Raspberry Pi Zero can read a micro SD card. Therefore, the OCR and TTS software systems were embedded to the Raspberry board by installing them on the SD card. A Raspberry Pi Zero board is shown in Figure 17 [37].

The Raspberry Pi Zero specifications are as follows:

- Processor specifications: 1 GHz single-core CPU.
- Ports: Mini HDMI port, micro USB OTG port, micro USB power.
- Memory specifications: 512 MB RAM.
- Camera support: Composite video and reset headers and a CSI camera connector (v1.3 only).

There are many operating systems that work with Raspberry Pi, such as Raspbian Jessie and Minibian-both Debian-based Linux operating systems, as well as Windows 10 IoT Core operating system [38]. During the development phase, we chose to work with Raspbian Jessie, because it has a convenient graphical user interface (GUI) that makes the development of the code easier, with the help of an Integrated Development Environment (IDE). However, a minimized operating system (without a GUI) would be more practical for production, since the GUI requires considerable memory and CPU resources. Freeing those resources would enhance the performance of the program. (Raspbian Jessie Lite is an example of such a minimized operating system.)

Fig. 16. TTS hardware components block diagram.



Fig. 17. Raspberry Pi Zero chip architecture.



The camera used for capturing the text images is a Raspberry Pi camera module, version 2. This camera has a resolution of 8 megapixels, a rolling shutter, and a fixed focus. Since the reader pen will be used to capture really closeup images, the camera focus had to be adjusted using a lens adjustment tool.

The camera is also connected to an infrared-based obstacle detection sensor, which consists of an infrared transmitter and receiver. The infrared transmitter emits an IR signal and, when an obstacle appears, that object reflects the IR light into the receiver. The receiver then signals the camera to start capturing. (The infrared sensing system has an adjustable detection distance.)

To make the reader pen portable, it had to be connected to a battery. However, it is not easy to find a battery that is small, affordable, and capable of providing the power requirements for the Raspberry Pi [39]. The battery we found closest to the requirements is a lithium polymer battery with a voltage of 3.7 volts. A boost circuit is needed to boost that voltage to 5 volts. There are several different models and manufacturers for this boost circuit [40].

Choosing the type of audio output for the Raspberry Pi Zero was difficult, given the fact that it does not have a sound card or even a standard audio jack output. However, the Raspberry Pi Zero W model has a Bluetooth module, which allows it to connect to a Bluetooth headphone. This increases the portability of the device. Figure 18 shows a photo of the prototype.

Fig. 18. The reader pen prototype.



## 5 EXPERIMENTAL EVALUATION

This section describes the experimental methods used to evaluate the OCR (including image preprocessing) and the TTS modules. Our aim was to evaluate the performance of the reader pen in recognizing text and producing speech and make sure that the pen meets the real-time constraints. At first, each of those two modules is evaluated separately. Then, a more general real-time usability testing is performed to provide the final experimental evaluation.

The evaluation tests were performed on a Raspberry Pi Zero W with a single-core 1 GHz CPU, 512 MB RAM, and the Raspbian Jessie operating system.

## 5.1 Evaluation of OCR (Including Image Pre-processing)

Toevaluate the effectiveness of the OCR program (including image pre-processing) experimentally, a set of metrics was used, along with a dataset of Arabic text images. The evaluation focused on two aspects: the accuracy and the response time of the OCR.

The dataset used for testing must be general enough to provide a useful measurement. Arabic Printed Text Image (APTI) [41] is a public dataset that is widely used for evaluating Arabic OCR. It is a word-level dataset, where each text image contains only one Arabic word. This is similar to what a reader pen camera will capture. The APTI text images contain 10 different Arabic fonts, with four styles for each font (plain, italic, bold, and bold italic), as well as different font sizes, from 6 to 24 points. The average image dimension is around 48 × 48 pixels, depending on the font size.

The first metric used was the overall character accuracy for all the tested images, which is the percentage of ground-truth characters that are recognized correctly in an Arabic text image. It is evaluated by comparing the ground-truth text file to the OCR output text file. The character accuracy is calculated by Equation (2):



where c is the number of characters that are recognized incorrectly, and m is the total number of characters in the reference text.
