where e is the number of words that are recognized incorrectly, and w is the total number of words in the reference samples.

The third performance metric is the average response time of the OCR engine. One recent study compared the most common Arabic OCR systems, based on the impact that the quality of the input images (i.e., image resolution) had on the accuracy of these OCR systems [42]. However, the quality of the input images also affects the response time of the OCR. Our experiment tests the response time of the OCR engine for camera-captured images and digital images, over a range of different image sizes.

## 5.2 Evaluation of TTS

In general, there are two methods to evaluate speech quality: (1) the subjective approach, where test subjects are asked to judge the quality of the speech that they hear, and (2) the objective approach, where equipment is used to measure the physical properties of the speech signal [43].

The subjective approach is more time-consuming. However, it is more commonly used, because the end user of a TTS-system is a human listener. Current objective methods (such as signal-tonoise ratio) are better suited to voice communication systems, where the received speech signal can be compared to the original speech signal. No original signal exists when synthesizing speech from text [44].

The Mean Opinion Score (MOS) is a subjective test that has been standardized by the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) and is widely used to measure audio and video quality. It is most commonly used for evaluating synthesized speech quality. Therefore, the MOS test was chosen to evaluate the speech quality of the reader pen [45].

The MOS result is a rational number in the range 1-5, where 1 is lowest quality and 5 is the highest quality. The MOS scale for speech quality is shown in Table 1, while Table 2 shows the scale for rating the listening effort, and Table 3 shows the scale for rating speech loudness [45].

Table 3. Loudness-preference MOS Scale

| Loudness preference         |   Score |
|-----------------------------|---------|
| Much louder than preferred  |       5 |
| Louder than preferred       |       4 |
| Preferred                   |       3 |
| Quieter than preferred      |       2 |
| Much quieter than preferred |       1 |

The MOS is the arithmetic mean over a series of N individual ratings (R1 - Rn) provided by subjects, as they listen to a set of N audio stimuli during a subjective quality evaluation test (see Equation (4)):



ITU recommends the use of seven different questions to evaluate: Listening Effort, Comprehension Problems, Voice Naturalness/Humanlike Voice, Voice Quality, Loudness, Intonation, and Confidence.

The individual speech samples should consist of random simple meaningful sentences. They should be easy to understand, and they should not include technical or scientific terms. The test listeners can be any native speaker of the language, with no hearing disability. The recommended number of listeners should be between 6 and 40 [45].

The reader pen MOS experiment was conducted using an online audio database consisting of seven speech samples that were all synthesized by the TTS software of the reader pen and seven survey questions for each speech sample. The seven survey questions are shown in Table 4. The total number of subjects was 40 listeners, the same seven samples were played for each listener.

## 5.3 Real-time Usability Testing and Evaluation

The purpose of this usability study is to ensure that the proposed Reader Pen is usable and useful, as determined in real-time by a set of target end-users. It measures user satisfaction, in terms of ease of use, and user-friendliness. It also provides design recommendations for the next version of the prototype.

The Higher Council for the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (HDC) introduced us to people with visual disabilities. Ten people participated in our real-time usability testing for the proposed reader pen assistive device. Their task was to read a text using the pen. The subjects were given a tutorial on how to use the pen. They were also asked to comment on the device by filling a usability evaluation form orally. The evaluation sheet is shown in Table 5 [47-49].

The instructions given to the subjects were as follows:

- You are requested to read the following text using our proposed assistive device 'Reader Pen.'
- The Pen will read every word in the text and convert it to speech.
- You are then requested to evaluate the Pen, using the following evaluation sheet. Please indicate, on a scale from 1 to 5, how well you agree with each of the following statements. Ascore of '5' in the form means that you 'strongly agree' with the statement, while a score of '1' means that you 'strongly disagree' with the statement.

## 6 RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

In this section, we present and discuss the results of our experiments regarding the OCR accuracy, the OCR response time, the speech quality, the real-time constraints, and the usability study.

## 6.1 The OCR Accuracy

Figure 19 shows the overall character accuracy percentage for nine different Arabic fonts in plain style in five different font sizes. The fonts were selected because they are most commonly used in Arabic textbooks, due to these fonts being provided in Microsoft Word by default. These overall accuracies were calculated across the 113,284 words in the APTI database.

Figure 20 shows the overall word accuracy percentage for nine different Arabic fonts in plain style in five different font sizes. The overall accuracy was calculated across the 113,284 words in the APTI database.

These accuracy results show that the fonts with the highest character and word accuracy percentage are the Simplified Arabic and the Arabic Transparent fonts. These are the most commonly used fonts in books and newspapers. However, the accuracy results are low for some fonts, such as Andalus, DecoType Naskh, and DecoType Thuluth. The training examples used to train the system were Arabic pages taken randomly from books and newspapers. Some Arabic fonts are not easy to read and are less popular. Therefore, they occurred less frequently in our random training dataset. The result was a much lower recognition accuracy for those fonts.

Figure 21 shows the overall character accuracy percentage in four different image sizes. The overall accuracy was calculated across the 113,284 words in the APTI database for Simplified Arabic font.

## 6.2 The OCR Response Time

The response times for different image sizes are shown in Figure 22.

The results in Figure 22 show that the response time of the OCR program (including image preprocessing) is affected by the quality (i.e. the resolution) of the input images. That response time increases with increasing image dimensions, because larger images fill more memory and require more processing at runtime. According to the results in Figure 21 and Figure 22, the chosen image size for the reader pen is in between 490 × 250 and 750 × 350 to obtain a reasonable response time and an acceptable accuracy.

Fig. 19. Font size versus overall character accuracy.



## 6.3 Speech Quality

The MOS results are shown in Table 6. These results show that most of the features of the speech were judged to be in the Fair-Good range, and users were able to understand the speech. The system achieved an overall MOS score of about 3.54, which is better than the results shown in previous related works. However, the average MOS score for speech naturalness was relatively low, compared to the rest of the scores.

Future work will focus on enhancing the MOS results of the TSS module using state-of-the-art TTS, including Arabic statistical parametric speech synthesis.

## 6.4 Meeting Real-time Constraints

We have designed our Arabic Reader Pen system to be able to meet real-time constraints, which means the system should meet the specified deadline, regardless of the workload. As mentioned in Section 3, the proposed reader system algorithm consists of three main processes: image preprocessing, optical character recognition (OCR engine), and Text-To-Speech conversion (TTS engine). The evaluation of real-time constraints for the OCR module (including image pre-processing) is demonstrated in Section 6.2, where the response time is affected by the image size and quality, as well as other parameters. Keeping these other parameters fixed and adjusting the image size and quality before passing the image to the OCR will ensure that the software meets the real-time constraint. Based on the results of Figure 21 and Figure 22, the optimal image size for the reader pen system to meet the real-time constraints, with an acceptable accuracy, is between 490 × 250 and 750 × 350. Thus, we chose an image size of 640 × 480 for real-time usability testing. As for the TTS module, we used the MBROLA algorithm, which is designed and implemented to meet real-time constraints [35].

Fig. 20. Font size versus overall word accuracy.



Fig. 21. Image size versus overall character accuracy.

- The pen is helpful for users who have low vision and users with reading difficulties such as Dyslexia.

- The size of the pen prototype needs to be smaller and lighter weight.
- The speaking rate and volume should be a user setting, so each user can change it to their preference.

- The speech quality is considered slightly robotic compared to the Voice Over and Talkback screen readers used in iPhone and Android platforms.

The above recorded results suggest that the proposed Arabic reader pen is easy to use and that the users can feel confident while using it. The results also suggest that the pen is useful in reading and understanding printed Arabic text and provides a good solution to enable people with visual and/or learning disabilities to access printed Arabic material in real-time. Of most importance, the proposed pen is fast and suitable in delivering the speech, and thus meets the real-time constraints. Finally, the users would be willing to buy and use the proposed pen if it was available for sale.

However, the results suggest that more work is needed in the overall design and look of the pen. At least two aspects of the design should be considered. First, the pen should not draw any unwanted attention to its users. For example, its size should be smaller, and its weight should be lighter. Second, the pen should provide more control to the users over its operations, such as speaking rate and volume.

Taken together, with an overall average score of agreements of 3.9, the proposed Arabic reader pen is pleasant and satisfying to use. The results of this device can contribute to make printed Arabic material accessible to visually impaired persons and people with learning disabilities.

## 7 CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK

In this article, we proposed to answer the following the research question:

Q: How could we build a real-time assistive embedded system that serves as a Text-To-Speech reader pen for the Arabic language?

A: We developed a real-time assistive reader pen for Arabic that employs Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and Test-To-Speech (TTS) conversion to allow people with visual disability to access printed Arabic text. The system employs LSTM neural networks for optical character recognition, and Arabic speech synthesis is achieved through concatenation synthesis, followed by the MBROLA algorithm. The performance of the OCR module achieved an accuracy of 88%. The performance of the TTS module achieved a Mean Opinion Score (MOS) of 3.53 (out of 5)indicating that the users were able to understand the delivered speech. The current prototype of the Arabic reader pen was used in real-time usability testing with 10 subjects. Overall, the results presented in this article suggest that this prototype was judged to be helpful by people with low vision.

As for future work, the current prototype of the proposed Arabic reader pen assistive device has room for enhancement in the following areas:

- Enhancing the OCR accuracy for some Arabic fonts by adding training data for these fonts and adding text correction stage after the OCR.
- Enhancing the human-like factor in the TTS module.
- Improving the MOS results of the TTS module by using state-of-the-art TTS, including Arabic statistical parametric speech synthesis.
- Evaluating the TTS module objectively by comparing phone duration, F0, and energy values with the target ones.
- Evaluating the TTS module subjectively, through Degradation MOS (DMOS) and preference tests.
- More work will be done on the overall design and look of the Pen to reduce its size and weight.
- The next version of the prototype will provide more control to the users over its operations, such as speaking rate and volume.

Abstract -  The term special needs mean the special educational  needs  that  the  students  who  suffer  from  learning disabilities must have due to several reasons. Learning impairment  is  a  condition  of  the  neurological  system  that impairs one's capacity to efficiently acquire and process knowledge.  Failures  in  diagnosing  the  people  with  learning disabilities have been repeatedly highlighted and remain unpopular  among  people  in  the  developing  countries  like  Sir Lanka. Dyscalculia (difficulties in math), dysgraphia (difficulties in writing) and dyslexia (difficulties in reading) can be  considered as some of the major learning disability issues. The 'mobile application based' solution  'Sankalpa  Math Master'  has  been  created  to  offer  a  game  based  all-in-one solution including screening, and intervention to identify one of the  above-mentioned  learning disabilities  called  'Dyscalculia'. Dyscalculia is generally distinguished by challenges in learning math,  including  organizing  problems,  multi-step  calculations, transposing numbers, distinguishing directions, and understanding  mathematical  signs,  leading  to  confusion  with basic  operations  and  facts.  The  provided  solution  has  been accurate  with  the  use  of  machine  learning  and  deep  learning techniques. In the process of screening with the use of Support Vector Machine (SVM) machine learning algorithm 99.77% of accuracy  level  has  been  obtained.  The  skill  level  prediction process has acquired an accuracy level of 97% with the use of Random  Forest machine learning algorithm. Sri  Lankan traditional education system will be vastly benefited by the high level of accuracy in screening, skill predicting, and other game and voice chat-based activities. The students with special needs will  gain  more  effective  and  personalized  learning  experience which will improve their learning abilities and help to close the technology gap in education.

KeywordsDyscalculia, Probability identification, skill prediction, Image processing, voice enabled chat

## I. INTRODUCTION

The  concept  of  'Special  Educational  Needs'  or 'Special  Needs'  encompasses  students  with  intellectual  or developmental disabilities, and learning disabilities, as examples. When it comes to different parts of the world the Jayawardena C.P.U Dept of Computer Science and Software Engineering Sri Lanka Institute Of Information Technology Malabe, Sri Lanka it20228576@my.sliit.lk

Sanath Jayawardena Dept of Computer Science and Network Engineering Sri Lanka Institute Of Information Technology Malabe, Sri Lanka sanath.j@sliit.lk

term  'special  educational  needs'  has  been  described  in different  ways.  But  in  general,  the  term  'special  education needs'  is  related  to  the  students  who  are  experiencing  the learning difficulties that make them harder to engage in the normal learning process than the students who are in the same age [1]. Learning disability is a diverse set of neurological conditions that affect language  processing,  resulting in difficulties with reading, writing, math, and communication. Several types of learning disabilities exist in the world such as  Dyscalculia,  Dysgraphia,  Dyslexia,  etc.  Referring  to developing  countries  like  Sri  Lanka,  the  term  'learning disabilities' is not amiable with the people due to the lack of knowledge and traditional mind set.

Poor  mathematics  aptitude  imposes  an  enormous cost on both society and affected individuals. This is called 'Dyscalculia' in medical terms [2]. This is one of the abovementioned learning disabilities that have consistent difficulties  using  fundamental  arithmetic  procedures  and memorizing  math  information.  Dyscalculia  is  defined  by difficulty processing numbers and amounts that often appear during  years  of  preschool.  Children  with  dyscalculia  have difficulty with fundamental computations and face difficulties  in  dealing  with  more  complicated  problems  in mathematics.  Computation  rules, deficits in math  facts retrieval processes and Inability to switch from calculation to counting can be identified as such difficulties.

In  the  world  there  are  a  considerable  number  of children suffering with  learning  disabilities  and  remain undiagnosed  due  to deficiency in correct identification process  or  due  to  the  technological  gap.  There  are  several existing  applications  that  have  been  developed  to  screen dyscalculia. But none of them provides 'all in one service' to these children. This problem heavily affects the developing countries like Sri Lanka and undeveloped countries such as Yemen. Children neither get a chance to enjoy the school life nor make a positive bond with studies [3] [4]. When it comes to Sri Lanka, students with learning disabilities can be mostly found themselves out of the main education stream resulted in escalation of high school 'drop-out' rate. Within traditional society,  especially  in  the  countries  like  south  Asia,  parents and  school  authority  pays  a  high  attention  on  talented students over  weak students.  They even do not believe the technology  as  a  remedy  for  the  educational  weakness  of  a child. As per United Nations International Children's Emergency Fund (UNICEF) calculations, 23.5% of children within  the  age  limit  of  5-14  years  are  excluded  from  the normal  educational  stream  and  reduce  participation  in  the general educational activities [5].

Within this research school students from grade 1 to 8  have  been  taken  as  the  sample  to  discuss  the  abovementioned learning disability. Main objective of this research is to carry out a solution to help the school students with a self-study friendly application solution, including screening, intervention,  and  a  skill  prediction  process  for  dyscalculia. The  intervention  includes  'finger  math  concept'  [6]  based activities and 'voice chat bot' [7] based self-support system. During the prediction, guardians can access the application and get the chance to track the development of the children. This has been planned to deliver among school students in both primary and secondary classes.

## II. LITERATURE REVIEW

Learning  disabilities  are  a  neurological  disorder hindering  information  processing,  without  known  cures  or therapies. Limited awareness among parents and instructors in Sri Lanka  leads  to undiagnosed  cases.  International research groups aim to develop tools for dyscalculia detection in children, yielding various solutions through their efforts. Often, solutions aim to identify multiple disabilities, but lack crucial  functionalities.  Some  require  supervision,  making accurate  diagnosis  and  treatment  challenging.  Users  face difficulty  in  diagnosing  conditions  and  require  multiple solutions for comprehensive treatment and predictions.

The 'Dyscalculia Screener' [8] has been developed by Brian Butterworth with the aim of identifying the students between age 6-14, who are suffering with learning disabilities in  mathematics.  He  had  used  several  kinds  of  quizzes including dot enumeration, Number Comparison (also referred to as Numerical Stroop) and Arithmetic Achievement test which only contains addition and multiplication  related  questions.  This  application  is  a  low interactive application used in desktop computers.

' TALASIA' mobile application by Meister Cody is another approach [9]. This was designed by Prof. Dr. JörgTobias Kuhn and Dr. Christin Schwenk. They have provided a  test  to  identify  the  dyscalculic  students  and  have  also provided several training sessions to improve number skills. The activities in this application are mainly based on a land called 'TALSIA' and around a magician and dragons in that country.  This  focuses  the  elementary  students  with  an  age limit of 2 - 4.

But  when  studying  the  process  of  both  above applications  there  were  few  similar  drawbacks  such  as  not using any voice commands to support children, not using IQ test to accurate the result and no skill prediction service for students.

Fingermath - Arithmetic Hand Gesture Game is an Interactive game-based approach for early childhood education [10]. This has been developed especially with the purpose  of  teaching  counting  and  basic  mathematics  skills like addition and collection.  The innovative 'jarimajic' method provides an engaging and effective way for young learners  to  grasp  these  concepts.  Use  hand  images  to  do calculation  games.  But  a  few  downsides  of  this  can  be addressed  as  limited  multiplications  and  low  interactive approach in using hand gestures.

"Nana Shilpa" is a mobile app designed to assist in screening and addressing various learning difficulties [11]. It focuses on verbal dyscalculia, lexical dyscalculia, operational dyscalculia, pragmatic dyscalculia, dysgraphia, and numeric dysgraphia.  They  also  provide  several  small  games  and activities to train the skills of the students. The app utilizes deep learning methods for more effective screening. But as a downside  it  does  not  use  Intelligence  Quotient  (IQ)  level testing, student skill prediction or finger math concepts to get more accuracy to the project.

'MathFun: A Mobile App for Dyscalculia Children' is research done by Rizawati Rohizan, Lim Hean Soon and Dr. Siti Azreena Mubin [12]. This was a mobile application built to help dyscalculic students in learning and engaging in math. It contains learning and exercise processes. They focus on helping students to familiarize themselves with mathematical symbols. Development has been done according to the 'Calculic Model'. But this approach lacks the Dyscalculia detection process, skill prediction process or finger math concepts.

Mohamad  Firdaus Che Abdul Rani, Rizawati Rohizan,  and  Nor  Azlina  Abd  Rahman  developed  a  webbased  solution  for  primary  students  with  dyscalculia  and dyslexia [13]. The solution provides specialized activities and game-based  interactions  to  enhance  their  knowledge  in  an engaging  manner.  There  are  several  counting  and  writing activities  provided.  This  is  mainly  based  on  helping  the students with activities. It does not focus on the screening of the disability.

'Mobile  application for dyscalculia children in Malaysia'  which  has  been  developed  by  Mazeyanti  Mohd Ariffin, Fiqa Azureen Abd Halim, and Norshakirah Abd Aziz [14]is an application that is focusing on the teaching concepts for the dyscalculic students. This application mainly focused on  counting  numbers,  counting  objects,  subtraction,  and addition related operations. This is a  much  more improved application as this has been developed based on the characteristics  of  dyscalculic  students.  The  activity  in  this application  is  based  on  finger  counting  and  motivational sounds like clapping sounds are also included.

Both  above  solutions  are  based  on  only  activitybased  gaming  environment.  These  solutions  lack  some functions like dyscalculia screening, skill prediction, a voice enabled chatting system and fingermath concepts.

Development  and  Standardization  of  Dyscalculia Screening Tool (DST) [15] is the latest dyscalculia screening approach  that  has  been  created  to  screen  the  dyscalculia disability.  In  this  approach  the  participant  has  to  answer several  questions  by  simply  selecting  the  'Yes'  and  'No' buttons.  Selecting  'Yes'  button  adds  0  mark  to  your  total mark and selecting 'No' adds 1 mark to your total mark. The result will be given by the participant based on the total marks obtained. This application only focusses on several predesigned questions but does not focus on the participants' current skills and IQ knowledge.

After  clearly  analyzing  all  the  drawbacks  of  the existing  approaches,  'Sankalpa'  Math  Master  has  been proposed. This new approach provides a more accurate and more  interactive  experience  for  the  students  using  new technologies. Simple and interactive screening process, voice enabled chat bot as a digital instructor, fingermath concept to train the skills and skill prediction process has been supplied in this new approach for this learning disability.

## III. METHODOLOGY

The 'Sankalpa' is a learning platform for students who are suffering from dyscalculia. This mobile application provides some  features such as identifying dyscalculia probability of the student, Voice enables chat bot, Arithmetic learning  system  using  finger  math  concepts  and  provide performance analysis skill level predication. Fig 1 illustrates the system overview of the 'Sankalpa' mobile application.

Fig. 1. System Overview Diagram



- A. Identify the probability of having dyscalculia and determine the study focus area

Fig. 2. Dyscalculia identifying tests component interfaces.



In the Probability identification, several steps were carried out  to  do  the  screening  process  to  identify  the  low  or  high probability of having dyscalculia among school students. To start with, an IQ test was given as shown in the Figure 1, to check the IQ level of the  student.  Meanwhile,  a  small quiz with a few questions was also raised for the guardian to get the data  of  the  student  in  his/her  point  of  view.  Finally,  an interactive mathematical quiz has been carried out to identify the probability of having dyscalculia.

Moving on to the model training process, 551 quiz results have been collected from students who are both dyscalculic and non-dyscalculic. The students belong to both primary and secondary level classes in school. If consider the age, they all belong to the age group between 6-13 years. The model was trained using python language using Jupiter lab. Scikit-learn (Sklearn)  library  was  used  to  create  the  model.  For  the mathematical quiz 2 sets of separate quizzes have been created according to age groups. Only 10 quizzes will be given in one attempt for a one student to face. Each quiz gets 30 seconds to give  the  answer  and  if  a  student  is  unable  to  answer  the question will be skipped with zero marks. MongoDB has been used as the database.

In this context, the process involves performing classification by utilizing a Support Vector Machine (SVM) supervised learning algorithm. Eemploying the SVM algorithm  is  aimed  at  locating  the  hyper-plane  in  order  to accurately  classify  future  data  points.  This  SVM  algorithm helps  to  predict  whether  the  student  has  a  low  or  high probability  of  having  dyscalculia.  To  get  more  accurate models using a non-linear dataset, the polynomial kernel has been used in the training process.

For the probability identification process, the marks of the IQ test that was answered by the student, marks of the questionnaire  answered  by  the  parent  or  the  guardian,  and marks  of  the  mathematical  quiz  performed  by  the  student, have been used. All these features have been fed into the SVM model.  This  helps  to  get  the  output  of  the  SVM  model  to identify the students low or high probability level of having dyscalculia. The student may see the marks they have got for several questionnaires and the final prediction result at the end of the process in a separate page as a summary report.

If the student has a high probability of having dyscalculia, they  will  be  informed  of  the  facilities  provided  within  our application to help them. They will be given a guide of how to use the in-app facilities for their improvement. After getting the results  and  guidance, students can head  on  to the dashboard of the application to start using the other facilities. Students can use this facility again if they need to see whether they  are  cured  or  not.  After  more  medical  professional consultations,  the  decision  has  been  made  to  elevate  the guideline providing facility to a higher level.

- B. Developing a voice-enabled chat bot to assist children with dyscalculia..

Fig. 3. Chatbot  component interfaces.



This voice-enabled chatbot has been designed for children to  offer  an  interactive  and  engaging  arithmetic  learning experience. The chatbot communicates amiably, converting voice  inputs  to  text  for  on-screen  interaction.  It  analyzes children's  questions,  corrects  errors,  and  provides  feedback for better understanding. By suggesting answers and displaying  results,  the  chatbot  acts  as  a  supportive  virtual instructor, enhancing math comprehension, problem-solving skills,  and  fostering  a  positive  learning  atmosphere  for children. [16]

This  employs  Python's  speech  recognition  for  its speech-to-text  capability.  It  effectively  translates  spoken words into text, facilitating seamless user-chatbot interaction.

Utilizing  the  library,  the  chatbot  processes  verbal  input captured  through  the  device's  microphone.  This  versatile library  excels  in  converting  audio  into  corresponding  text, accommodating various sources like  microphones or audio files. Support of it for the multiple voice recognition engines and Application Programming Interface (API)s allows developers to choose the most suitable one, ensuring accurate language support and compatibility across different operating systems.

Once the voice input has been captured and translated to text,  it  can  continue  processing  and  analyzing the  text-based  input  to  extract  necessary  information.  The 'Multinomial  Naive  Bayes  algorithm'  is  used  for  Natural Language Processing (NLP) in the development of the voiceenabled  chatbot.  The  model  has  been  built  using  a  dataset consisting of math-related questions along with their corresponding  answers.  With  the  use  of  this  dataset,  the chatbot  can  be  trained  to  comprehend  user  queries  and provide the most accurate responses. The Multinomial Naive Bayes algorithm was selected for its efficiency when dealing with  text  classification  problems,  which  fits  well  with  the intention of the chatbot, which is to comprehend queries from users and provide appropriate responses. Based on the Bayes theorem,  this approach  assumes  that  characteristics are conditionally independent given the class. It determines the probability that a given text belongs to a specific class and chooses  the  class  with  the  highest  probability  to  be  the predicted class. The chatbot learns from the dataset during the training  phase  by  estimating  the  Multinomial  Naive  Bayes model's parameters. To comprehend the patterns and connections  between  various  concepts  in  mathematics  and related  queries,  it  analyzes  the  question-answer  pairs.  This procedure helps the chatbot to determine the purpose of user inquiries and obtain pertinent information from its knowledge base.  After  the  model  has  been  trained,  the  chatbot  could apply the Multinomial Naive Bayes algorithm to assess user queries. For the provided question, it determines the probabilities  of  different  classes  (such  as  math  topics)  and chooses  the  most  likely  class.  The  chatbot  searches  its knowledge  base  for  the  appropriate  response  based  on  its predicted class and responds to the user with it.

## C. Develop interactive arithmetic learning system

Fig. 4. Finger maths learning component interfaces.



Integrating Image Processing Technology into childhood lessons  fosters  a  dynamic  learning  environment,  tailoring education  to  individual  needs  and  enhancing  engagement. This approach accelerates learning and produces educational activities utilizing image processing software for basic math problem-solving using fingers. The initiative aims to create a reliable classroom tool and contribute to understanding image processing's effectiveness as a teaching aid for  young children, enriching educational practices and knowledge.

For example, one way may  entail employing cameras  to  capture  photos  of  children's  fingers  while  they answer  math  problems.  The  Image  Processing  Technology may  then  evaluate  the  photos  to  determine  whether  the calculations are right. This not only teaches numerical skills but also helps youngsters to learn and build finger coordination [17].

The  use  of  image  processing  technology  to  solve simple math concepts using hand gestures and finger counting is an underutilized solution in online learning.

Utilizing finger math techniques to create lessons on addition, subtraction, and basic multiplication (6 to 10) with interactive live practical tests. Doing that can elevate children's effectiveness and efficiency. And they can easily understand arithmetic concepts and practice arithmetic problems on their own. Make the learning experience more interactive and  fun for children. Children  can  actively participate in the learning process through hand gestures and finger counting. This provides them with immediate feedback on their understanding of math concepts and helps to increase their  engagement  and  motivation.  It  has  the  potential  to enhance the learning experience for children, especially in the early childhood years, by making  it more  interactive, engaging, and effective.

First children can access the lessons and refer to how to  solve  arithmetic  problems  using  finger-math  techniques and they can interact with the device using their hands and fingers to solve arithmetic problems that they learned in the lessons and practice and get the feedback live. The system will generate different types of arithmetic problems automatically and constantly. When children struggle to give the correct answer, the system will help to solve that problem by giving feedback to the children.

To develop a Finger count identification and display finger overlay system first tried using open-cv with a custom dataset. However, after developing a system using Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architecture and many preprocessing techniques, the system struggled a lot. Need perfect lighting conditions, it is hard to identify both hands and  hard  to  display  the  finger  point  overlay.  Performance issues, Lack of accuracy.

This  system  should  be  very  fluid  and  accurate because this system has been designed for small children with Dyscalculia.  And  especially  this  is  a  mobile  application therefore  it  needs  to  be  very  efficient  and  run  on  low-end mobiles.  The  MediaPipe Library developed by Google has been found when searching for different types of technologies to solve these problems. The library also supports displaying finger landmarks overlay on top of the camera feed, which is a significant advantage  for  this system  as  it  enhances interaction  and  greatly  benefits  small  children.  The  Media pipe  library  can  identify  both  hands  at  the  same  time  and detect  21  landmarks  pointing  in  a  single  hand  in  a  single frame. By employing that library and custom finger landmark point values designed for children, the system is refined to accurately  recognize  the  finger  count  on  both  the  left  and right hands. And  the system can identify the fingers respectively  as  their  name.  Using  those  details,  the  system can  identify  fingermath  techniques  and  the  answers  to  the system-generated test question and help the student to interact and learn basic mathematics in a more relaxed fun way.

## D. Dyscalculia Student's Academic Performance Skill level predication

Fig. 5. Teacher Dashboard and Student's skill level predication component interfaces



The  proposed  system  called  'Sankalpa'  provides  the ability to predicate the skill level of the dyscalculia student and more other features to enhance the quality of education for students who suffer from dyscalculia. Teachers can use the skill prediction process to input the assignment marks of their  students  and  other  details.  The  marks  have  been collected and analyzed to assess the mathematical abilities of the students and identify any challenges they may face due to dyscalculia. Parameters such as class test marks, assignment marks, and overall performance in mathematical assignments are  considered.  This  data  has  been  subsequently  used  to predict  the  skill  level  and  academic  performance  of  each student.

To  develop  the  prediction  model,  the  application utilizes Machine Learning (ML) techniques. The model has been trained using a dataset that includes information on the performance of dyscalculia students in their class assignments. Based on this training data, the ML model can analyze the assignment marks provided by the teacher and provide  a  level indicating each  student's skill level in mathematics  and  their potential  academic  performance. Jupyter notebook has been used to implement this process. It is  open-source  software,  open  standards,  and  services  for interactive computing across multiple programming languages. The data has been organized using this tool. Then supervised neural network has been designed to train the data and extract information from the data. In our experimental case,  we predict the student's performance. In this system, student  performance  has  been  predicted,  and  the  accuracy percentage has been determined. Once the prediction process has  been  completed,  the  application  presents  the  results, including  the  predicted  skill  level,  academic  performance score,  and  any  additional  insights  or  recommendations. Teachers  can  utilize  this  information  to  understand  their students' mathematical abilities and plan appropriate teaching strategies.

If  the  prediction  suggests  that  a  student  may  have difficulties or a lower skill level in mathematics, the application provides intervention options that are accessible to  teachers.  These  interventions  may  involve  personalized study plans, additional practice exercises, or recommended educational resources designed to address the specific needs of each student.

Additionally,  the  application  allows  teachers  to access comprehensive reports that include the results of the Skill  prediction  process  and  could  notify  the  feedback personally  to  the student  profiles.  This  feature  enables teachers to  monitor the development of their students over time and make informed decisions about ongoing interventions and academic support.

The  Sankalpa  application  provides  a  teacherfocused feature that allows for the input and analysis of class assignment  marks  to  predict  the  skill  level  and  academic performance of dyscalculia students. It offers targeted interventions  and  support,  empowering  teachers  to  guide their  students  toward  improved  mathematical  abilities  and academic success.

## IV. RESULTS AND DISCUSSIONS.

## A. Identify the probability of having dyscalculia and determine the study focus area

The SVM model was fed with the data that were collected from  schools  and  therapy  centers.  The  above-mentioned features were used to train the SVM classification algorithm. 99.77% accuracy could be achieved by the algorithm for the probability  detection.  The  test  accuracy  was  shown  nearly 98.5%.

## B. Developing a voice-enable chat bot to assist childern with dyscalculia.

The Multinomial Naive Bayes algorithm has been used as the algorithm to proceed with the voice enabled chat bot. The model has been trained using this algorithm and this uses a theorem called Bayes theorem to proceed. The data set has been  fed  into  the  algorithm  and  trained  to  get  the  best accuracy in test and result data.

## C. Develop intractive arithmatic learning system

Media  Pipe  Hand  is  an  exceptional  machine  learningbased library that stands out with its real-time hand detection and  tracking  capabilities,  providing  precise  21  2D  hand landmarks.  It's  ensuring  real-time  performance  on  mobile devices.  With  an  impressive  accuracy  of  95.7%  for  palm detection and 91% for hand landmark detection, it can reliably handle occlusions and lighting variations, delivering consistent and robust results. Its unique ability to detect and track  multiple  hands  simultaneously  makes  it  particularly valuable for complex hand interactions and group scenarios.

## D. Progress analysis and Skill performance level predication

The  Random  Forest  model  was  utilized  to  analyze  a dataset consisting of 1024 samples. This dataset was employed as training data for the Random Forest classification  algorithm.  The  model  was  trained  using  five specific  features  to  predicate  children's  skill  level  in  four development phases. The results demonstrated a remarkable accuracy rate of approximately 98% in skill predication.

To  evaluate  the  model's  performance  further,  1/3  of instances  were  selected  for  testing  purposes.  Impressively, the Random Forest model correctly classified testing accuracy  rate  of  97%.  Only  one  instance  was  incorrectly predicted, highlighting the model's effectiveness in accurately predicting the skill level of the student.

## V. CONCLUSION

There  were  limited  research  projects  conducted  in the field of learning disabilities, particularly in fulfilling the requirements  mentioned.  However,  an  innovative  mobilebased  solution  called  "Sankalpa"  has  been  developed  to address this gap. This solution offers various features, including the ability to identify the probability of dyscalculia in  students,  a  voice-enabled  chatbot,  an  arithmetic  learning system using finger math concepts, and Skill level predication for dyscalculia school students.

Currently, the "Sankalpa" application is available on the  Android  platform  and  supports  the  native  language, Sinhala. However, there are plans to expand its reach in the future. The goal is to make the solution accessible in multiple languages, including support for platforms like iOS, and even provide a web-based version. By pursuing these enhancements,  the  aim  is  to  develop  a  comprehensive  and improved solution that fulfills the aforementioned requirement.

## Self-adaptive  Learning  Algorithm as  a  Tool  for  the  Development and  Strengthening  of  the  Dyslexic Student's  Skills  in  the  Study  of  Musical Composition

## Michele  Della  Ventura

Abstract In  this  period,  the  topic  of  Artificial  Intelligence  (AI)  is  at  the  center  of various  discussions  that  mainly  concern  the  teaching/learning  system  and  the  contribution  that  AI  can  make  in  the  classroom.  From  a  naturally  inclusive  perspective, technologies  (based  on  AI)  from  the  early  stages  of  design  and  development  must take  into  consideration  the  needs  of  all  students,  without  neglecting  dyslexic  students. In  that  sense,  the  main  problem  is  represented  by  the  ability  of  these  tools  to  support the  dyslexic  student  in  studying  and  not  in  carrying  out  the  assigned  tasks  for  him/ her.  This  research  paper  presents  an  algorithm  (which  combines  the  Viterbi  algorithm  with  the  Markov  process)  designed  and  developed  to  enhance  the  learning process  of  a  dyslexic  student  in  the  area  of  Music  Composition,  in  particular,  in  the harmonization  of  a  melodic  line.  The  harmonization  of  a  melodic  line  involves  many cognitive  processes  and  systems  and  a  learning  disability  may  lead  to  over-fatigue and to a psychological  distress  of the student, with the  subsequent  loss  of  confidence  and  personal  motivation.  The  algorithm  looks  like  a  tutor  able  to  support  the student  through  suggestions  during  the  harmonization  of  a  musical  melody  (and  not by  providing  the  solution).  The  experimental  results  show  that  the  algorithm,  given a  melodic  line,  is  able  to  correctly  generate  a  bass  line  as  well  as  harmonize  each sound  of  the  melodic  line.  It  is  also  demonstrated  (through  a  case  study)  that  the  algorithm  can  have  a  positive  impact  on  dyslexic  students'  motivation  and  engagement in  learning.  Finally,  educational  implications  and  research  suggestions  are  provided based  on  the  research  results.

Keywords Artificial  intelligence · Dyslexia · Educational  technology · Hidden Markov  Model · Melodic  harmonization

## 1 Introduction

Nowadays,  the  introduction  of  Artificial  Intelligence  (AI)  in  the  classroom  represents  a  necessary  breakthrough.  However,  this  tool  must  be  used  with  awareness  and knowledge  of  the  facts:  with  proper  use,  AI  can  represent  a  valid  and  valuable  aid for  the  learning  process.  The  use  of  technology  (based  on  AI)  in  the  classroom  is, however,  one  of  those  divisive  issues.  In  fact,  it  is  very  often  commonly  believed that  too  much  technology  limits  creativity  and  at  the  same  time  offers  shortcuts  for students  (and/or  teachers).  Instead,  it  is  necessary  to  become  aware  of  the  many  possibilities  that  these  tools  offer  and  of  the  importance  they  cover,  whether  we  like  it  or not,  in  the  learning  process  of  students  in  general  but  above  all  of  dyslexic  students. These  tools  should  not  provide  the  student  with  the  solution  to  a  problem,  but  help the  student  find  the  appropriate  solution  to  the  problem.  This  necessarily  implies  that AI-based  tools  must  be  adequately  designed,  through  a  fruitful  and  fertile  integration of  multiple  strategies  that  can  avoid  the  creation  of  educational  resources  that  are by  their  nature  deficient  [1].  The  growing  openness  of  the  Educational  Technology World  to  inclusion  can  be  traced  in  the  trend  of  the  main  teaching  tools  to  satisfy the  needs  of  personalized  learning  [2]  where  the  software  should  act  as  an  empathic mediator  to  strengthen  motivation,  awareness,  and  mastery  of  the  student's  learning process  [3].  New  technologies  must  guarantee  the  acquisition  of  skills  useful  for individual  growth,  and  therefore,  combine  the  use  of  resources  and  tools  with  the possibility  of  developing  critical  thinking  and  producing  multimedia  artifacts  from scratch.  To  enhance  the  creativity  and  aptitudes  of  individual  students,  it  is  necessary to  stimulate  their  aptitudes,  generating  curiosity,  and  introducing  them  to  new  fields of  study  [4].

In  the  field  of  music  and  more  specifically  in  the  area  of  musical  composition, several  algorithms  have  been  developed  that  are  able  to  compose  music,  using  Markov chains  [5-7]  or  neural  networks  [8-10].  The  most  recent  advances  in  the  field  of deep  learning  have  opened  the  way  for  a  number  of  new  methods  for  generating music  [11-14].  However,  all  of  these  systems  for  music  composition  focus  largely on  autonomous  generation:  little  work  in  this  domain  has  been  addressed  regarding issues  related  to  the  support  of  the  student  (and  not  of  the  'musician')  in  educational activities.

In  the  educational  field  (in  general  but  more  specifically  in  the  music  field),  the AI  should  help  the  student  to  improve  his/her  critical  thinking  [15]  and  consequently his/her  creative  thinking  [16]:  the  AI  should  teach  the  student  to  look  at  things  from different perspectives, to test hypotheses, and to find creative solutions to  problems.  Critical  thinking  helps  the  student  to  make  informed  decisions,  solve  problems effectively,  and  develop  independent  thinking.  This  is  important  for  all  students  but becomes  crucial  for  the  dyslexic  student.

Starting  from  these  assumptions,  this  paper  presents  an  algorithm  able  to  support the  dyslexic  student  in  harmonizing  a  melodic  line,  providing  visual  suggestions  that have  the  purpose  of  guiding  the  student  toward  the  search  for  a  solution:  harmonization  of  each  sound  of  the  melodic  line  avoiding  the  errors  provided  by  musical grammar.  The  algorithm  is  based  on  the  concept  of  deep  learning,  and  thanks  to  the training  phase  it  is  able  to  support  the  student  through  the  Markov  Decision  Process.

The  structure  of  this  paper  has  been  organized  as  follows.  Section  2  explains  the principles  behind  the  harmonization  of  a  melody.  Section  3  explores  the  concept of  'dyslexia',  which  underlies  the  proposed  algorithm.  This  is  followed  (Sect.  4) by a description of the method  used  to achieve the goal. Section 5  shows  some experimental  evidence  illustrating  the  effectiveness  of  the  proposed  method.  Finally, in Sect. 6, the paper concludes with concluding remarks on current issues and future  research  possibilities  with  respect  to  the  efficient  improvement  of  educational practices  and  technologies.

## 2 Melody  Harmonization

Along  with  rhythm  and  melody,  harmony  is  one  of  the  three  constitutive  elements of  the  music.  Leaving  aside  the  concept  of  rhythm  which  is  not  the  object  of  this research,  the  melody  can  be  defined  as  a  succession  of  sounds  with  complete  meaning (see  Fig.  1a),  while  the  harmony  represents  the  simultaneity  of  two  or  more  sounds built  under  each  sound  of  the  melody  (see  Fig.  1b)  [17].

Harmonizing  a  melody  line  means  arranging  a  melody  in  a  harmonic  context, submitting  a  sound  texture  to  the  music,  and  choosing  and  evaluating  the  alternatives between  the  possible  chords  [17,  18].  The  musical  chord  consists  of  the  superimposition  of  several  sounds  that  are  performed  simultaneously  (see  Fig.  1b).  When  a chord  is  arranged  in  overlapping  thirds,  it  is  said  to  be  in  the  fundamental  state  (see Fig.  2a):  in  this  case,  the  lowest  note  is  called  fundamental,  and  the  other  two  notes are  called  third  and  fifth  (seventh,  …).  If,  on  the  other  hand,  the  chord  is  in  a  position in  which  the  root  is  not  the  lowest  note,  it  is  said  that  the  chord  is  in  an  inverted  state: first  position  and  second  position  (see  Fig.  2b).  From  this,  it  follows  that  each  sound of  the  melody  can  belong  to  different  chords  (see  Fig.  3).

During  his  harmonization,  the  student  must  understand  which  chord  each  sound belongs  to on the basis of the previous chord and how  the following  chords  are intended  to  be  developed.  When  choosing,  two  important  sounds  must  be  taken  into consideration:  the  upper  and  lower  sound  of  the  chord  which  represents  the  bass,  and the  soprano  (the  lower  note  gives  depth  to  the  chord  and  the  upper  one  is  the  most perceptible  to  the  human  ear)  [18].

Fig.  1 Example  of  melody  and  its  harmonization



Fig.  2 Example  of  musical chords

Fig.  3 Examples  of  possible musical  chords  for  the  C  note of  the  melody





For  this  reason,  before  harmonizing  a  melodic  line,  the  student  learns  to  harmonize a  bass  line  (which  makes  it  easier  to  learn  the  many  musical  grammar  rules)  trying  to build  an  interesting  melodic  line.  For  each  sound  of  the  bass  line,  the  student  is  able to  precisely  define  which  are  the  other  sounds  of  the  chord  (tenor,  alto,  and  soprano) and  only  has  to  decide  their  arrangement  to  develop  the  melody  (see  Fig.  4).  Being that  the  harmonization  must  be  done  in  4  voices  (see  Fig.  1c)  and  that  instead  a  chord is  composed  of  only  3  sounds,  the  musical  grammar  imposes  that  a  sound  of  the chord  is  doubled  in  one  of  the  4  voices,  according  to  the  scale  degree  of  the  bass  line sound.  This  offers  the  possibility  to  modify  the  trend  of  the  melodic  line  (see  Fig.  4a and  b).

In  harmonizing  the  melody,  on  the  other  hand,  the  student  must  understand  which chord  each  sound  belongs  to:  it  is  an  important  choice  that  requires  time  (due  to  the many  possibilities  that  each  sound  can  have,  as  seen  in  Fig.  3)  and  concentration  and which  therefore  it  can  lead  the  student  (especially  dyslexic)  to  lose  motivation  and abandon  the  exercise.

The  algorithm  presented  in  this  document  intends  to  help  the  dyslexic  (and  nondyslexic)  student  in  the  harmonization  of  the  melody,  suggesting  (where  necessary) which  sound  can  be  present in the bass line for each sound  of the  melody.  This allows  the  student  to  know  the  two  most  important  sounds  of  the  chord  (bass  and soprano)  and  to  apply  the  previous  knowledge  acquired  during  the  harmonization of  the  bass  line:  the  graphical  representation  (as  written  in  paragraph  3)  helps  the dyslexic  student  to  memorize  certain  situations  and  to  know  how  to  recognize  and reproduce  them  when  they  arise.

Fig.  4 Example  of  different  bass  line  harmonization



## 3 Dyslexia  Versus  AI  (and  Vice  Versa)

How  can  AI  support  the  learning  process  of  the  dyslexic  student?

Dyslexia  does  not  depend  on  subjective  psychological  factors,  low  motivation to  study,  or  low  intelligence.  Dyslexia  consists  of  the  difficulty  of  automating  the process  of  decoding  the  graphic  signs  that  characterize  the  written  text  [19].  This difficulty  has  repercussions  on  the  performance  which  is  often  characterized  by  low reading  speed  and/or  poor  accuracy  and  this  can  compromise  the  understanding  of  the text  [20].  This  may  mean  difficulties  in  understanding  the  rules  of  musical  grammar and  consequently  little  or  no  practical  application  of  the  concepts,  i.e.,  difficulties  in harmonizing  the  sounds  of  the  melody.

The  natural  compensatory  tool  of  the  person  with  dyslexia  is  the  development of  the  prediction  skill,  i.e.,  ' guessing  the  words  while  reading ' [20,  21].  In  harmonizing the melody,  it is necessary  to  avoid  this  instrument  becoming  the  lifeline: harmonization  requires  a  lot  of  energy  and  concentration,  because  it  is  necessary  to identify  the  sounds  of  each  chord  and  these  depend  on  the  sounds  that  make  up  the previous  chord  and  how  you  intend  to  build  harmony  in  subsequent  chords.  Trying to  'guess'  the  sounds  of  the  chord  could  lead  the  student  to  make  mistakes  (based  on musical  grammar).  Dyslexia  involves  a  reading  difficulty  that  can  be  compensated  if the  information  is  provided  through  oral  channel  support  (such  as  an  audio  message, an  audio  file,  …)  [22]  or  the  visual  one,  for  example,  using  images  [23].  It  is  immediately  clear,  therefore,  how  important  it  is  for  the  dyslexic  student  the  use  of  study material  that  is  not  only  present  in  written  mode,  but  also  in  graphic  mode.  In  textbooks,  the  rules  of  musical  grammar  are  always  explained  by  the  written  text  (rich  in specific  technical  terminology)  followed  by  images  representative  of  the  final  result that  would  be  obtained  from  their  application.  In  other  words:  given  some  sounds of  the  melody  is  proposed  an  image  that  shows  its  harmonization  on  the  basis  of  the rules  explained,  and  it  is  up  to  the  student  to  understand  the  movement  of  the  sounds of  the  various  voices  between  the  chords  that  follow.  The  difficulty  of  understanding the  written  text  is  added  to  the  difficulty  of  interpreting  the  image.  It  goes  without saying  that  it  is  not  enough  to  simply  change  the  mode  of  presentation  to  eliminate any  difficulty [24]: it is necessary,  in fact, that the  student  with  dyslexia  learn to recognize  certain  melodic  situations  (for  example,  a  melodic  progression,  a  stylistic feature,  …)  and  to  harmonize  them  (adding  to  each  melody  sound  the  sounds  that characterize  the  musical  chord  and  making  the  sounds  move  correctly  between  one chord  and  the  next).

In  order  to  acquire  an  effective  method  of  study,  the  student  with  dyslexia  must be supported [25] by the teacher and by the use of appropriate educational and technological  tools  called  'compensatory  tools'.  Compensatory  tools  (IT  or  not)  are always  aimed  at  the  acquisition  of  autonomy  [22]:  they  need  an  initial  learning  phase to  be  used  at  their  best  and  their  aim  is  to  improve  skills  and  autonomous  learning. Basically,  a  good  compensation  tool  is  one  that  requires  little  effort  in  learning  how  to use  it,  that  is  simple  and  immediate  and  that  leaves  intact,  in  its  user,  the  resources  and energies  to  decide  on  the  activities  of  study  and  understanding  of  concepts.  It  should be  stressed  that  compensatory  technologies  do  not  'compensate  in  themselves'.  In order  for  users  to  be  effective,  they  must  also  develop  in  parallel  a  'compensatory competence',  that  is,  a  strategy  that  allows  them  to  make  the  best  use  of  the  tool  and integrate  it  effectively  in  the  learning  phases.

Compensatory  tools,  based  on  AI,  can  play  a  fundamental  role  in  the  implementation  of  inclusive  teaching.  Through  the  use  of  technologies,  the  dyslexic  student  can be  allowed  to  do  what  he  otherwise  could  not  do,  or  to  do  it  with  less  expenditure  of energy,  or  to  do  it  in  a  more  independent  or  safe  or  psychologically  more  acceptable way  [26].

The  algorithm  object  of  this  research  takes  its  cue  from  the  above  considerations and  presents  itself  as  a  support  tool  for  the  dyslexic  student,  with  the  aim  of  guiding him  in  the  correct  harmonization  of  a  melodic  line  through  the  suggestion  of  the possible  sounds  of  the  bass  line,  leaving  the  completion  of  the  tenor  and  contralto lines to the student. In this way, the student has the possibility to observe (and memorize)  how  the  movements  of  the  melody  and  the  bass  line  vary  without  the interference  of  other  sounds.

## 4 The  Proposed  Model

This paragraph  illustrates the general architecture of the  algorithm  designed  and developed  on  the  basis  of  the  concepts  presented  in  paragraphs  2  and  3.  In  summary:

- (1) the  melodic  line  and  the  bass  line  represent  two  fundamental  elements  of  the harmony  of  a  musical  piece:  the  trend  of  the  first  is  closely  connected  to  the second  (and  vice  versa);
- (2) the  ascending  or  descending  movement  of  the  sounds  of  the  melodic  line  depends on  the  movement  of  the  sounds  of  the  bass  line  (and  vice  versa):  these  determine the  arrangement  of  the  sounds  of  the  other  voices  (tenor  and  alto);
- (3) the  ascending  or  descending  movement  of  a  sound  of  the  melody  depends  on the  degree  of  the  scale  of  the  sound  of  the  bass  line,  and  therefore,  on  which sound  of  the  chord  is  doubled  (see  example  in  Fig.  4);
- (4) the  graphic  representation  is  an  important  compensatory  tool  for  the  dyslexic student:  it  represents  the  educational  mediator  to  recall  content  related  to  specific concepts  [23];
- (5) in  the  harmonization  of  the  melody,  the  possibility  to  define  the  sounds  of  the bass line with the of the AI prevents the dyslexic student from  resorting to the  use  of  the  prediction  skill  and  allows  him/her  to  do  what  he/she  otherwise would  not  could,  or  to  do  it  with  less  expenditure  of  energy,  or  to  do  it  in  a  more independent  or  secure  or  psychologically  more  acceptable  way:  in  other  words, AI  can  be  a  useful  tool  to  motivate  the  student.

The  algorithm  starts  from  a  fundamental  assumption: a  sound  of  the  melodic  line has  an  ascending  or  descending  movement  that  depends  on  the  sound  of  the  bass line,  which  makes  it  possible  to  identify  the  degree  of  the  musical  scale  to  which  the chord  belongs,  which  in  turn  defines  the  sounds  of  the  chord  and  which  ones  can  be doubled.

Fig.  5 Example  of  transition  matrix



This  can  be  represented  by  a  transition  matrix Pt that  is,  for  Markov  chain  { X } at time t, a  matrix  containing  information  on  the  probability  of  transitioning  between states.  In  particular,  given  an  ordering  of  a  matrix's  rows  and  columns  by  the  state space  S,  the  ( i , j )th  element  of  the  matrix Pt is  given  by



For  the  algorithm,  the  matrix  represents  the  probability  that  one  degree  of  the  musical scale  Xt resolves  on  another  degree  of  the  musical  scale  (Fig.  5a,  column  1  and  row 1)  [5].

However,  this  is  not  enough  to  describe  the  movement  of  the  sounds  of  the  melody in  the  transition  from  one  chord  to  another.  It  is  necessary  to  consider  simultaneously both  the  ascending  or  descending  movement  of  the  sound  of  the  melodic  line  (Fig.  5b, column  3  and  row  3)  and  the  number  of  semitones  that  characterize  this  movement (Fig.  5b,  column  2  and  row  2).

The  probabilities  calculated  on  the  training  corpus  are  associated  with  the  possible transitions  between  the  various  states  [27]:  starting  from  any  state Si ,  the  next  sound of  the  melody  will  be  attributable  to  a  given  state Sj with  a  certain  probability



where C ( Si , Sj )  is  the  count  in  the  corpus  of  occurrences  of  the  sequence Si  S j , C ( Si ) is  the  count  in  the  corpus  of  occurrences  of Si and N is  the  number  of  states.  All probabilities P ( Si | Sj )  are  entered  into  the  transition  matrix.

If  with  the  transition  matrix,  it  is  possible  to  describe  the  trend  of  the  melody, to  define  the  bass  line  (which  will  determine  the  degree  of  the  musical  scale,  and therefore,  allow  the  identification  of  the  sounds  of  the  chord  and  their  arrangement), it  is  possible  to  use  the  Viterbi  algorithm  (associated  to  the  transition  matrix),  which with  a  dynamic  programming  approach,  allows  to  analyze  the  paths  between  states starting  from  the  initial  state  going  through  the  successive  states  identifying  the  best path  in  relation  to  the  given  emissions  [27].  The  probability  of  the  most  probable path  ending  in  state k with  observation i is



where i represents  the  probability  of  observing  element i in  state l , j represents  the probability  of  the  most  probable  path  ending  at  position x -1  in  state k with  element j ,  and p kl represents  the  probability  of  the  transition  from  state l to  state k .

## Training  Phase

The  use  of  the  algorithm  has  provided  a  training  phase  consisting  in  the  reading  of musical  pieces  composed  in  the  form  of  a  4-voice  choir  (soprano,  alto,  tenor,  bass) which  included  fifth  chords  (such  as  C-E-G)  and  seventh  chords  (such  as  C-E-G-B), the  inversions  of  these  types  of  chords  and  that  there  were  no  modulations  (i.e.,  key changes).  The  musical  pieces  were  in  MIDI  format:  a  digital  format  that  does  not require  complex  information  decoding  operations  (therefore,  greater  speed  in  the phase  of  chord  analysis  and  compilation  of  the  transition  matrix)  and  of  which  it  is possible  to  find  a  well-stocked  database  online.  The  transition  matrix  did  not  have any  default  setting  regarding  the  dimensions,  but  on  the  contrary,  it  was  automatically resized  during  the  reading  of  the  chords  (based  on  the  type  of  each  chord,  the  degree of  the  scale  of  the  chord,  the  ascending  or  descending  movement  of  the  melody  sound in  the  concatenation  of  two  consecutive  chords).

## Testing  Phase

During  the  training phase, the algorithm  was  tested  to verify its functionality. In particular,  the  algorithm  was  asked  to  read  a  melody  and  propose  possible  solutions for  the  bass  line.  The  goal  was  to  look  at  the  algorithm  as  it  was  defined  and  inspect it  carefully  for  imprecisions,  so  as  to  be  able  to  identify  which  melodic  passages represented  an  obstacle  for  the  algorithm,  create  set  tests  suitable  for  verifying  the overcoming  of  those  defects  and  prepare,  therefore,  an  update  of  the  training  phase with  the  reading  of  musical  pieces  with  specific  characteristics.

It  emerged  that  (see  Table  1),  as  the  reading  of  the  number  of  possible  cases  of concatenation  of  musical  chords  increased  (training  phase):

- -the  possibility  of  the  bass  line  not  being  completed  decreased  (Table  1  column  2);
- -the possibility that the sounds  of  the bass line represented  grades  of  the scale whose  sequence  was  not  correct  (according  to the rules  of  musical  grammar) decreased  (Table  1  column  3);
- -the  possible  solutions  for  the  bass  line  (corrected  from  the  point  of  view  of  musical grammar)  increased  (Table  1  column  4).

Table  1 Analysis  of  the  algorithm  solutions

|   Number of chords |   Uncompleted bass line (%) |   Uncorrected grade sequence (%) |   Possible solutions (%) |
|--------------------|-----------------------------|----------------------------------|--------------------------|
|                500 |                          96 |                              100 |                        0 |
|               1000 |                          87 |                               81 |                        1 |
|               1500 |                          72 |                               67 |                        1 |
|               2000 |                          59 |                               55 |                        1 |
|               3000 |                          31 |                               41 |                        2 |
|               4000 |                          28 |                               26 |                        2 |
|               5000 |                          24 |                               18 |                        3 |

As  already  demonstrated  by  the  various  experiences  of  deep  learning,  for  a  better performance  of  the  algorithm,  it  is  necessary  to  analyze  a  large  number  of  cases.  As regards  the  present  research,  it  was  important  to  maximize  the  number  of  possible solutions  of  the  algorithm  (corrected  according  to  the  rules  of  musical  grammar) (see  Table  1  column  4)  to  support  the  student  with  greater  accuracy  avoiding  loss  of motivation,  and  to  give  the  student  interpretative  freedom  (creativity).

## 5 Evaluation:  A  Case  Study

The  first  tests  to  verify  the  algorithm  were  carried  out  by  3  teachers  of  music  composition,  who  had  the  task  of  verifying  the  proposed  solutions  and  identifying  possible integrations  of  the  training  data.  Subsequently,  a  group  of  students  (identified  by  the 3  teachers)  was  asked  to  use  the  algorithm.

The  test  was  conducted  for  a  time  period  of  4  months  (from  January  2023  to  April 2023)  and  involved  12  students,  5  girls,  and  7  boys  (aged  15-16),  of  which  6  were affected  by  dyslexia:  all  of  them  had  similar  educational  backgrounds.

During  the  first  month,  the  students  participated  in  the  lessons  and  carried  out  the proposed  activities,  without  using  the  algorithm.  The  teacher  monitored  the  students' behavior  and  corrected  the  exercises  by  providing  suggestions  and  further  explanations  (where  necessary).  At  the  end  of  the  month,  an  examination  was  passed  in  the classroom  consisting  of  the  harmonization  of  a  melody,  identical  for  non-dyslexic and  dyslexic  students.

The  result  supplied  important  information  so  as  to  be  able  to  continue  with  the project.  In  particular,  it  emerged  that:

- 6  students  harmonized  all  the  melody  (of  which  1  dyslexic  student);
- 2  students  (with  dyslexia)  harmonized  less  than  40%  of  the  melody.
- 4  students  harmonized  about  60%  of  the  melody  (of  which  3  dyslexic  students);

In  February,  the  teacher  introduced  the  algorithm  to  the  students,  who  were  able to  start  using  it  while  carrying  out  exercises.

At  the  end  of  the  month,  a  classroom  examination  was  carried  out,  assigning  the same  test  to  all  students  and  allowing  them  to  use  the  algorithm.  The  results  supplied the  hoped-for  information:

- 9  students  harmonized  all  the  melody  (of  which  3  dyslexic  students);
- 1  student  (with  dyslexia)  harmonized  about  80%  of  the  melody.
- 2  students  (with  dyslexia)  harmonized  about  90%  of  the  melody;

In  the  following  two  months  (March  and  April)  the  students  continued  to  use  the algorithm  during  the  various  activities  proposed  by  the  teacher,  acquiring  greater autonomy  which  was  confirmed  in  the  last  test  proposed  at  the  end  of  the  course:  it harmonization  of  a  melody  without  using  the  algorithm.

The  results  were  satisfactory:

- 8  students  harmonized  all  the  melody  (of  which  2  dyslexic  students);
- 2  students  (with  dyslexia)  harmonized  about  70%  of  the  melody.
- 2  students  (with  dyslexia)  harmonized  about  85%  of  the  melody;

Beyond  the  numerical  results,  one  of  the  important  things  that  emerged  concerns the  increase  in  motivation  (and  therefore  self-esteem)  of  dyslexic  students.  In  fact,  it was  observed  that,  at  the  beginning,  if  the  algorithm  stopped  because  it  was  unable to  give  a  suggestion,  the  dyslexic  student  also  stopped;  subsequently,  the  student was  able  to  go  ahead  with  the  harmonization,  even  if  only  for  a  few  chords.  This had  tangible  feedback  on  each  student's  performance,  which  improved  their  grades. The  learning  improvement  also  appeared  for  students  who  already  drew  a  high  profit because  they  learned  to  find  more  than  one  possible  solution  for  the  harmonization of  the  same  melody.

## 6 Discussion  and  Conclusions

Artificial  Intelligence  can  certainly  bring  innumerable  advantages  within  the  musical composition  learning  process:  on  the  one  hand,  it  will  be  essential  to  educate  students to  understand AI algorithms (promoting  an aware use of the technological platforms  that  surround  them),  on  the  other  hand,  the  same  algorithms  will  facilitate  the discovery  of  many  details  of  the  learning  processes  that  are  now  difficult  to  detect (therefore  useful  for  the  improvement  of  the  algorithms).

It  is  important  to  underline  two  aspects  to  keep  in  mind  when  creating  educational software:  the  centrality  of  the  student  in  the  learning  process,  and  the  importance  of teacher  training,  who  will  not  have  to  be  replaced  by  algorithms,  but  who  will  be able  to  use  these  tools  for  an  effective  teaching  activity  and  deep  learning.

In  this  paper,  an  algorithm  has  been  presented  to  support  the  dyslexic  (and  nondyslexic) student in the field of the study of musical composition, which is the harmonization  of  the  melody:  a  complex  and  demanding  operation  that  can  lead the student  to lose  motivation,  and  therefore,  to  negative  results.  The  simple  and intuitive  graphical  interface  allows  the  dyslexic  student  to  be  able  to  benefit  from  a presentation  of  information  through  the  visual  channel.

The  results  obtained  are  promising  both  in  terms  of  the  ability  of  the  algorithm  to harmonize  a  melody  (or  just  generate  the  bass  line)  and  in  terms  of  the  motivational aspect  of  the  student  (dyslexic  and  non-dyslexic)  which  has  led  to  an  improvement in  educational  achievements.  Despite  this,  it  is  possible  to  highlight  how  this  type of  activity  has  tried  to  make  the  concepts  that  underlie  the  learning  process  experiential  and  directly  tangible  at  a  cognitive  and  metacognitive  level,  and  therefore, it  is  necessary  to  perfect  the  training  phase  by  reading  a  greater  number  of  chord concatenation,  allowing  the  algorithm  to  present  alternative  solutions  for  the  same melody.

## Paper Source: Text to Audio Listener Tool in Tamil Language for Dyslexics
