## TEXT  TO  AUDIO  LISTENER  TOOL  IN  TAMIL  LANGUAGE  FOR    DYSLEXICS

Prathipa S Department of Computer Science and Engineering Sri Sairam Engineering College Chennai,Tamil Nadu,India. prathipa.cse@sairam.edu.in

Nishanthi G Department of Computer Science and Engineering Sri Sairam Engineering College Chennai,Tamil Nadu,India. sec21cs032@sairamtap.edu.in

Abstract -Our  project  introduces  customizable  text-to-speech technology  in  Tamil  to  enhance  literacy  development  for  dyslexic children, addressing their phonological-core deficits. This adaptable system identifies text within PDFs and vocalizes it while allowing dyslexic users to customize word presentation. Additional modules include sound recognition, letter and object identification, and kinesthetic activities  for  multisensory learning.Extensive user testing with dyslexic children yielded promising results, significantly  improving  reading  comprehension  and  engagement. This  research  contributes  to  education  technology  and  learning disabilities  by  offering  a  comprehensive  solution.  As  technology's role in education expands, tailored interventions hold transformative potential, promising inclusive and effective literacy development.

Keywords Dyslexia Text-to-Speech Technology Literacy Development Inclusive Education Gamification

## I. INTRODUCTION

Promoting literacy is integral to education, fostering cognitive growth and societal engagement. However, dyslexic children, constituting 5-10% of the population, face formidable barriers to  reading  due  to  phonological  processing  difficulties.  Our research seeks to empower these children through customizable  text-to-speech  technology  in  Tamil.  Beyond PDF  text  recognition  and  audible  conversion,  our  system stands  out  for  its  adaptability,  enabling  users  to  tailor  word presentation. Supplemental modules, including sound recognition,  letter  and  object  identification,  and  kinesthetic activities, address dyslexic children's challenges holistically.

Extensive user testing demonstrated significant gains in reading comprehension and engagement. This research potentially revolutionizes education technology by providing a personalized,  inclusive  tool  for  dyslexic  children's  literacy development. Our paper covers theoretical foundations, methodology,  system  modules, and outcomes, aiming  to advance inclusive education and create an accessible learning environment by merging technology, education, and learning difficulties.

Karthiga AV

Department of Computer Science and Engineering

Sri Sairam Engineering College Chennai,Tamil Nadu,India. sec21cs055@sairamtap.edu.in Deepa Lakshmi S Department of Computer Science and Engineering Sri Sairam Engineering College Chennai,Tamil Nadu,India. sec21cs068@sairamtap.edu.in

## II.MOTIVATION

This project is driven by the fundamental importance of literacy development in education, fostering cognitive growth, self-expression, and societal engagement. However, it recognizes the significant hurdles that dyslexic children, comprising 5-10% of the population, face in achieving reading proficiency due to phonological processing difficulties.

The primary motivation behind this research is the urgent need to  address  these  challenges  and  ensure  equitable  learning opportunities for dyslexic children. Dyslexia's association with phonological-core deficits  demands  tailored interventions that transcend  traditional  teaching  methods.  This  project  is  fueled by  the  desire  to  empower dyslexic  children  by  granting  them control  over  their  learning  experiences  while  enhancing  their reading comprehension.

Through the development of customizable text-to-speech technology  in  Tamil,  we  aim  to  dismantle  the  barriers  to literacy  for  dyslexic  learners,  potentially  reshaping  education technology.

## III . OUTLINE OF THE PROJECT

In the pursuit of enhancing literacy development for dyslexic children, this research has introduced a novel and customizable text-to-speech technology tailored to the Tamil language. Through a comprehensive examination of dyslexia's challenges and the limitations of existing solutions,  this  project  addresses  a  critical  gap  in  assistive technology. By providing dyslexic learners with the ability to  customize  word  chunking  and  formatting,  our  system offers  a  personalized  learning  experience  that  empowers them to overcome phonological-core deficits. The evaluation results underscore the effectiveness of our solution in improving reading comprehension and engagement levels among dyslexic children. The incorporation of sound recognition, letter and object identification, and kinesthetic activities further enriches the learning process, catering to different learning styles and sensory preferences. The  broader  implications of this research  extend  to  inclusive  education  and  the  field  of education  technology.  The  ability  to  adapt  technology  to meet  the  unique  needs  of  dyslexic  learners  demonstrates the potential of technology to bridge educational gaps and foster equity.. In conclusion, this project represents a significant step towards creating a more inclusive learning environment. By combining technology, languagespecificity, and customization, we aspire to     contribute    to   the   ongoing   dialogue   on     how assist technologies can transform the educational landscape and empower children with dyslexia to embark on successful journeys of literacy and learning.

## IV.LITERATURE REVIEW

'Adaptive  Reading  Assistance  for  the  Inclusion  of Students with Dyslexia:  The  AGENT-DYSL  Approach" (2008):  In  2008,  P.  Tzouveli,  A.  Schmidt,  M.  Schneider,  A. Symvonis, and S. Kollias proposed  the  AGENT-DYSL approach aimed  at facilitating the inclusion of dyslexic students. This adaptive reading assistance system was developed  to  cater  to  the  unique  needs  of  dyslexic  learners. The  study  contributes  to  inclusive  education  by  leveraging technology  to  support  dyslexic  students  in  their  learning journey.

"The  Implementation  of  Interactive  Multimedia  in Early Screening of Dyslexia" (2012): In 2012, H. M. Ekhsan, S.  Z.  Ahmad,  S.  A.  Halim,  J.  N.  Hamid,  and  N.  H.  Mansor explored  the  utilization  of  interactive  multimedia  for  early dyslexia screening. Their research emphasized the importance of  timely  identification  and  intervention,  showcasing  how multimedia tools could aid in the early detection of dyslexia, thereby improving educational outcomes for affected children.

"Machine Learning-based Learning Disability Detection  using  LMS"  (2020):  In  2020,  M.  Modak,  O. Warade,  G.  Saiprasad,  and  S.  Shekhar  delved  into  machine learning  techniques  for  detecting  learning  disabilities  within Learning Management Systems (LMS). Their study introduced an innovative approach to identifying and supporting  students  with  learning  disabilities  in  the  online learning environment, addressing the evolving needs of modern education.

"A Heuristic Evaluation of an Educational Game for Children  with  Dyslexia"  (2018):  In  2018,  N.  Ouherrou,  O. Elhammoumi,  F.  Benmarrakchi,  and  J.  El  Kafi  conducted  a heuristic  evaluation  of  an  educational  game  designed  for children  with  dyslexia.  Their  critical  assessment  provided valuable  insights  into  the  usability  and  effectiveness  of  the game,  aiming  to  better  cater  to  the  educational  needs  of dyslexic children .

Sampath, H., Sivaswamy, J., and Indurkhya, B. (2010):  In  their  2010  paper  titled  "Enhancing  Supportive Systems  for  Dyslexia  and  Autism  in  Children,"  Sampath, Sivaswamy, and Indurkhya focus on improving systems designed to aid children with dyslexia and autism. Published in ACM SIGACCESS Accessibility and Computing, Issue 96, in January, their work contributes to the development of assistive technologies for these special needs learners.

Mirza,  A.,  Fayyaz,  M.,  Seher,  Z.,  and  Siddiqi,  I. (2018):  The  paper  by  Mirza,  Fayyaz,  Seher,  and  Siddiqi, presented  at  the  2nd  Mediterranean  Conference  on  Pattern Recognition  and  Artificial  Intelligence,  discusses  the  use  of textural features for detecting Urdu caption text. Their research,  presented  in  2018,  explores  innovative  methods  for detecting  text  within  images,  particularly  in  the  context  of Urdu language.

Raza, A., Siddiqi, I., Djeddi, C., and Ennaji, A. (2013): In their 2013 contribution to the 12th International Conference on Document Analysis and Recognition, Raza, Siddiqi, Djeddi, and Ennaji delve into the realm of multilingual artificial text detection using sequential transformations. Their research explores techniques to detect and analyze text in multiple languages, contributing to the field of document analysis and recognition

Rana,  A.,  and  Lehal,  G.  S.  (2015):  Published  in  the Indian Journal of Science and Technology, Volume 8, Issue 35, Rana  and  Lehal's  work  in  2015  focuses  on  optical  character recognition  for  the  Urdu  language  in  offline  mode.  Their approach  involves  segmentation  based  on  ligatures  in  the Nastaliq  script,  contributing  to  the  advancement  of  character recognition technology for Urdu, particularly in offline scenarios .

## V LIMITATIONS AND CHALLENGES

The  project's  focus  on  the  Tamil  language  may  limit  its applicability to regions where  Tamil is not the primary language, necessitating adaptations for broader use. Implementing  customizable  text-to-speech  technology with multiple modules requires substantial computational resources and  may  pose  challenges  in  resource-constrained  educational environments.Dyslexic  children  and  educators  may  require time  to  adapt  to  and  fully  utilize  the  system's  customization features,  potentially  affecting  immediate  user  adoption  and efficacy.While  the  system  is  tailored  for  dyslexic  children, individual learning needs vary, making it challenging to create a  one-size-fits-all  solution.The  long-term  sustainability  of  the project, including updates and maintenance, may  require ongoing support and funding.

## VI  SYSTEM DESIGN

The proposed dyslexia project is structured into two distinct but interconnected phases: Text-to-Speech Conversion and Gamification Modules. These phases are designed to holistically address the challenges faced by dyslexic individuals in learning to read and comprehend text. The methodology for each phase is outlined below: Text-toSpeech Conversion:

## A.Outline of proposed system :

## a . Research and Analysis:

The  initial  phase  of  our  project  involves  a  comprehensive examination of current text-to-speech (TTS) technologies and their applicability in assisting dyslexic learners. This review is crucial  to  identify  the  strengths,  limitations,  and  potential effectiveness of TTS  systems in addressing the unique challenges faced by individuals with dyslexia. The following steps  outline  the  approach  taken  in  this  review:Identify  and analyze a range of existing TTS technologies that have been used  or  proposed  for  aiding  dyslexic  learners.  This  includes commercial TTS software, open-source solutions, and specialized dyslexia-focused applications. Evaluate the features offered by each TTS technology, particularly in terms of customization. Investigate whether the TTS systems allow adjustments for speech rate, emphasis  on     syllables,    pronunciation,    and other parameters to cater to dyslexic learners' needs.

## b )Model Selection and Optimisation:

Selecting an appropriate text-to-speech (TTS)  engine  or framework is a critical step in the project's methodology. The chosen TTS technology should provide the necessary customization options and flexibility to tailor the synthesized speech  to  the  specific  needs  of  dyslexic  learners.  Research and  Evaluation:  Conduct  an  in-depth  analysis  of  available TTS  engines,  frameworks,  and  platforms.  Consider  both commercial and open-source options.

## c)Gathering and preparing data:

The  process  of  curating  a  dataset  of  dyslexia-friendly  texts involves collecting a diverse range of text materials that cater to dyslexic learners' unique needs and challenges. The aim is to create a comprehensive collection that encompasses different  difficulty  levels  and  subjects,  ensuring  that  the synthesized  speech  addresses  various  literacy  requirements. Difficulty  Levels:  Select  texts  that  span  different  difficulty levels,  from  beginner  to  advanced.  This  allows  dyslexic learners  to  gradually  progress  in  their  reading  abilities  and build their comprehension skills over time. After curating the dataset, the next step involves preprocessing the text data to optimize it for accurate speech synthesis. This process includes  segmenting  the  text  into  smaller  units,  such  as phrases or sentences, to ensure that the synthesized speech

## maintains clarity and natural flow.

d)Model Training and Tuning : Training the chosen text-tospeech (TTS) model on the curated dataset involves using machine learning techniques to enable the  model to generate accurate and intelligible speech from text input. The process of training and fine-tuning the model  aims  to  optimize  its performance for dyslexic learners' needs. Data Preprocessing: Prepare the curated dataset     by        formatting        it     into        a        suitable  input format for the TTS  model. Convert text segments into tokenized representations that the model can understand.

## e).Clarity Enhancement:

Implement adjustments to the TTS model to prioritize clear pronunciation  of  phonemes  and  syllables.  This  ensures  that speech is easily discernible and promotes phonological awareness for dyslexic learners. Pacing and Pauses: Incorporate  modifications  that  introduce  appropriate  pauses and  pacing  in  the  generated  speech.  This  aids  in  providing learners with sufficient time to process and comprehend the content.  User  Feedback  Loop:  Collaborate  with  dyslexic learners  and  educators  to  gather  feedback  on  the  modified speech  synthesis.  Iterate  based  on  their  insights  to  refine modifications for optimal comprehension.

## B.Gamification Modules:

## a)Game Design and Objectives:

Collaborate  with  game  designers,  educators,  and  dyslexia specialists to conceptualize engaging and educational games. Define  clear  learning  objectives  for  each  game,  targeting specific cognitive deficits and literacy skills.

## b)Multisensory Approach:

The  process  of  integrating  auditory,  visual,  kinesthetic,  and tactile  elements  within  each  game  involves  designing  game environments that cater to diverse learning styles. By engaging multiple senses, the games create a richer and more effective learning experience for dyslexic learners.

i)Auditory  Elements: Incorporate  auditory  cues  such  as  clear speech instructions, sound effects, and background music that support the game's narrative and provide auditory reinforcement for learning objectives.

ii)Visual Elements : Design visually appealing game interfaces with dyslexia-friendly fonts, high contrast color schemes, and clear  graphics.  Visual  elements  can  include  text,  images, animations, and visual   cues   that   aid   in  comprehension.

iii) Kinesthetic Elements : Integrate  interactive elements that require physical actions or movements.

These  can  include  touch  gestures,  dragging  and  dropping items, or motion-based interactions that engage learners kinesthetically.  Tactile  Elements:  Utilize  haptic  feedback  or tactile sensations through touch screens or devices to provide sensory  input.  For  instance,  providing  vibration  or  touch feedback upon completing tasks or achieving milestones in the game.

## c)Content Creation and Adaptation:

Create game content using dyslexia-friendly fonts, colors, and layouts. Adapt game content to offer varying levels of difficulty, ensuring a gradual learning progression.

## d)User Experience Optimization:

Focus on intuitive user interfaces, minimizing distractions and cognitive load for dyslexic players.Incorporate customizable settings to adapt the games to individual preferences and needs.

## e)User Testing and Iteration:

Conduct extensive user testing sessions with dyslexic children to evaluate the effectiveness and engagement of the games. Analyze user interactions, gather feedback, and iteratively refine game mechanics based on collected data.

Integration with Text-to-Speech: Integrate the synthesized speech from Phase 1 into relevant aspects of the gamification modules, enhancing audio support and comprehension. The methodology outlined  above emphasizes collaboration with experts, iterative design based on user feedback, and a usercentric      approach.

Keywords-  Dyslexia, Speech Therapy, Image Processing, Gesture  recognition,  Mobile  solution,  Voice  recognition,  Reading and speaking weaknesses

## I. INTRODUCTION

Dyslexia  is a disorder, characterized by trouble with reading despite normal  intelligence. Different people are affected to varying degrees. Problems may include difficulties in  spelling  words,  reading  quickly,  writing  words,  "sounding out" words in the head, pronouncing words when reading aloud and understanding what one reads. Often these difficulties are first noticed at school.

Dyslexia  is  believed  to  be  caused  by  both  genetic  and environmental factors. Some  cases run in families. The underlying  mechanisms  of  dyslexia  are  problems  within  the brain's  language  processing  Dyslexia  is  diagnosed  through  a series of tests of memory, spelling, vision, and reading skills. Dyslexia is separate from reading difficulties caused by hearing or vision problems or by insufficient teaching [1].

Treatment involves adjusting teaching methods to meet the person's  needs.  While  not  curing  the  underlying  problem,  it may  decrease  the  degree  of  symptoms.  Treatments  targeting vision are not effective. Dyslexia is the most common learning disability and occurs in all areas of the world. It affects 3-7% of the population; however, up to 20% may have some degree of  symptoms [2].  While  dyslexia  is  more  often  diagnosed  in men,  it  has  been  suggested  that  it  affects  men  and  women equally. Some believe that dyslexia should be best considered as a different way  of learning, with both benefits and downsides [3].

## II. BACKGROUND

Dyslexia is a specific reading disability in word recognition,  spelling  and  decoding.  Students  with  Dyslexia require special adjustments to the text and text environment to be able to read better. Current studies have shown that many assistive  technologies  such  as  software  application  and  other tools  are  available  in  aiding  Dyslexia's  student  in  reading. However, websites that support Dyslexia's student in reading are very minimal. This discourages Dyslexia's student to use the  Internet.  Therefore,  there  is  a  need  to  identify  userinterface  requirements  for  web  readability  for  students  with Dyslexia. The requirements are font style, font size, font color, background color and spacing [4].

Dyslexia includes a large variety of literacy-related difficulties,  which  demands,  in  most  cases,  a  personalized intervention.  However, as dyslexia affects a large fraction of the population, schools cannot provide individual care for each student. The Hope application provides a tool for students to work on their literacy skills following a personalized teaching program. The design of the game and adaptation mechanisms integrated with it is aimed at maintaining student engagement for the duration of an open-ended number of playing sessions, while using a limited quantity of assets and literacy content.

By  focusing  on  maintenance  of  engagement,  we  hope  to improve learning outcomes and motivate students to also play the game outside of school [5].

People with developmental dyslexia show different levels of difficulties in psychoacoustic and psycholinguistic processing.  It  has  been  proposed  that  dyslexia  are  linked  to temporal processing deficits [6]. A recent study by Ziegler et al tested the perception of global versus local pitch patterns in children  with  dyslexia [7].  In  this  study,  dyslexics  showed deficits  in  local  pitch  perception  but  not  in  global  pitch perception, compared  to the non-dyslexic controls.  Such temporal processing in dyslexics has been further argued to be related to the phonological processing deficit [8]. One example is a recent study by Cheung et al who investigated the perception of lexical tones and aspiration contrasts in Cantonese in dyslexic children and he proposed that dyslexic children have lower degree of categorical perception of tones and aspiration contrasts than age-matched controls [9].

## III. METHODOLOGY

The ultimate  goal  of  executing  this  research  project  is  to build  up  a  virtual  reality  application  for  the  people  who  are suffering  from  Dyslexia  spread  in  all  over  the  world  and  the main objective of the application is to provide a reliable and well accurate product to overcome the weakness of Dyslexia by using a user friendly mobile application with virtual reality.

Primarily the application will detect whether the user is in the  ideal  mental  and  intelligence  level  according  to  the  age. Dyslexia has many  stages. Then  the application has to recognize  the  stage  of  Dyslexia  by  giving  the  user  few activities. The main three weaknesses of Dyslexia are reading, speaking  and  writing.  For  detect  the  writing  weaknesses  we develop a hand glove and it connected to the application via Bluetooth.  User's  hand  gestures  are  recognized  by  the  hand glove  and  for  the  reading  and  speaking  weaknesses,  user's voice will recognize by voice recognition.

Application  will  run  in  stage  by  stage  to  overcome  the weaknesses since the game load the user the stages dynamically. This whole application will run according to the 'Speech Therapy' that currently use to treat Dyslexia patients completely manually. The device will guaranty that the output information  is  accurate  and  consistence.  The  beneficiaries  of the  proposed  device  will  be  the  people  who  suffering  from Dyslexia  and  anyone  who  willing  to  improve  their  reading, writing  and  speaking  skills.  Using  'The  Hope'  application, they can overcome their weaknesses by using the application.

The application run stage by stage, when the user completes the  tasks  successfully,  then  only  user  can  go  to  the  next activity.  Completing  an  activity  means  the  user  is  overcome that  weakness.  There  are  mini  tasks  in  every  activity.  As  an example,  some  patients  can't  write  2  letters  words,  3  letters words, 4 letters words etc.

Therefore, for patients who are straggled to write 2 letters words  there  are  different  kind  of  activities  and  for  3  letters words  there  are  different  kind  of  activities  for  the  user  to follow.  The  activities  and  stages  will  arrange  dynamically after  recognizing the stage of Dyslexia of the user.

## A. Detecting the stage of dyslexia

Dyslexia  is  a  disorder  and  it  has  many  stages.  As  an example, one who is suffering from Dyslexia may have weak in writing and fluent in speaking. Another one may have weak in reading but good in writing and speaking. Writing also can divide  into  many  stages  that  are,  3  letter  word  weakness,4 letters  word  weakness,  5  letters  word  weakness,  weak  in writing  sentences  etc.  So,  detecting  the  stage  of  Dyslexia  is very important to deliver the best therapy to the user.

When the user starts the application, it recognizes whether the user is in the ideal mental and intelligence stage according to the age. Application give some activities to decide the stage user like, an 8-year-old child can recognize objects and scenes.

'The Hope' supports virtual reality.  It  helps  to  recognize the  object  and  it  is  a  creative  way  to  deliver  an  activity  to  a kindergarten child. Children with Dyslexia are not very social and they are like step aside of the society. They are not fluently communicating  with  an  unknown  person  who  is  doing  the therapy  as  the  current  solution  to  this  matter.  Therefore, bringing a 3D virtual world to the unsocial child is an effective way  to  overcome  the  weaknesses  and  get  an  improvement better than the current manual solution called 'Speech Therapy'  in  hospitals,  schools,  special  educational  units  etc. And  treating  without  figuring  out  what  stage  is  the  user  in Dyslexia, is not accurate.

First task is to decide the stage of Dyslexia. The first-time user will face an aptitude test to detect that the user can write, read  and  speak  3  letter,  4  letter,  5  letter  and  6  letter  words. After  considering  the  performance  of  the  user  it  will  be compared  with  a  well-trained  predefined  data  set  that  has  a 100% accuracy by using the SVM algorithm[10][11].

Figure 2 shows how the SVM algorithm that we use to train the data set to detect the Dyslexia stage works.

Figure2: Functionality of SVM algorithm [12]



## B. Dyanamic therapy generator

After  detecting  the  stage  of  dyslexia,  now  the  user  is ready  for  the  treatment.  This  treatment  currently  doing  by manually in hospitals and special educational units in front of a doctor or a therapist. Using 'The Hope' application user can do it with a guardian or the parent by following the guidance of the application. After detecting the stage of dyslexia, it will go to the next step as an input.

After arriving the stage of Dyslexia, system will show the therapies that user must follow. These therapies are lining up dynamically  by  considering  the  performance  of  the  aptitude test  that  the  user  has  faced.  As  an  example, if a user poor in writing  the  therapy  generator  give  the  priority  to  the  writing therapies. If the user poor at reading therapy generator give the priority to the reading therapies.

Therapy generator make sure that the user follows the ideal and the most accurate therapy list by delivering and lining up the therapies dynamically. Therapies have sub therapies cause the  dyslexia  cover  a  wide  range  of  disorders.  By  lineup  and generate  the  therapies  dynamically  therapy  generator  makes sure that the user follows the most suitable treatment that the user wants to overcome the weaknesses of Dyslexia. User just should click the next button and follow the therapies will show the  user  friendliness  of  the  application.  Fig.3  shows  how  the therapy  generator  works.  It  shows  how  the  Dyslexia  stage become an input to the therapy generator.

Figure 3: Work Hierarchy of therapy generator



## C. Writing skills improver

Handwriting  is  a  unique  skill  that  a  person  possesses. Handwriting skill is heavily affected from dyslexia. Areas that affected by dyslexia are

- Master the rules of spelling &amp; grammar
- Write letters numbers and symbols in the correct order
- Listen &amp; take notes

Most  of  the dyslexia patients flips letters, and  also patients write letters incorrect or incompletely [12].

Figure 4 shows the letters that make dyslexia patients confuse are simple letters like b, d, f, g, h, j, n, p, q, r, t, y.

Figure 4: Dyslexic Alphabet [13]



To  prevent  this  problems  and  confusion  'The  Hope' writing skill improver area will help out. Writing skill improver will first get the handwriting as an input. The written input  will  be  convert  to  an  image,  image  will  be  recognized and  convert  to  symbolic  form.  This  will  be  then  compared with the predefined data set, and show the errors.

Handwriting recognition means the ability of the computer to analyze hand written document (paper, photographs,  touch  screen  and  other  devices)  inputs  and recognize the characters, words, sentences.

Figure.5  shows  the  procedure  of  writing  skills  improver that use to detect the hand gestures of the user.

Handwriting interpretation, what happen is determining the meaning of the recognized symbolic form. [14]

## D. Speaking skills improver

The  main  motive  of  developing  this  app  is  to  provide  a support  for  children  suffering  from  vocal  disabilities  due  to dyslexia.  Primarily,  this  app  will  aid  doctors  to  assess  how severely  a  child  is  suffering  from  dyslexia.  Via  the  'HOPE' app, doctors will experience a faster, more efficient method of diagnosis  compared  to  the  older,  slower  ways.  Furthermore, this app will enable parents of dyslexic children to help their children speak, in the comfort of their own homes.

HOPE  has  been  developed  focusing  mainly  on  younger children,  whereby  the  interfaces  have  all  been  designed  in  a child  friendly,  colorful  and  attractive  theme  that  appeals  to younger audiences.

The  app  works  by  providing  paragraphs  and  words  of increasing complexities for the child to read as they progress further. For example, a beginner to this app will get words like 'Cat',  'Dog', 'Cake' etc., and  as they progress further they will be introduced to words like 'Come', 'Running', 'Swimming' etc., and finally they will be introduced to more complex words such as 'Caterpillar', 'Lawnmower' etc.[15]

The app recognizes individual words spoken by the child this process is instantaneous, and allows us to come to a clearer conclusion  on  their  level  of  speech.  If  a  word  has  been pronounced incorrectly, the app then repeats the word repeatedly till the child gets it right, but there is also a 'SKIP' option in order to avoid frustration. The data gathered by the app is then presented in a graphical form for analysis by the doctors/parents.  Furthermore,  the  app  is  also  enabled  with  a function that allows doctors to add their own activities to the software.

## IV. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION



Hand  writing  is  associated  with  recognition,  interpretation. The  language  represented  by  the  graphical  form  will  be converted into symbolic form in recognition part. In Server The  main  result  of  this  research  is  to  overcome  all  the weaknesses  of  Dyslexia  and  improve  writing,  reading  and speaking skills. This is an Android based mobile application. In the  analysis,  we  used  Unity  game  engine  and  MATLAB.  To give a different experience to the children who using this and to be more accurate, 'The hope' supports virtual reality too. Data set that we generate by using the information we collected from Lady Ridgway Hospital, was perfectly match for our requirements.  We  used  several  algorithms  like  SVM,  SVM Linear and SVM Gaussian Etc.

Figure 5: System Diagram

In machine learning, support vector machines are supervised learning models with associated learning algorithms that analyze data used for classification and regression analysis. Given a set of training examples, each marked as belonging to one or the other of two categories, an SVM training algorithm builds a model that assigns new examples to one category or the other, making it a non-probabilistic binary linear classifier [16].

An  SVM  model  is  a  representation  of  the  examples  as points in space, mapped so that the examples of the separate categories are divided by a clear gap that is as wide as possible. New  examples  are  then  mapped  into  that  same  space  and predicted to belong to a category based on which side of the gap they fall. There were some problems when implementing this application [17].

Generate the data set was the first task to detect the stage of the  disease.  We  had  to  visit  Lady  Ridgway  Hospital  and Victory Special education school several times. Another hard task was to detect the hand gestures and get a clear image to image  processing.  We  developed  a  hand  gesture  glove  that work as  a  mouse  to  help  the  user  to  write.  Furthermore,  the user can see his/her improvement in a graphical way. Application gives points to motivate the user, as we give the priority  to  the  children  who  are  suffering  from  Dyslexia. Anyone  who  willing  to  improve  their  reading,  writing  and speaking skills can use the application.

According  to  Artificial  intelligent,  image  processing  and voice recognition components, it was revealed that detect the stage of Dyslexia and weaknesses of Dyslexia can overcome. It  provides  more  accurate  results  than  the  current  solution, 'Speech  therapy'.  Detecting  the  Dyslexia  stage  is  100% accurate  by  using  SVM  algorithm.  User  can  use  the  hand gesture  glove  or  use  the  mobile  screen  as  a  doodle.  Hand gesture glove makes the application user friendly.

Speech recognition is the ability of a machine or program to identify  words  and  phrases  in  spoken  language  and  convert them  to a  machine-readable  format.  Rudimentary  speech recognition  software  has  a  limited  vocabulary  of  words  and phrases, and it may only identify these if they are spoken very clearly.  More  sophisticated  software  has  the  ability  to  accept natural  speech.  Speech  recognition  works  using  algorithms through acoustic and language modeling. [18]

Acoustic  modeling  represents  the  relationship  between linguistic units of speech and audio signals; language modeling matches  sounds  with  word  sequences  to  help  distinguish between words that sound similar. Speech recognition performance is measured by accuracy and speed. Accuracy is measured with word error rate. WER works at the word level and identifies inaccuracies in transcription, although it cannot identify  how  the  error  occurred.  Speed  is  measured  with  the real-time  factor.  A  variety  of  factors  can  affect  computer speech recognition performance, including pronunciation, accent, pitch and volume and background noise [19].

'The Hope' developed for English language and can only improve English writing, reading and speaking skills. Authors are  planning to deliver a new update for Sinhala language in future.

Currently  the  application  is  running  for  android  devices. Supporting for IOS is the next task. It will be a huge advantage for  the  IOS  users  because  the  application  support  for  virtual reality too.

## V. CONCLUSION

In  this  research  paper,  the  researchers  have  presented  an application to overcome the weaknesses of Dyslexia, writing, reading  and  speaking.  The  main  outcome  of  research  is  to improve  the  writing,  reading  and  speaking  skills.  Virtual Reality  offers  a  real  visualization  of  the  final  product  for customers,  and  will  be  an  advantage  while  it  increases  the dedication and the interest of the user. This study proves that a business  plan  like  this  is  more  effective  and  accurate  than  a manual process to overcome a disorder

## The Use of NN to Detect Learning Styles of Children with Learning Disabilities in E-Learning System

Oussama Elhammoumi ( &amp; ) , Fatima Ezzahra Benmarrakchi , Nihal Ouherrou, and Jamal El Ka fi

Computer Science Department, Chouaib Doukkali University, El Jadida, Morocco

{elhammoumi.o,benmarrakchi.f,ouherrou.n, elkafi.j}@ucd.ac.ma

Abstract. Every child learns differently and possesses a dominant or preferred learning style in certain ways. The cognitive development of children with learning disabilities (LDs) is often different than that of children without LDs. However, understanding how it differs from normal child development is important to understand how learning style identi fi cation can assist children with LDs. The aim of this paper is to propose an automatic learning style detection that works by the way of children interaction with the system. In this study, an Arti fi cial Neural Network is used to predict the learning style of children with LDs.

Keywords: Learning disabilities  VARK model  Dyslexia  Learning style  Arti fi cial neural network

## 1 Introduction

Learning styles are the most important and interesting element in the learning process since they may help learners become more self-aware of their strengths and weaknesses especially for children with learning disabilities (LDs) [1]. LDs refers to a disorder in one or more of the psychological processes involved in understanding or using spoken or written language. The term LDs does not involve learning problems that are primary the result of visual, hearing disabilities or mental retardation [2]. It is used to describe the most common types of learning disabilities such as dyslexia, dysphasia, dysgraphia, dyspraxia, and dyscalculia [3].

Children with LDs have speci fi c cognitive abilities and different learning needs [4] and preferences [5]. The cognitive development of children with LDs is often different than that of children without LDs. However, understanding how it differs from normal child development is important to understand how learning style identi fi cation can assist children with LDs.

Various learning styles models and theories have been proposed to identify students ' learning style and most of them focus heavily on the ability to think and how individuals acquire, retain, and retrieve information, and tend to collect style dimensions to provide a pro fi le of a learner ' s style [6, 7]. The traditional way to identify learning styles is to ask learners to complete questionnaires. However, these instruments present some disadvantages such as the lack of motivation to fi ll out a questionnaire and lack of self-awareness of their learning preferences or sometimes when learners fi ll out the questionnaire they feel bored because of the number of questions and they do not even understand the aim of the questions. To solve these limitations, numerous approaches for automatically detecting learning styles have been proposed. However, most of these approaches have been applied for adults or learners without LDs and did not include children with LDs. Hence, in this study we propose an automatic learning style detection for children with LDs.

© Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2020 M. Ezziyyani (Ed.): AI2SD 2019, AISC 1102, pp. 210 -216, 2020. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-36653-7\_21

This study tends to build a detection model of VARK learning styles. VARK learning style is one of the relevant methods used in e-learning systems and is characterized by the many learning objects or teaching materials available in online environment. We used an Arti fi cial Neural Network to predict the learning style of children with LDs. We present the description of the proposed model and discuss some limitations, implications and research gaps that can be helpful to researchers working in the fi eld of learning styles.

## 2 Related Work

Learning style can be de fi ned as the composite of cognitive, affective, a psychological characteristic that serve as an indicator of how an individual interacts with and respond to the learning environment. Various learning style models and theories have been proposed to identify individuals learning style such as; David Kolb ' s model , Peter Honey and Alan Mumford ' s model , Neil Fleming ' s VAK/VARK model , Anthony Gregorc ' s model , Felder -Silverman learning style , and Gardner ' s theory of multiple intelligences . Every learning style model has its own assessment tool in a form of a questionnaire and it includes various questions about personality, study attitude and behavior.

Neil Fleming ' s VAK/VARK [7, 8] model is the most widely accepted and used model which de fi nes how learners like to receive information. The model bases on the basic human observation channels; vision, hearing and feeling. VAK theory is considered to be one of the classical learning theories in the educational fi eld, it de fi nes three sensory modalities: Visual (see), Auditory (listen) and Kinesthetic (doing).

VARK is an acronym for Visual, Auditory, Read/write and Kinesthetic. It is a learning style model that has been modi fi ed from VAK model, to VARK learning style by Fleming in 2006. R is a second ' visual ' modality for Read/write learners. According to [3], it seemed obvious that some students had a distinct preference for the written word whilst others preferred symbolic information as in maps, diagrams, and charts. These two preferences were not always found in the same person. There is more acceptance of this distinction today than in the 1980s.

Visual learning style (V) involves the use of seen or observed things. Auditory (A) learning style involves the transfer of information through sounds. Kinesthetic (K) learning styles involves physical and practical experiences.

Kolb learning style model [6] is one of the model includes cycle of learning as a central principle in his experiential learning theory expressed by the following stage of learning: abstract conceptualization (AC), concrete experience (CE), active experimentation (AE), and reflective observation (RO). Kolb ' s learning theory sets out four distinct learning styles types for which Kolb used the following terms: diverging (CE/RO), accommodating (CE/AE), converging (AC/AE), and assimilating (AC/RO).

Felder -Silverman learning style ( FSLSM ) [9] is the most popular model used in adaptive learning for adults, it become now a widely accepted learning style and is increasingly being adopted in many online learning systems. It describes four learning style dimensions, which indicate the student ' s preferences for certain poles of the dimensions; Active and reflective, sensing and intuitive, visual and verbal, sequential and global.

There exists a variety of research within the areas of LS detection and e-learning systems. Among the studies there is a study conducted by [10], the researchers presented an approach to recognize automatically the learning styles of individual students according to the actions that he or she has performed in an e-learning environment and the recognition technique was based on neural networks. Similar works can be found in the work of, the researchers proposed an approach using ANN to identify students ' learning styles based on the Felder-Silverman learning style model (FSLSM).

## 3 Our Proposed Approach

The aim of this study is to offer to children with LDs a personal and a unique learning experience based on their learning preferences. For this purpose, we propose an adaptive approach for learning, which considers the learning preferences of children with LDs in e-learning systems. We used Arti fi cial Neural Networks (ANN) to identify children with LDs learning styles based on the VARK learning style model. While there exist many learning style models, we selected the VARK model because it seems to be most appropriate for the use in educational systems for our target learners. According to [5] VAK learning style model uses the three main sensory receivers (vision, audition and kinesthetic) to determine a student ' s preferred or dominate learning style and provides a different perspective for understanding a student ' s strengths. Its use can be helpful with children with LDs to fi nd out their learning styles and provide a general idea about their preferences in learning environments. Table 1 represents the description of the VARK learning style model and recommendations in e-learning system that support the learning style.

ANN are a type of machine learning that is inspired from the human brain. These days, ANN are able to perform what has been termed deep learning. An ANN is based on a collection of connected units or nodes called arti fi cial neurons that transmit a signal from one neuron to another. The essential building block of ANN is a perceptron which accomplishes simple signal processing, and these are then connected into a large network.

Using ANN can help determine the learning style of a learner in both online and offline environments, unlike the traditional way of giving questionnaires to learner to be fi lled and infer the learning style from them. A Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) for multi-class Softmax Classi fi cation Neural Network has been proposed to classify the learning style of children. The network is composed of an input layer of two hidden layers and an output layer as shown in Fig. 1.

Fig. 1. The MLP model to classify the learning style of the learner.



Before feeding the data to the network a preprocessing step of normalizing the data, every feature linearly rescaled to the [0,1] interval using the min-max normalizer with the following formula:



Using Recti fi ed Linear Unit (ReLU) as an activation function for each layer and the Softmax function for multi-classi fi cation. Relu function is calculated using the following formula f x ð Þ ¼ max 0 ; x ð Þ where x is the input to a neuron. Softmax function calculates the probability that any of the classes are true, it is calculated using the following formula:



Where z is a vector of the inputs to the output layer and j indexes the output units. The model is initialized with random weights, in the forward propagation the network calculates the output and compare the result with the target, then the error is calculated.



Since all the hidden units have contributed to the error in the output layer, the output error signals are transmitted backwards from the output layer to each unit in the hidden layer that immediately contributed to the output layer. This process is repeated layer by layer, until each unit in the network has received an error signal that describes its contribution to the overall error. Once the error signal for each node has been determined, the errors are then used by the unites to update the weights until the network converges to a state that allows all the training patterns to be encoded.

The output vectors for each type of Visual is [0 0 0 1], for Auditory it is [0 0 1 0], for Reading -Writing it is [0 1 0 0], and for Kinesthetic it is [1 0 0 0].

The proposed NN architecture aims to fi nd a mapping between children with LDs actions in the e-learning system and the learning style that they best fi t. To achieve this goal, we must identify the inputs of the network, its outputs and the meaning of their possible values as shown in Table 2. V1, V2, V3 and V4 are the inputs of the network, each one consists of the number of clicks or visits of an element such as videos, games, audio fi les, puzzles.

Table 1. Description of the VARK learning style model and recommendations in e-learning system.

## 4 Conclusion and Future Works

In this paper, we proposed an adaptive approach for learning, which considers the learning preferences of children with LDs in e-learning systems. We used ANN to identify children with LDs learning styles based on the VARK learning style model. For future work, we are planning to collect the data from questionnaires to train and test the network, the questionnaires will be answered by the children, and from the result of the questionnaires will assign one of the four classes based on the number of clicks or visits to the elements of each input.

## Use of recommendation models to provide support to dyslexic students

Gianluca Morciano a, ∗ , Jos´ e Manuel Alcalde Llergo a , Andrea Zingoni a , Enrique Yeguas Bol´ ıvar b , Juri Taborri a , Giuseppe Calabr` o a

a Department of Economics, Engineering, Society and Business Organization (DEIM), University of Tuscia, 01100 Viterbo, Italy ordoba,

b Department of Computing and Numerical Analysis, C´ ordoba University, 14071 C´ Spain

## Abstract

Dyslexia is the most widespread specific learning disorder and significantly impair different cognitive domains. This, in turn, negatively affects dyslexic students during their learning path. Therefore, specific support must be given to these students. In addition, such a support must be highly personalized, since the problems generated by the disorder can be very different from one to another. In this work, we explored the possibility of using AI to suggest the most suitable supporting tools for dyslexic students, so as to provide a targeted help that can be of real utility. To do this, we relied on recommendation algorithms, which are a branch of machine learning, that aim to detect personal preferences and provide the most suitable suggestions. We hence implemented and trained three collaborative-filtering recommendation models, namely an item-based, a user-based and a weighted-hybrid model, and studied their performance on a large database of 1237 students' information, collected with a self-evaluating questionnaire regarding all the most used supporting strategies and digital tools. Each recommendation model was tested with three different similarity metrics, namely Pearson correlation, Euclidean distance and Cosine similarity. The obtained results showed that a recommendation system is highly effective in suggesting the optimal help tools/strategies for everyone, with an error less then 12%. As a further evidence of the effectiveness of the implemented system, its precision was 0.85 and its recall was 0.83. The best performing filter was the hybrid one, when Pearson's correlation is used to measure the distance among users and/or items. In addition, in a final testing performed on 50 students, dyslexic students who used the recommendation algorithm increased their academic scores of almost 1 point in a 1 to 10 scale, showing higher learning performance compared to students who did not use it. This demonstrates that the proposed approach is successful and can be used as a new and effective methodology to support students with dyslexia.

Keywords: Specific Learning Disorders, Dyslexia, Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Recommendation Systems, Education.

## 1. Introduction

Dyslexia is a neurodevelopmental disorder that can negatively impact several cognitive abilities that are crucial for learning. Therefore, a timely diagnosis and the use of valid support systems are of outmost importance in order to help the children to cope with their difficulties. The diagnosis of dyslexia can be done by using standard pen-and-paper tests (Schulte-K¨ orne, 2010) or by using machine learning (ML) algorithms. An example of the use of ML to diagnose dyslexia can be found in (Palacios et al., 2016). After the diagnosis, however, the use of effective support items is crucial to help the children to overcome some of their difficulties. ML and virtual reality (VR) represent ways in which support methods can be created and used by dyslexic children. For instance, in (Maresca et al., 2022) VR was used to enhance cognitive abilities in dyslexic children while in (Yeguas-Bol´ ıvar et al., 2022) was used to determine the difficulties of each tested student. ML and, in particular, recommendation systems are used to customize the learning experience of students with or without cognitive difficulties (Urdaneta-Ponte et al., 2021; Hoic-Bozic et al., 2015; Rodr´ ıguez et al., 2015). Our work compares three recommendation systems using three different similarity metrics. The goal is to select the best model to assist university students with dyslexia in choosing the most effective learning tools and studying strategies for their needs. To provide a comprehensive understanding, the following sections will delve into the relevant literature (Section 2) and the methodologies employed in this study (Section 3). Subsequently, Section 4 will present the results, leading to a succinct conclusion in Section 5 summarizing the key insights gained from our investigation.

## 2. Related works

Specific learning disorders (SLDs) are a set of neurodevelopmental disorders that affect around 10% of the worldwide population (Narimani et al., 2016) and impair, to different degrees, specific cognitive skills such as reading, writing and performing mathematical operations correctly (Shaywitz, 1998). Depending on the severity and the type of the impaired skill, three categories of SLDs can be distinguished (Toffalini et al., 2017): (i) dyslexia, if the subject has strong difficulties in reading; (ii) dysgraphia, when impaired writing skills are predominant and (iii) dyscalculia, if the mathematical skills are the most affected. In addition, there is a high rate of comorbidity between these SLDs, thus often two or more disorders are present together. Among them, dyslexia has the highest prevalence (Wagner et al., 2020). Dyslexia affects not only reading but also attention (Bosse et al., 2007), working memory (Smith-Spark &amp; Fisk, 2007) and phonological processing (Galaburda et al., 2006). Also, abilities such as note-taking, text composing and organizing the study activity are negatively influenced (Mortimore &amp; Crozier, 2006). These deficits can significantly impact the learning experience of dyslexic students. However, numerous studies show that if dyslexia is detected early during childhood, it is possible to reduce the severity of the symptoms by employing supporting methodologies that help in addressing the specific difficulties of the child (Battistutta et al., 2018). Therefore, diagnosing dyslexia as early as possible is of paramount importance.

Among the methods used to diagnose dyslexia, the most common are the cognitive tests (Schulte-K¨ orne, 2010). These, are used to examine general cognitive abilities, using the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS) for adults or the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children (WISC) (Wechsler, 2014) for children, or to assess specific cognitive abilities such as verbal and phonological processing (Pothos &amp; Kirk, 2004), generally compromised in dyslexia.

If the diagnosis of dyslexia does not arrive early in life, during childhood or adolescence, or if it fails, the difficulties produced by dyslexia tend to be more accentuated and acting to mitigate them becomes even more difficult (Battistutta et al., 2018). In addition, these issues can influence self-esteem and future aspirations (Ghisi et al., 2016) which increase the risk of developing generalized anxiety (Mammarella et al., 2016) or depression (Mugnaini et al., 2009). In light of this, finding support tools for dyslexic students is of utmost importance. This support can come in the form of standard tools or digital tools or a combination of those. For instance in (MacCullagh et al., 2017), the authors interviewed dyslexic students about the support tools perceived as most useful. The students reported that one of the most effective standard support tool was attending face-to-face lectures and recording them. This was best coupled with the use of visual slides.

An example of digital tool that is currently studied to help dyslexic students is the VR (Alcalde-Llergo et al., 2023). For instance, in (Maresca et al., 2022) dyslexic students were divided and trained through classical neuropsychological treatments or using VR. The VR treatment was composed of different exercises aimed at improving cognitive functions such as memory, attention, language, spatial-temporal orientation and executive functions. The results show that the students that underwent the VR treatment improved their abilities across all the cognitive domains analyzed. This study shows the potential of using VR in supporting dyslexic students.

However, even if providing standard and digital support tools helps dyslexic students, this may not be enough. As highlighted before, dyslexia has a high comorbidity with other SLDs. In addition, dyslexia has a comorbidity with other neurodevelopmental disorders such as attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) (German` o et al., 2010), executive functioning disorder (Gooch et al., 2011) or obsessive compulsive disorder (Pauc, 2005). Therefore, the presence of two or more disorders translates in two or more cognitive deficits co-existing and this leads to increased issues during the learning path of each student. Furthermore, greater deficits in learning can result in higher risk of developing psychological issues during childhood and adolescence. In light of this, it appears evident that different dyslexic students can have different difficulties and thus, the support strategies and tools designed to help them during their learning path must be personalized. With the recent advancements in machine learning (ML) algorithms, today it is possible to develop supporting methodologies that can ameliorate the difficulties encountered by dyslexic subjects during their life, especially during their education path (Ciolacu et al., 2017), (Baglama et al., 2018), (Zingoni et al., 2024). For instance, in (Hamid et al., 2015), researchers use a hidden Markov model to predict challenges in learning the Malay language among primary school students with dyslexia. The model analyzes errors in phonology, spelling, reading, and writing exercises, emphasizing the necessity for personalized support interventions. Similarly, (Mpia Ndombo et al., 2013) adopts a comparable approach but incorporates students' behavior into the model training. The outcome is a computer-assisted learning system that, based on predictions, leads to a substantial 60% improvement in dyslexic students' skills compared to traditional support tools. Meanwhile, the primary goals of (Rajapakse et al., 2018; Thelijjagoda et al., 2019) are focused on creating an assistive learning platform tailored for both primary and secondary school students, by using object character recognition and a neural network (NN) in the former or a support vector machine (SVM) in the latter.

Among the ML algorithms, recommendation systems (RS) are a natural candidate to provide a personalized learning experience to students (Masruroh et al., 2021) as they are specifically designed to detect user preferences and recommend items accordingly (Khalid et al., 2022). RSs can be generally categorized in collaborative filtering (CF), in which items are recommended based on the preference of similar users (Herlocker et al., 2004), content-based (CB), in which items are suggested to the user based on the description of the item (Marana et al., 2023), knowledge-based (KB), which focuses on the knowledge of the users' need for a particular item (Carrer-Neto et al., 2012) and hybrid system which is a combination of the algorithms described above (Burke, 2002). In the field of education, several RSs were proposed to enhance the learning experience of the students (Nabizadeh et al., 2020) . For instance, in (Hoic-Bozic et al., 2015) the authors combined a set of RSs such as knowledge-based, CB and CF along with Web 2.0 tools to provide teachers with suggestions on how to design a course and students with indications on what activities to choose such as attending seminars, participating in e-courses, summaries of subject matter and solving online tests. Thanks to this method, students achieved better final course results. In (Rodr´ ıguez et al., 2015) the authors created an hybrid model in which a CF, a CB and a KB algorithm were combined in order to recommend learning objects to students that have similar learning styles. This hybrid recommendation approach increased the relevance of the recommended educational material and improved the students' learning process.

The studies reported above and in Table 1 show a prominent role of RSs in education. Unfortunately, the majority of RSs focus on students without SLDs such as dyslexia. Moreover, little to no effort is done in creating study support tools to dyslexic students at university except for (Zingoni et al., 2021, 2024) that mixes AI and virtual reality to create a platform to support dyslexic students.

Our work was developed with the goal of exploiting ML to customize the learning experience of students by recommending specific support tools. In particular, three RSs were compared to determine which algorithm recommend the best learning strategies and study tools according to the needs of each student. Lastly, the best performing algorithm has been used to recommend learning tools and study strategies to dyslexic and non-dyslexic students and their learning rate was assessed by experienced professors. This work is framed within the VRAIlexia project, which aims at provide specific support to university stu- dents with dyslexia, by relying on new technologies, like VR and AI (vrailexia consortium).

## 3. Methodology

In this work, the goal was to compare the efficacy of three RSs, a userbased, an item-based and a hybrid model, in suggesting the best study tools and learning strategies to university students with dyslexia. Along with these RSs, three similarity metrics were tested as well namely, the Euclidean distance, the Cosine distance and the Pearsons' correlation. After the collection of the dataset, the hybrid model was implemented by combining the user-based and the item-based with different weights, as shown in (Badaro et al., 2013). In order to select the best set of weights, the mean absolute error was computed, and subsequently, the algorithm's performance using these weights was further validated using other commonly used metrics, such as precision and recall at k. Finally, the best performing model was used to help students with and without dyslexia during their learning path.

## 3.1. Dataset collection

The dataset used in this work was collected from a questionnaire aimed at assessing the issues that each dyslexic student has experienced and the learning strategies and study tools they have used and found useful to ameliorate their difficulties. Questions were also asked about the main problems caused by dyslexia, on the basis of which the most useful tools were able to be recommended in (Yeguas-Bol´ ıvar et al., 2022). In addition, demographic information has been collected in the dataset, but were used for other purposes such as shown in (Benedetti et al., 2022). The different learning methodologies presented in the questions were selected with the help of experts in SLDs. Here, participants can describe how much the supporting tools and strategies presented were considered helpful by choosing different options: 'not at all', 'very little', 'little', 'medium', 'much' and 'very much'. However, to include the possibility that users never tried or did not know one or more items, two other answers ('never tried' and 'I don't know') were added. These two responses were used to identify tools and strategies that were not sufficiently known to users, enabling the promotion of their application to obtain more accurate ratings in future analyses. In order to quantify a qualitative answer, and use it profitably in RSs, the different options have been converted into a range of numerical values between 0 and 5, were 0 corresponded to 'not at all' and 5 to 'very much'. Regarding responses labeled as 'never tried' and 'I don't know' they will be treated and preprocessed as missing values. The algorithm will process these data in the form of a ratings matrix, where the rows will represent different students, and the columns will represent support tools and study methodologies that may be proposed by the system. This representation follows a format similar to the one illustrated in Figure 1encompassing all the students and the dyslexic support methodologies under consideration.



The questionnaire was created by skilled psychologists by starting from an interview carried out on 20 dyslexic university students about the best tools and strategies they have adopted to overcome those issues. The questionnaire was then administered to other 30 dyslexic students, in order to check for its accessibility and clearness. The final version, comprising 17 support tools and 22 learning strategies, totaling 39 items, was distributed to 1,237 dyslexic students, in accordance with the following criteria: having a valid diagnosis of dyslexia, being native Italian speakers, being 18 years old or more, and attending univer- sity or having finished or abandoned it less than five years before the filling of the questionnaire. The distribution of the participants was nearly even, concerning gender (54% female students against 46% male students) and age (an almost uniform distribution was observed within the selected range). In addition, the above-described information we collected about the received support, the type of high school attended, the category of student (full-time student, worker student, commuter etc.) and the family context allowed us to verify that all these variables were quite uniformly distributed. This limit potential biases. On the contrary, a surely present bias is given by the fact that only Italian-speaking participants took part to the questionnaire but, as reported previously limiting the work only to one language is strictly necessary, since dyslexia-related issues vary a lot from a language to another (Miles, 2000) and, thus, it is opportune to analyze each language by itself. It is worth mentioning that it was not possible to gather information concerning variables like the socioeconomic situation of the students and their ethnicity, which may have an impact on the system. However, at least the second one does not represent a great issue for the considered Italian university context, since this is less ethnically heterogeneous than other European countries, with only a 3% presence of non-Italian students. The acquired data have been treated according to the article 13-14 of the GDPR 2016/679 (Parliament) of the European Union. In particular, they have been processed completely anonymously and used only for research purposes. Table 2 presents the questions related to the issues, the tools and the learning strategies gathered by the questionnaire. However, it is important to note that the difficulties will not be taken into account when generating recommendations by the system.

Among the various techniques employed in this domain, collaborative RSs and contentbased approaches stand out as two distinctive methodologies, each with its ered.

unique strengths and limitations. Content-based systems require a big amount of information about items' features, instead of focusing on the relationships obtained through feedback from users through ratings. For this reason, the collaborative systems approach has been considered more appropriate for our data set. Still, the content-based approach will be considered in future work to compare performance against collaborative methods, and ultimately provide the best possible advice to dyslexic students.

Data were analyzed using three types of CF RSs implemented as (Badaro et al., 2013). The three types CF systems were: a user-based (Zhao &amp; Shang, 2010) in which the similarity between users guides the recommendation of the different methodologies, an item-based (Wang et al., 2006) in which item similarity is analyzed to suggest the most relevant tools and strategies to the users, and a hybrid approach (Badaro et al., 2013) which combines the above mentioned approaches through a weight system. The motivation to use a hybrid model is given by the differences presented between the user-based and item-based approaches. User-based approach make recommendations based on the similarity between users, which means the algorithm will recommend items liked by users similar to the student. On the contrary, in the item-based approach recommendations are made based on similarities between items, computing this similarity according to the given ratings. The differences between the two approaches are visually depicted in Figure 2.

Hybrid approach was implemented by combining the user-based and itembased methods with different weights. This involved assigning specific relevance or weight to each of the predicted ratings using the equation below:



where α is the weight and ̂ r u is the predicted rating for the user-based approach, whereas (1 -α ) is the weight and ̂ r i is the predicted rating for the item-based algorithm.

These weights were used to reduce the error deriving from predicted ratings

To select the final weights to be assigned to each of the models, a preliminary experimentation has been carried out. After that, coinciding with the results obtained by (Sarwar et al., 2001), it was found that higher weights for the itemsbased method (1 -α ) provided better results. Therefore, a scale of values for the weights has been selected to emphasize higher values for the item-based weight, starting with an user-based weight value ( α ) twice as large as the item-based one, and concluding with item-based weight values seven times larger than α . All the considered cases are illustrated in Table 3.

| #2     | 1 / 2 | 1 / 2      |
| #3     | 1 / 3 | 2 / 3      |

It is worth noting that by assigning α = 1 or α = 0 the fully user-based approach and the fully item-based approach are obtained, respectively. Thus, by properly tuning α it is possible to include all the analyzed cases within the formula 1.

To compute similarities among users or items, three widely used metrics in CF systems were considered and compared: the Pearson correlation coefficient(Sheugh &amp; Alizadeh, 2015), the Euclidean distance and the Cosine distance

(Vinh et al., 2018; Hofmann, 2004). These metrics aim to identify the n most similar users to the test user (in the case of user-based), or the n most similarly evaluated items according to the ratings given by the test user(in the case of item-based). These three metrics are defined as follow:







where N is the number of users or items; x i and y i are the individual ratings; and ¯ x and ¯ y are the sample mean.

The Pearson coefficient is employed for direct calculation of similarities among all users or objects. Then, most similar neighbors are obtained by taking the n most correlated ones. In contrast, the Euclidean and Cosine distances are applied as distance metric within a K-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) algorithm, and the n nearest neighbors are directly extracted from the obtained model. Another important aspect to take into account is the number of nearest neighbors considered in the similarity calculation. After conducting numerous tests with various potential values for the number of neighbors, we determined that optimal results are achieved with n values in the range of 3 to 11. Therefore, in the final experimentation, we will consider the number of neighbors to be 3, 5, 7, and 11. Algorithm 1 contains the pseudocode of the process for the similarity computation depending on the different considered metrics. The method returns the n neighbors most similar users or items sorted according the computed similarity measure, stored in top similarities .

The objective of the final learning methodologies RS is to predict the ratings of tools and strategies for a particular user. The prediction is made by computing the average of the ratings given by the most similar users in the case of user-based approach or, in the case of item-based approach, the ratings of the most similarly scored items. In the case of the hybrid method, the prediction is obtained with the result of the sum of the user-based and object-based predictions multiplied by their corresponding weights.

The entire process described above is reflected in Algorithm 2 and Algorithm 3, corresponding to the user-based and item-based recommendation systems, respectively. Both algorithms generate a list of key-value pairs, referred to as recommendations , comprising the tools and strategies to be recommended along with their respective ratings assigned by the recommendation system. To achieve this, both algorithms distinguish the data they will utilize for similarity computation, data similarities . In the case of user-based, only the training data, data train items , and the test user's data, text user for whom the recommendation is to be made, are needed. Conversely, in the case of item-based, it is necessary to consider each test item, from data test items , separately to generate their respective ratings without taking into account the rest, treated as unknown to the user. Finally, recommendations is completed with the average rating values obtained for the different test items from the n neighbors most similar users or objects.

To assess the accuracy of the used methodologies, the mean absolute error (MAE) between the score predicted by RS and the respective score actually given by the user will be obtained. MAE is calculated by averaging all the N absolute errors of the rating-pairs ( p i , q i ). Since lower MAE reflects a better accuracy the choice of the weights must be done in order to minimize it:



where N is the total number of tools and strategies considered to be recommended, p i is the predicted value and q i the actual value.

Finally, one of the main challenges faced by RSs is the cold-start problem, which can be presented as a user cold-start or item cold-start (Sejwal &amp; Abulaish, 2022). The user cold-start problem stems from the challenge of addressing new users for whom the system lacks any pre-existing information (Cosley et al., 2003). On the other hand, the item cold-start appears when a new item is being introduced to the dataset (Schein et al., 2002). The former concern has been addressed through the solicitation of opinions from new users regarding the system's methodologies for profile generation, which are subsequently compared with those of other users. Regarding the item cold-start, it is not expected to pose a problem for our existing system. Indeed, new learning methodologies are not implemented very often due to this kind of strategies occasionally appears. The developed system will demonstrate its robustness by considering both test users and items when evaluating its performance.

## 3.3. Data analysis

From the 39 items used in the questionnaire, T4 support tool (Using the Easy Reading font) was discarded since more than 48% of the participants did not know it. Therefore, the actual number of support tools used was 16, to which are added 22 learning strategies for a total of 38 items. The data were partitioned, with 75% (947 users) utilized for training the model and the remaining 25% (290 users) designated for the test set. Subsequently, a 10-fold cross-validation was applied to the training dataset to optimize the configuration parameters of the model before validating its performance on the test set. In addition, another separation of the data has been carried out to get some test learning methodologies and use them for the evaluation of the system. This split has been done taking randomly a 20% of the learning methodologies along different epochs to check the robustness of the system in making predictions for different combinations of unknown items.

## 3.4. Assessment

Finally, to test the algorithm on a real case, the best performing model found was used to assess the efficacy of recommending specific learning tools and strategies to students with or without dyslexia. 50 subjects, 53% male and 47% female, participated to the testing campaign. Among them, 40% are dyslexic, whereas the remaining are not affected by any learning disorders. The subjects are university students or students that finished university but that are still completing their academic formation with a master, a doctorate or corporate training courses. The test consisted in providing specific textbooks of 3 disciplines (political science, communication, and economics) to students currently enrolled in affine degree, PhD or master courses, and ask them to study a portion of a book each. 50% of the students, equally divided in dyslexics and non-dyslexics, tried the RS that was found to perform best, and obtained personalized suggestions about tools and strategies that should help them in studying. The other 50% received random recommendations, instead of the specific ones output by the RS. Then, all the students were asked to follow the suggested methodologies during the study phase and the level of knowledge of the studied disciplines was assessed by university professors, on a scale from 0 to 10, 6 being the minimum sufficient score. A comparison was made between the results of the ones that benefited of the RS and the ones that do not. Differences among dyslexic and non-dyslexic students were also examined.

During this initial experiment, the optimal number of neighbors to be considered to compute the similarities will be also calculated. Additionally, this evaluation will incorporate the results obtained with the three different metrics employed for calculating similarities. Subsequently, we will perform a comparative analysis of the three considered approaches: user-based, item-based, and hybrid RSs.
